On overall analysis of the intent of Article 311(2), it is vivid that an employee holding a post in Union or State ought not to be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to the one by which he was appointed. It is further specified that a person shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank after an inquiry supplying the charges if any against him and giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges. The applicability of the said clause is restricted in a situation wherein his conduct led to his conviction of criminal charges or where the authority empowered who dismissed, removed or reduced in rank records reason in writing upon satisfaction that it is not 'reasonably practicable' to hold an enquiry against him. In addition, where such power has been exercised by the President or the Governor it may be in the interest of security of the State or if not expedient to hold such an enquiry, then exceptional power under clause (c) of second proviso to Article 311 ought to be exercised. [Para 40]

■

In case such a decision invoking the extraordinary power is taken by the competent authority in light of the judgment Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel 1985 taxmann.com 1415 (SC)/(1985) 3 SCC 398 within the parameter as discussed, the scope of judicial review is available to the Constitutional Courts wherein the reasons as assigned for satisfaction of the authority must be reasonable, valid, justified and in writing. In addition, the satisfaction as recorded must be the objective satisfaction on the basis of material brought on record which ordinarily the disciplinary authority may take as a prudent person. Otherwise, dispensing with the enquiry is not permissible in law. In the present case, Section 21 of the 1978 Act confers power of punishment and Section 22 prescribes the procedure for awarding such punishment. The procedure as contemplated has been elaborated under the 1980 Rules. In the present case, in the Court’s view, the power exercised by the authority is completely without application of mind, thus, the question of recording of satisfaction as affirmed by the appellate authority, the CAT and the High Court does not arise. Therefore, it can be held that the order dispensing with the regular procedure of inquiry is arbitrary and consequently the order of dismissal of the appellant is liable to be quashed and the orders of the CAT and the High Court affirming the said dismissal order stand set aside. [Para 41]

■

In light of the above discussion, the irresistible conclusion is to set aside the order passed by the CAT and the High Court and to quash the order of dismissal passed by the DCP and confirmed by the appellate authority. In consequence, the appellant shall forthwith be reinstated with continuity of service. He shall be entitled for all consequential benefits notionally. Since, the appellant is found involved in a criminal case, therefore, in the facts of the case, back wages from the date of dismissal till reinstatement are restricted to 50%. [Para 42]

■

The setting aside of the order passed under Article 311(2) proviso (b) of the Constitution and direction for reinstatement shall be without prejudice to the right of the respondent to take recourse as permissible by initiating a departmental enquiry in accordance with law. Accordingly, and with the aforesaid directions, the present appeal stands allowed to the extent indicated. Parties to bear their own costs. [Para 43]

headnotes.text: It is desirable that if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry is being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending the final disposal of the criminal case. It would be particularly appropriate to adopt such a course where the charge against the workman is of a grave character, because in such a case, it would be unfair to compel the workman to disclose the defence which he may take before the criminal court. But to say that domestic enquiries may be stayed pending criminal trial is very different from anything that if an employer proceeds with the domestic enquiry in spite of the fact that the criminal trial is pending, the enquiry for that reason alone is vitiated and the conclusion reached in such an enquiry is either bad in law or mala fide.

Held, that it was desirable that when the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry was being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending final disposal of the criminal case. In view of the accepted principles of law, in the event thepetitioner was convicted in the criminal trial, he would automatically be dismissed and/or removed from service, without taking recourse to formalities of departmental proceedings and, in the atternative, if the criminal case failed for want of evidence, by an order of discharge and not acquittal, in that event also, the departmental authorities would be entitled to proceed with the departmental enquiry, even after passing of such order of discharge by the criminal court. Therefore, during the pendency of the criminal trial, the employer would be restrained from proceeding further with the departmental enquiry against the petitioner.
Domestic enquiry—Pendency of Criminal case or appeal—Employer need not wait for its decision—Enquiry may be proceeded with.

There is no legal prohibition which prevents the holding of a domestic enquiry into an act of misconduct by a workman just because a criminal case is pending against the workman. The domestic enquiry in which the workman is answerable to his master and which may end in a departmental penalty is entirely different from the criminal proceeding in which the same person in respect of the same act is prosecuted for violation of the penal law of the land, which may end in conviction and sentence.

The decision to hold or not to hold a domestic enquiry, during the pendency of a criminal trial in respect of the same allegation, against a workman, is that of the employer to be taken at his discretion and if the employer decides to hold such enquiry, he cannot be prevented from doing so by the issue of a writ of prohibition.
The principles of natural justice do not require that the employer must wait for the decision of a criminal case or an appeal before proceeding with a domestic enquiry. 1960(1) L.L.J. 520, Approved.

In the instant case it was held that the Industrial Tribunal was in error when it characterised the result of the domestic enquiry as mala fide partly because the enquiry was not stayed pending the criminal proceedings against the concerned workman.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Domestic enquiry started by employer against employee—Simultaneously criminal proceedings initiated by CBI on same charges—Principles of law—Employer should stay domestic enquiry pending final disposal of criminal case

A writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of a domestic enquiry by an employer into alleged acts of misconduct by a workman can be issued only if there was total lack of jurisdiction in the authority holding the enquiry. No such writ can be issued preventing an authority having jurisdiction to hold the enquiry, even if criminal proceedings are pending in respect of the same matter.
Domestic enquiry—Stay of domestic enquiry pending disposal of criminal case—Desirability—Inference of mala fide where enquiry not stayed

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Criminal proceedings pending on same charges—Is no bar to domestic enquiry being held by employer—No right in employee to obtain temporary injunction against continuation of domestic enquiry.

The petitioners have no legal right to insist that the enquiry proceedings against them are to be stayed till such time the Criminal Court concludes its trial. Possible prejudice to the interest of the employer also might have to be noticed, as it cannot be a one way traffic, and they are not expected to silently suffer in the bargain.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Criminal case pending on same matter—Employer can decide whether to hold domestic enquiry or not—Employer cannot be prevented by writ of prohibition from proceeding with enquiry.

It is not necessary to examine the question as to whether the domestic enquiry was vitiated in law when simultaneous criminal proceedings were pending against the petitioner on the same charge and as such in consequence the order of dismissal becomes bad in law.

Departmental Enquiry—Criminal Proceedings—Staying of departmental enquiry—Charge-sheet in domestic enquiry founded upon same facts on which a criminal case pending—Petitioner had not chosen to file any petition to stop department from proceeding with departmental enquiry—Petitioner did not file any petition for restraining employer to proceed in departmental enquiry on alleged ground—Not fit case where petitioner fulfills litmus test laid down by Supreme Court in case of Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., 1999 (82) FLR 627 (SC) as requirement—No complicated questions of fact and law involved—Department not under obligation to stay domestic enquiry. [Para 12]

Domestic enquiry—Commencement of criminal proceedings on same set of facts—Whether both proceedings can be continued simultaneously—Depends on facts of each case though there is no legal bar—No hard and fast rule can be laid down.

It is not a requirement of the principles of natural justice that an employer should not hold against his employee a departmental enquiry in respect of the very same charges which are pending trial in a criminal court till the termination of such trial and there is no legal right in an aggrieved workman to obtain an order of temporary injunction from the court to restrain the continuation of the departmental proceedings against him. Nor are the courts under any obligation to grant such injunction.
Domestic Enquiry—And criminal trial—Can proceed simultaneously—Decision in criminal case would not materially affect the outcome of domestic enquiry. [Para 5]

It cannot be held as a general rule that whenever a person is acquitted by a criminal court, no further disciplinary action can be taken as the scope, purpose and object of the two enquiries are different and the standards of proof are also different and all depends upon the facts of each case. Where a criminal offence is committed, it is for the management to charge-sheet the employee and conduct a domestic enquiry and if the misconducts are proved, to punish the employee. The management is also free not to conduct the enquiry but to wait for the criminal court judgment.

Domestic enquiry—Alleged misconduct by employee—Simultaneous criminal proceedings and disciplinary action—Should not be permitted when both are based on same grounds—Disciplinary proceedings should be stayed—That criminal proceedings had not yet commenced or that accused employee had already put in his defence in disciplinary proceedings not relevant.

(b) If the criminal case against the delinquent em­ployee is of a grave nature which involves complicated questions of law and fact, then it would be desirable to stay the departmental proceedings till the conclusion of the criminal case.

It is well-settled that a domestic enquiry and a criminal trial can proceed simultaneously and the decision in the criminal case would not materially affect the outcome of the domestic enquiry. The nature of both the proceedings and the test applied to reach a final conclusion in the matter, are entirely different. The charge-memo dated 17.8.1987 records charges of grave indiscipline, misconduct, dereliction of duty and involvement in the criminal case. Obviously, the charges in the domestic enquiry and before the criminal Court were not similar.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry against workman—Pendency of criminal proceeding against workman no bar to domestic enquiry—Writ of prohibition against holding of domestic enquiry—Will issue only when there is total lack of jurisdiction.

There is no legal prohibition for the holding of disciplinary proceedings just because a criminal case is pending. It is also well settled that a writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of a domestic enquiry can issue only when there is total lack of jurisdiction and no such infirmity exists in this case.

Domestic enquiry—Criminal case and disciplinary proceedings based on same set of facts—Proceedings simultaneously conducted—Defence in the criminal case would be affected—Disciplinary proceedings to be stayed—On facts held that no justification to stay disciplinary proceedings.

The criminal proceedings and the domestic proceedings are not based on the same set of facts. Even otherwise, assuming that both the proceedings are based on same sets of fact, in my view, there is no provision of law empowering the Court to stay the departmental proceedings merely because criminal proceedings are pending in a Criminal Court.

Where an employee is alleged to have committed an offence in assaulting an officer, in the proceedings taken by the employer taking disciplinary action against the employee, it is the duty of the employer to accept and treat as conclusive the finding of the Criminal Court which tried the offence. The employer, in such case, of course, need not wait for the decision before taking action; except in grave cases. In simple cases, he can proceed with his own domestic enquiry and decide on the disciplinary action to be taken against the employee. In a case of acquittal of the employee by the Criminal Court, the management must accept the same, otherwise his bona fides will be questioned. In such a case the Industrial Tribunal would be justified in interfering with the order of the employer terminating the services of the employee.

Therefore, the High Court cannot entertain a petition for a writ of prohibition against the employer restraining him from proceeding with a domestic enquiry on the ground that some of the witnesses proposed to be examined were police officers who would be giving evidence against the workman in the criminal case in respect of the same matter.

There is no legal bar for both criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings going on simultaneously against a Government servant. But, in certain situations, it may not be “desirable”, “advisable” or “appropriate” to proceed with the disciplinary enquiry when a criminal case is pending on identical charges. The staying of disciplinary proceedings is a matter to be determined taking into consideration all the facts and circumstances of the particular case and no hard and fast rule can be enunciated in that behalf. The only ground constituting a valid ground for staying the disciplinary proceedings is that the defence of the employee in the criminal case with charges of a grave nature and involving complicated questions of fact and law may not be prejudiced.

The law as enunciated by the Supreme Court leaves no scope for doubt that all said and done, there is no bar for simultaneous proceedings being taken against the delinquent in the form of criminal action and also disciplinary proceedings unless the charges are extremely serious and grave requiring the judicial determination in preference to the verdict in the domestic inquiry proceedings. In the instant case, even though the criminal action and disciplinary proceedings are grounded upon the same sets of fact, in my view, there is no provision of law empowering the Court to stay the departmental proceedings merely because criminal prosecution is pending in the Criminal Court.

It is well settled that criminal and disciplinary proceedings by the department are different and they are not inter-connected. Therefore, in this case it has been rightly held by the second respondent that the pendency of the criminal case was no ground to bar the domestic enquiry and also the Labour Court has clearly found that the Manager was entitled to hold the enquiry and award the punishment in the terms of Standing Order. Therefore, in the above circumstances it is the categoric contentions of the respondent that merely because the petitioner and the other two workmen were acquitted by this Court, it cannot be said the domestic enquiry was vitiated or the findings of the enquiry officer were not justified. Further in this case it is significant to note that the petitioners herein and other were charged for misconduct under Standing Orders 23.11 riotous and disorderly behaviour, 23.12 acts subversive of discipline, 23.25 causing danger to the security of the life of the co-worker whereas the criminal case was for the offence of murder. Therefore, I see every force in the various contentions raised by the respondents. In the above circumstances of these cases, I am of the clear view that the impugned award of the second respondent does not suffer from any error of law or jurisdiction calling for interference by this Court.

(vii) That because of the unsettled legal position as to whether a departmental enquiry in respect of the same charge, which is pending in the criminal court, can be initiated especially when the criminal case is pending, the appellant-bank bona fide thought that they could not initiate the enquiry. Therefore, inevitable delay had occurred which could not be said to be a reason for nullifying the enquiry.

Departmental Enquiry and Criminal Proceeding—On same charges—No bar to the two proceedings being carried out simultaneously—Departmental proceedings—When to be kept in abeyance—Detailed with reference to principles laid down by the Apex Court in case of (Capt.) M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd. 1999 (82) FLR (SC). [Para 15]

Where an employee is placed under suspension pending domestic enquiry into alleged misconduct in accordance with the conditions of his service, the fact that the employee is acquitted by a criminal court before the domestic enquiry ends will not result in the termination of the order of suspension ds the suspension was pending the domestic enquiry and not pending the criminal trial. Hence it cannot be contended that once he is acquitted in the criminal case, he should be reinstated in service. The suspension order will continue till the domestic enquiry is over unless it is terminated by another order of the authority concerned.

Dismissal for misconduct—Assault by workmen of Manager of factory alleged—Arrest of workmen and Criminal case—Finding by Criminal Court that case was concocted—Non-participation of workmen in Departmental enquiry Refusal of company to postpone enquiry till after decision of Criminal case—Victimisation for union activities alleged.

The continuation of the departmental proceedings cannot be said to be of such a nature where the same need to be stopped pending adjudication by the criminal court of the case filed against the petitioner.

The law is well settled that the inquiry officer can come to a different conclusion than arrived at by a Criminal Court and that it is immaterial whether the charges were identical or the witnesses were the same, as long as the power exercised by the Criminal Court and the inquiry under the relevant law and the service law was distinct and separate. There is no bar for holding a disciplinary proceeding during the pendency of the trial though the basis may be one and the same. It is for the disciplinary authority to decide as to whether in a given case it should keep the domestic inquiry pending till the outcome of the criminal trial or not.

It is now a settled legal principle that the domestic enquiry under the standing order and/or disciplinary proceeding under the service rule qua criminal proceeding on the identical fact situation, there is no embargo of simultaneous proceeding of both the two matters. It is also settled legal position now that the domestic enquiry and/or departmental proceeding relates to adjudication of the conduct of the workman and/or employee concerned upon being charged for misconduct on issue of factual matrix as mentioned in the article of charge, whereas in a criminal proceeding on the identical fact situation, determination and decision of the Court is to find the guilt of the person concerned in terms of the criminal offence either relating to Indian Penal Code or any other penal statute. Furthermore, it is a settled legal principle that proof of fact and the degree of such proof varies in respect of the two proceedings. In a criminal proceeding, charge is required to be proved without any doubt and strictly following the Evidence Act, whereas in a domestic enquiry and/or departmental proceed­ing preponderance of probability would suffice for determining the conduct of the delinquent. Even if in identical fact situation, it is now settled that even after acquittal of an accused from a criminal proceeding, domestic enquiry can be completed and punishment can be imposed. Hence, pendency of a criminal proceeding or adjudication of a criminal proceeding on the identical fact ipso facto will not destroy the findings of the domestic enquiry. Judgments of all these legal propositions are based on: Union of India v. Sardar Bahadur. 1972 Lab IC 627 Nelson Motis v. Union of Indiaand another. 1992 (65) FLR 853 (SC) State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena, 1996 (74) FLR 2550 (SC) and Depot Manager, Andhra State RoadTransportCorpn. v. Mohd.Yusuf Miya. 1997 (77) FLR 9 (SC)

Sometimes both the criminal trial and departmental enquiry go on. There is no bar against that. But, if a departmental enquiry is withheld till the decision of the criminal trial, then that decision should be taken into account and cannot be overridden by continuing the departmental enquiry thereafter on the identical charges. Furthermore, if a departmental enquiry is not at all launched but a criminal case is instituted and that ends in acquittal of the accused, it will not be proper for the department again to proceed on the same charges.

It is held by the Supreme Court in Noida Entrepreneurs Association v. Noida and others, 2007 (112) FLR 1139 (SC) that mere acquittal in criminal case would not affect outcome of the enquiry proceeding which is based on the evidence recorded during the domestic enquiry.

Therefore, it cannot be contended that where the criminal case lodged against a workman-driver had resulted in his being acquitted, on the same charge he could not be subjected to a domestic enquiry and punished.

[The court accordingly, on the facts, ordered stay of the disciplinary proceedings until disposal of the criminal trial. However, having regard to the consequences to the employer-company, liberty was granted to the company to apply to the criminal court on the basis of a copy of the judgment for an immediate expedited disposal of the trial in view of the fact that the company was otherwise required to continue paying the subsistence allowance almost indefinitely.]
The Respondents are directed to stay further proceedings in the departmental proceedings till the disposal of the criminal case.

The Hon’ble Apex Court after taking into account various earlier judgments has held that departmental proceedings and proceedings in criminal case can proceed simultaneously, as there is no bar in their being conducted simultaneously, though separately. It has been further held that if the departmental proceedings and criminal case are based on similar set of facts and charges in criminal case against delinquent employees is of grave nature which involves complicated questions of fact and law, it would be desirable to stay the departmental proceedings till conclusion of criminal case.

Discharge—Company having two alternatives either to discharge concerned workmen under standing orders or to take disciplinary action—Holding of disciplinary enquiry—Propriety—Enquiry almost parallel to disciplinary enquiry pending before criminal court—Exercising power under standing order and discharging of workman held proper.

Departmental enquiry—Criminal case proceedings and departmental proceedings—Founded substantially on same set of facts—Disciplinary proceeding ought to have been kept stayed/deferred/suspended until decision of the criminal trial.(Gau. H.C.–I.B.) XE "Departmental enquiry—Criminal case proceedings and departmental proceedings—Founded substantially on same set of facts—Disciplinary proceeding ought to have been kept stayed/deferred/suspended until decision of the criminal trial.(Gau. H.C.–I.B.)" [Para 8]

The company had two alternatives, either to act under standing order 47, or to take disciplinary action and hold a domestic enquiry. But the latter course would have meant that the company would have to launch into an enquiry almost parallel to the one which was going on before the committing magistrate.

In the present case, scope of enquiry in both the proceedings being different based on different evidence and witnesses and since the petitioner has nowhere urged that departmental enquiry will seriously prejudice his defence in the criminal case, in the considered opinion of this Court, it is not a fit case where departmental proceedings against the petitioner should either be quashed or stayed during pendency of criminal proceedings.
Charges in the domestic enquiry were found proved on the basis of evidences led by the parties whereas, the criminal case has failed on account of the witnesses turning hostile.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Workman aquitted by criminal Court on ground that there was not sufficient evidence even to frame a charge—Bars domestic enquiry by employer on same charge—Dismissal on basis of domestic enquiry would be invalid.

facts.text:
’T’, an employee of the petitioner-company, failed to vacate the company’s flat after retirement, in spite of demand, and a complaint was filed against him under section 630. While the criminal proceedings were in progress, the company also filed a civil suit for recovery of possession of the flat for damages. ’T’ filed an application before the Trial Court for staying the criminal proceedings on the ground of the pendency of the civil suit. When this was rejected, he filed a revisional application. The Sessions Judge ordered that the judgment in the case under section 630 should not be delivered till the disposal of the civil suit.

On revision petition :

The petitioner was in employment of OP No. 2-company and while he was in service, he was extended the facility of residential accommodation. Subsequently, the petitioner’s service was terminated and the company asked him to vacate the residential quarter. In spite of notice and reminders, the petitioner did not vacate the premises and, therefore, he was alleged to have committed offence under section 630. The petitioner, by filing the instant petition, prayed for quashing the entire criminal proceedings initiated against him alleging that the termination of his service was illegal and the Government had referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication and, thus, under such circumstances, criminal proceedings under section 630 could not be initiated against him.

■

A charge-sheet dated 12 October 2012 was issued to the workman alleging misconduct under various Standing Orders. A domestic enquiry was conducted, and on 31 July 2014 the Enquiry Officer held the workman guilty; the report was forwarded on 6 October 2014. The workman submitted an apology on 16 October 2014, and the recognised Union also requested a sympathetic view. An industrial dispute was pending between the company and the recognised Union, and during its subsistence an MoU dated 14 August 2014 was executed stating that 13 of 18 suspended workmen would be taken back subject to conditions at the management’s discretion, while enquiries against the remaining five, including the workman, would continue. After considering the apology and the Union’s request, management decided to dismiss the workman, and he was terminated on 17 October 2014.

■

It was pleaded that he remained unemployed for about two years, then started a grocery business, and that the business suffered losses and was closed on 28 November 2021, after which he remained without gainful employment.

■

The workman filed a complaint under Section 33A challenging the dismissal as arbitrary and illegal and sought reinstatement with back wages, also alleging discriminatory treatment vis-à-vis 13 similarly situated workmen who were given minor punishment. By order dated 27 September 2019 on preliminary issues, the Tribunal held the domestic enquiry fair and proper and the findings not perverse.

■

By final Award dated 18 January 2024, the Tribunal declined reinstatement with back wages and awarded compensation of Rs. 7 lakhs, while recording that the termination occurred during pendency of References and thus amounted to breach of Section 33(2)(b).

■

On writ petitions before the High Court.

■

The petitioner–company engaged respondent No.1 as an underground loader. The company alleged that he remained absent from duty without authorization from December 1997, issued a charge sheet for misconduct, received his reply, and conducted a domestic enquiry in which the workman participated. The Enquiry Officer held the charges proved. After issuing a show-cause notice and considering the workman’s explanation along with the enquiry record, the Enquiry Officer’s report, and the past service record, the disciplinary authority dismissed the workman from service for misconduct.

■

Respondent No.2–union raised an industrial dispute on behalf of the workman. Conciliation failed, and the Government of India referred the dispute to the Central Government Industrial Tribunal on the question whether the dismissal was legal and justified, and the relief, if any, to the workman.

■

Before the Tribunal, an initial order held the domestic enquiry valid and fair. The parties filed documents; a medical certificate produced by the workman, not part of the domestic enquiry record, was admitted in evidence. In its final award, the Tribunal recorded that the workman had medical treatment and a certificate, found that he was not afforded fair opportunity in the domestic enquiry, held the enquiry devoid of fairness and propriety, declared the dismissal not legal or justified, directed reinstatement with back wages from the date of dismissal, excluded wages for the period of pre-disciplinary absence if not covered by leave, imposed a 25% cut in pendent lite wages, and directed disbursement of monetary benefits within a time frame.

■

On the petitioner’s writ to the High Court.

Respondent No. 2-complainant had filed the proceedings under section 630 against the applicant/accused, seeking his eviction from the accommodation allotted to him as a condition of his service inasmuch as he was not in its service. The applicant moved an application seeking for discharge of the proceedings on the ground that his ULP complaint against the termination of his service was pending before the Labour Court. His main contention was that the proceedings under section 630 were not tenable inasmuch as a Labour Court proceedings in ULP for setting aside the relevant order of termination issued by the complainant were pending and the applicant/accused therein had claimed reinstatement by seeking quashing of the order of illegal termination. The trial Judge rejected his application, and the said order was confirmed in revision application preferred by him.

On application under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 the applicant contended that it was obligatory on the part of complainant to obtain prior permission of the Labour Court under section 33(1) of the 1947 Act before resorting to filing of the complaint under section 630.

■

The petitioner–employee was named in an FIR lodged by the Superintendent of Police, Anti-Corruption Department, on a complaint by a private electricity consumer alleging demand of bribe under Section 13(1)(b) read with Section 13(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

■

The petitioner was confined in jail from 23.01.2015 to 18.12.2018 during the criminal trial and did not discharge duties during this period. The criminal case was not instituted at the behest of the respondent–corporation (employer). The employer did not create any hindrance or prevent the petitioner from working, and no departmental proceedings were initiated against him.

■

By order dated 23.04.2020, the employer declined to pay arrears/back wages for the period 23.01.2015 to 18.12.2018, applying the principle of 'no work no pay'.

■

Aggrieved, the petitioner challenged the said order seeking arrears/back wages for the aforesaid period.

The respondent-company approached the petitioner-company and ob- tained a Diesel Generator on hire purchase agreement. As cheques issued by the respondent-company were dishonoured, the petitioner-company filed a criminal complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instru- ments Act. While so winding up order was passed against the respondent-company. The Criminal Court stayed the proceedings on the ground that the petitioner had not obtained permission from the Company Court as required by section 446.

On application under section 446, the petitioner sought permission/leave to continue the pending criminal proceedings.

The petitioners originally filed a company petition under section 397/398 alleging oppression against the respondents. However, when the matter was listed for hearing and the petitioner had concluded his arguments, the petitioner registered a criminal case against the respondents for alleged tampering with shareholding of respondent No. 1-company and obtained an order under section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for investigation. In these circumstances, the respondents filed the instant application for stay of proceedings of the company petition on ground that the party could not adopt parallel proceedings/forum shopping to agitate its grievance. The respondents further contended that the company petition and criminal complaint being based on identical and similar facts and the nature of charge in the criminal case as filed by the petitioners being grave and because it raised complicated questions of facts and law, the company petition ought to be stayed.

Despite termination of applicant's services on 19-2-2002 by his employer-company, he did not vacate the quarter allotted to him during his employment with the company. On complaint under section 630, the trial court, finding prima facie case against the applicant, initiated proceedings under section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 by issuing summoning order. The applicant filed instant application for quashing of the said proceedings contending, inter alia, that his services were terminated without giving any show-cause notice, and that the termination matter was pending before the Labour Commissioner.

■

The appellant joined the respondent club and was allotted membership.

■

The appellant was found involved in corrupt practice of collecting bribe/motive by using club premises and he was charged by the police for the same. He remained in judicial custody for a long period of time and the prosecution of said criminal cases was pending.

■

The respondent club vide notice which was received by him, suspended the membership of the appellant on the sole ground of a pending criminal case and his consequent police detention.

■

The decision of the club which was conveyed to the appellant by a letter by virtue of which membership of the appellant was terminated due to pending criminal case against him and his name was omitted from the register of the club.

■

The appellant filed the instant appeal under section 59 against the suspension and termination from the membership of the club.

■

The appellant filed the instant appeal under section 59 seeking to set aside the decision of the termination of the appellant taken by the club and consequent letter sent to the appellant as well as suspension letter and also the direction to the club to register the name of the appellant in the records/ register of the club.

■

The appellant stated that the Articles of Association mandated the Managing Committee to conduct an enquiry, wherein in the instant case no enquiry was undertaken by the Managing Committee. The appellant also contended that under the Articles of Association of the club, neither the Managing Committee nor the Secretary nor any other person was authorized to suspend any of the members from its membership before the enquiry was conducted. Therefore, suspension of the appellant was illegal per se as the club being a company was bound by its Articles of Association.

■

The appellant argued that the proper inquiry was not made before taking action against him as envisaged in the Articles. He pointed out that as per the Articles, it was clear that the power to make enquiry and to suspend any member vested with the managing committee of the club and notice by which the appellant was expelled from the club does not refer as to whether any voting through secret ballot took place or not, therefore in absence mandatory requirements, all the action taken against the appellant was illegal per se.

■

A dispute arose between the appellant–Management and its workmen following a strike. The Management issued a show cause notice on 11-5-2011, placed the workmen under suspension, and issued charge memoranda. A domestic enquiry was conducted in which the workmen participated. The Enquiry Officer held the charges proved, following which a second show cause notice dated 17-8-2011 was issued. The explanations submitted by the workmen were rejected and orders of removal from service were passed on 20-8-2011. Aggrieved thereby, the workmen raised industrial disputes in I.D. Nos. 33, 34, 35, 36 and 37 of 2011 before the Labour Court, Pondicherry.

■

Before the Labour Court, the Management, in its written statement, specifically reserved its right to adduce additional evidence in the event the domestic enquiry was held to be unfair or defective. The parties adduced oral and documentary evidence. However, the Labour Court did not decide the fairness of the domestic enquiry as a preliminary issue; instead, while passing the final award, it held that the enquiry was not conducted in a free and fair manner and ordered reinstatement of the workmen.

■

The Management challenged the awards in writ petitions under article 226, but the writ Court confirmed the Labour Court’s awards.

■

Aggrieved thereby, the Management preferred intra-Court appeals before the High Court.

■

The respondent–workman, employed in a defence organisation (Gun Carriage Factory, Jabalpur), was charged with stealing brass and copper pieces. A departmental inquiry was initiated. On different dates the respondent did not appear; when he appeared, he admitted the charges, and on subsequent dates he again remained absent. The inquiry officer submitted a report holding him guilty. After issuing notice, the disciplinary authority imposed the penalty of removal from service.

■

The CGIT held that the termination was not proper and legal, quashed the penalty of removal, and awarded compensation of Rs. 2.5 lakhs to the respondent.

■

In the employer’s writ, the High Court upheld the quashing of the removal order but gave liberty to proceed with the inquiry from the stage of express denial of charges, directed that reasonable opportunity be afforded to engage a defence assistant, and that the inquiry be conducted under Rule 14 of the CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965. The High Court quashed the compensation, deemed the workman to be under suspension till conclusion of the inquiry, and directed that the inquiry be concluded expeditiously and preferably within six months.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the employer contended that the charges concerned theft in a defence factory; the respondent repeatedly remained absent; he had admitted the charges; the inquiry officer found him guilty; the disciplinary authority, after notice, removed him; and the CGIT exceeded its limited scope of interference, with compensation being unwarranted. The respondent contended he was coerced to accept the charges and that lack of a defence assistant led to miscarriage of justice.

■

The records reveal that on 11-4-2023, the workman filed his written statement. No reply thereagainst was filed by the Management. On 2-5-2023, 3 (three) issues were framed which have been already quoted herein above. The Management side thereupon appeared only on 21-6-2023 and prayed that they would like to adduce further witnesses. In the entire order sheet as well as the various applications filed by the Management, there is nothing on record to show that the Management at any point of time requested the Industrial Tribunal to first adjudicate the Domestic Enquiry and then to proceed with the adjudication on merits. [Para 30]

■

The observations of the Supreme Court in paragraph No. 61 of the judgment in the case of Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. v. Ludh Budh Singh (1972 taxmann.com 72 (SC)/(1972) 1 SCC 595) makes it clear that the Management can rely upon the Domestic Enquiry in the first instance and alternatively without prejudice to the said plea, simultaneously adduce additional evidence justifying its actions. It is also stipulated that when the Management relies upon the enquiry conducted and also simultaneously adduces evidence before the Tribunal, it is the duty of the Tribunal to first adjudicate on the legality and validity of the Domestic Enquiry and in the circumstance, the Tribunal holds the Domestic Enquiry to be valid, there is no requirement of considering the evidence adduced before it on merits. However, if the Tribunal holds the Domestic Enquiry to be not proper/valid, the Tribunal derives jurisdiction to decide on the merits and thereupon look into the evidence adduced by the Management in support of the action taken against the workman. It is also relevant to mention that the Supreme Court at paragraph No. 61(4) of the judgment makes it clear, that the management has to request the Tribunal to frame a preliminary issue. The Supreme Court also observed that it was open to the Tribunal to deal with the question of validity of the Domestic Enquiry report at the first instance. [Para 32]

■

The above analysis shows that it is the requirement of law that the Management has to take a plea in the written statement that it would rely upon the Domestic Enquiry as well as also take a plea without prejudice to the plea of the Domestic Enquiry to adduce evidence on merit. The reasons assigned for not allowing the plea of adducing evidence at a later stage after deciding the issue of validity of the Domestic Enquiry, is very relevant, in the opinion of this Court, inasmuch as delay in disposal of the Reference proceedings would wreck the morale of the workman and compel him to surrender to the mighty Management. It is in this perspective, this Court is of the opinion that merely taking a plea in the written statement and not drawing the attention of the learned Tribunal in the entire proceedings that a plea is taken as regards the validity of the Domestic Enquiry be decided as a preliminary enquiry, cannot be countenanced. It is the duty of the Management to bring it to the notice of theTribunal by filing an application or by submitting draft issues that the plea of validity of the Domestic Enquiry be decided as a preliminary issue. Failure to do so, it is also the opinion of this Court that such plea cannot be raised at a later stage after the Award is passed. The request to be made to the Tribunal to frame a preliminary issue on the validity of the Domestic Enquiry is also apparent from paragraph No. 61(4) of the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. v. Ludh Budh Singh (supra). [Para 36]

■

In the instant case, it would be seen from the facts delineated above that the workman was dismissed from service on 24-3-2008. The petitioner took the plea of relying upon the Domestic Enquiry and to adduce evidence on merits if the Tribunal decided against the Domestic Enquiry. However, the records of the entire proceedings would show that not only the Petitioner did not request the Tribunal to adjudicate the validity of the Domestic Enquiry as a preliminary issue but adduced evidence on merit thereby going against the plea taken at paragraph No. 21 of the written statement. The Petitioner further knew that three issues were framed and then also did not make any request that the validity of the Domestic Enquiry which was Issue No. 1 should be decided as a preliminary issue. [Para 37]

■

In that view of the matter, this Court cannot permit the petitioner to raise that objection to the impugned Award for not framing the preliminary issue, in the present proceedings. [Para 38]

The petitioner's contention that criminal prosecution cannot be initiated under Section 34 pending adjudication of the dispute under Section 10, where the allegations in both proceedings are one and the same cannot be accepted in absolute terms. In appropriate cases, there can be simultaneous proceedings under Sections 10 and 34. In some cases, the simultaneous proceedings may not be desirable. [Para 13]

■

While considering such a question on permissibility of simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication proceeding, in the context of two different enactments, the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO ([1984] 19 Taxman 1 (SC) /1984 (Supp) SCC 437), and Radheshyam Kejriwal v. State of West Bengal ([2011] 12 taxmann.com 107/108 SCL 406 (SC)/(2011) 3 SCC 581) has held that such criminal prosecution pending adjudication of dispute is permissible. On behalf of the respondent-Union, these two judgments are cited to justify the simultaneous application under Sections 10 and 34. [Para 14]

■

In P. Jayappan (supra), the Apex Court was considering Section 276-C of Income Tax Act, 1961 (Act, 1961) and in Radheshyam Kejriwal (supra), Section 56 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (Act, 1973). In both the enactments, the provisions of law provide for simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication of a claim or liability under the said Acts. [Para 15]

■

Section 276-C of Act, 1961 which provides for criminal prosecution, uses the expression "without prejudice to any penalty that may be imposable on him under any other provisions of this Act". Likewise, Section 56 of the Act, 1973, uses the expression "Without prejudice to any award of penalty by the adjudicating officer under this Act". [Para 16]

■

From the language employed in the aforementioned two provisions, it is explicit that, the simultaneous criminal prosecution for the violation of the provisions of the aforementioned two Acts, even before the adjudication takes place on the claim or liability under the respective Acts, is expressly provided. [Para 17]

■

In the Act there is no provision which uses similar expression which expressly provides for simultaneous criminal prosecution and adjudication of a claim or liability under the Act. Thus, in a way it is possible to urge a contention that, the simultaneous prosecution pending adjudication of the dispute alleging violation of the provisions of the Act is not permissible. [Para 18]

■

At the same time, one has to notice that there is no provision which specifically bars simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication of any claim or liability by any other authority/Tribunal/Court under the Act. [Para 19]

■

To answer the questions raised, the Court has to keep in mind the object of the Act. One of the objects is to provide efficacious remedy to the workmen against the violations of the provisions of the Act. At the same time, among other, the Act also aims in securing industrial peace. [Para 20]

■

If these two aspects are borne in mind, it is not permissible to accept the contention that the complaint under Section 34 alleging violation of the provisions of the Act is permissible only in a situation where the adjudication gets concluded by the authority/Court/Tribunal relating to the violation of the provisions of the Act. [Para 21]

■

At the same time it is not possible to accept the contention that every application alleging violation of the provisions of the Act, seeking permission to prosecute for alleged violation of the provisions of the Act, will have to be allowed pending adjudication of the dispute arising from such violations of the provisions of the Act. [Para 22]

In CIT v. Bhupen Champak Lal Dalal [2001] 248 ITR 830/ 116 Taxman 746 , the Supreme Court was mindful of the fact that the prosecution in criminal law and proceedings under the Act were undoubtedly independent proceedings and, therefore, there was no impediment in law for the criminal proceedings to proceed even during the pendency of the proceedings under the Act. However, the Supreme Court observed that wholesome rule will have to be adopted in matters of this nature where the Courts have taken the view that when the conclusions arrived at by the appellate authorities have a relevance and bearing upon the conclusions to be reached in the criminal case necessarily, one authority will have to await the outcome of the other authority. [Para 5]

The decision of the Supreme Court in K.C. Builders v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 135 Taxman 461, makes it more than clear that the proceedings under section 271(1)(c) would have a clear and definite bearing on those under section 276C. Insofar as the proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were concerned, the penalty against the assessee stood deleted. However, the department had preferred an appeal which was pending before the Court. Therefore, clearly, the assessee could not claim for quashing of the proceedings. The assessee submitted that although the initial application was filed by it for discharge, yet in the light of the decision of the Supreme Court, it was not at this stage claiming quashing of the proceedings and according to it, the order, keeping the criminal proceedings before the trial court in abeyance, need not be interfered with and the same should await the decision in the appeal before the Court. [Para 6]

In view of the decision of the Supreme Court, and in view of the submission made by it that it was not pressing for quashing, there was no reason as to why the impugned order passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, keeping the proceedings before the trial court in abeyance ought to be interfered with, particularly because the result of the proceeding under section 271(1)(c) has a clear bearing on proceedings under section 276C, as observed by the Supreme Court in K.C. Builders’ case (supra). Therefore, the order passed by the Additional Sessions Judge was in consonance with law and, therefore, called for no interference. The instant revision petition was to be dismissed. [Para 7]

It is settled that pendency of the reassessment proceedings cannot act as a bar to the institution of criminal proceedings for the offences punishable under section 276C or 277.

Further, the legal position is clear that if the criminal proceedings are launched against the assessee under section 276 C on the basis of the order of the ITO imposing penalty on the assessee and that if the said order is quashed subsequently by the appellate authority, the criminal proceedings are liable to be quashed. Moreover, the standard of proof required in criminal proceedings for convicting the accused is much more than what is required in penalty proceedings under the Act in view of the well-known principle of criminal jurisprudence that benefit of every reasonable doubt has to be given to the accused.

In the instant case, documentary evidence clearly spelt out that the accused firm had certainly maintained double records in order to evade payment of income-tax. Therefore, it could not be said that no prima facie case had been made out against the assessee firm.

The Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate had yet not taken cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused named therein but merely had referred the complaint to the police for investigation and to file a challan/charge sheet if there was evidence. From the above, it was clear that there was no criminal proceeding pending so as to tantamount to a parallel proceeding as contended by the respondents. The application for stay was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. [Paras 14 and 15]

The pleadings in the instant case were complete and no further disclosure was required to be made by the respondents against whom the criminal case was filed. Therefore, the arguments advanced by the respondents/applicants that they would be prejudiced by the continuance of the instant proceedings were without any basis and were not tenable. No prejudice was likely to affect them. Moreover, the CLB has consistently taken a view that if both the parties on similar grounds have filed another civil case, the CLB would not encourage parallel proceedings. There was nothing to prevent the CLB to proceed with the instant case when the criminal complaint filed was only at stage of investigation by the police. Relying on the judgment of the Supreme Court in Karamchand Ganga Pershad v. Union of India [1970] 3 SCC 694, it can be said that the proceedings before the CLB can continue even when criminal case is pending which may have been filed by either parties against each other. The matters before the CLB are to be decided in summary proceedings on the basis of evidence by way of affidavits filed by the parties. The overall assessment of the case led to the conclusion that the CLB could proceed with the case when criminal proceedings were pending. However, there was no need to proceed in the instant case for the reasons that the whole issue was evolving around the question of 55,005 shares held by the petitioner which had been fraudulently and by tampering certain documents allegedly were reduced to 405 shares. The question of tampering the documents fraudulently or otherwise had to be decided by the Criminal Court. That being the sole basis of the petition, the case was to be adjourned sine-die with certain directions to be followed. [Para 21]

The term ’employee’ is a wider generic term which would include workman also. In fact, the definition of workmen in section 529(3)(a) itself indicates that the Legislature has treated workmen as one of the categories of employees. The object of section 630 is to provide speedy remedy for enabling the company to obtain possession of its property where it is wrongfully obtained or wrongfully withheld by any officer or employee of the company. There will be no rationale in excluding workmen from the scope of section 630.

The provisions of section 630 do not suffer from the vice of any constitutional infirmity. In Petlad Bulakhidas Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat [1999] 92 Comp. Cas. 900/[1998] 18 SCL 438 (Guj.) it has already been held that the law in question is within the legislative competence. Even the challenge to the constitutional validity of section 630 on the ground that it is discriminatory or that it deprives the right to life under article 21 of the Constitution was also negatived.

There is no conflict between the powers of the Labour Court under the Industrial Disputes Act and the powers of the Criminal Court under section 630. When a workman is dismissed from service, he has the remedy of challenging such dismissal before the Labour Court by setting a reference made under section 10 of the I.D. Act. So long as the Labour Court hearing such reference does not give any declaration that the dismissal was illegal or so long as the Labour Court does not pass any other order staying the operation or any further implementation of the order of dismissal (assuming that the Labour Court has any such power), the order of dismissal would remain in force and the Criminal Court hearing the complaint under section 630 has to consider the situation in light of the order of dismissal/termination of service. Mere pendency of the reference before the Labour Court cannot and does not deprive the Criminal Court of its powers under section 630.

Section 33(1) of the I.D. Act intends to prohibit the employers from altering the conditions of service of workmen who have already raised an industrial dispute with respect to some other conditions of the service in existence. If workmen of a unit have raised an industrial dispute about wage revision, the employer cannot be permitted to nullify the reference by terminating the services of the workmen without obtaining permission of the concerned body before whom the dispute about wage revision is pending. It is in order to save the workman from this kind of retaliation that the Legislature has enacted section 33(1) of the ID Act.

The above provisions could not be applied in the case like the present one where there was no pending industrial dispute when the employee was dismissed from service. Upon such dismissal, all the logical consequences would follow including the stoppage of salary and all other benefits which went with the employment. The employee would, therefore, also lose the right to occupy the quarters allotted to him during his employment.

The consequential order of eviction of quarters came to be passed by the Magistrate when the order of dismissal was in full force and, therefore, the Magistrate was justified in giving a finding that in view of the order of dismissal the petitioner had no right to continue to occupy the quarters and that such continued occupation of the quarters even after receiving the notice of eviction from the respondent-employer was sufficient to bring the case within the scope of section 630. The Magistrate was not bound to await the disposal of the reference by the Labour Court in which the petitioner had challenged his dismissal of service.

Thus, the revision application, having no merit, was dismissed.

As per section 446 no suit or other legal proceedings if pending by the date of winding up order shall be proceeded against the company except with the leave of the Court. The section deals with the suits and other legal proceeding. The Marginal Note is regarding staying of suits on winding up order. Therefore, in the context of the object of framing the said section it is clear that the words 'other legal proceedings' is ejusdem generis to the term 'suit'. Thewords 'other legal proceedings' will not embrace proceedings like those under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The purpose of the section was to safeguard the assets and the property of the company which has been wound up under the Court's order. If any thing is to be realised from the assets or the property of the liquidated company, the same deserve to be done under the Court's permission only. Criminal Proceedings, particularly like section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act have no bearing whatsoever to the purpose for which the section has been enacted. The relief or provision incorporated in section 446( 1) of the Companies Act does not cover criminal proceedings of the type under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The use of the words 'other legal proceedings' is not meant to embrace proceedings of every nature as such. It is true that the words 'other legal proceedings' if taken literally would mean that all and every proceeding of any nature will fall under section 446. But having regard to the Marginal Note and the purpose of the enactment, the expression 'other legal proceedings' will have to be construed The said word cannot be and ought not to be read out cf its total context or in isolation. It has to be considered, in the light of the penal provisions, otherwise the penal clauses under the various Acts would be ineffective by invoking section 446. Hence, the operation of this section must be restricted to proceedings arising out of violations of the Companies Act and not to proceedings for violation of provisions of other criminal statutes. However, proceedings which are of criminal nature but arise out of the provisions under the Companies Act may perhaps fall under the term 'other legal proceedings'. The term 'other legal proceedings' in section 446 refers to civil proceedings as opposed to criminal proceedings under other Acts. Giving a wider meaning to 'other legal proceedings' would make ineffective many of the benevolent and social legislations like (1 ) Employees State Insurance Act (Section 86A); (2 ) Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (Section 14A); ( 3) Employment of Manual Scavengers Act, 1993 (Section 15); (4) Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (Section 32); (5) Minimum Wages Act (Section 22C) and several such other enactments, which are of piece of beneficial legislation to safeguard the public or the weaker sections of the society. Under such beneficial Legislations prosecution of the companies are permissible. If a simplistic view is to be taken of the application of section 446(1 ) all such prosecutions can become a sterile. Hence, it was not the purpose of enacting section 446.

The prosecutions under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are not covered by section 446(1) of the Companies Act. Therefore, for prosecuting pending criminal proceedings under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against a company, no leave is required to be obtained from the Company Court for prosecuting the said case. As far as the directors are concerned, section 446 of the Companies Act has no application even by stretching the provisions because the provision is only meant for prosecution against the companies and not against the directors.

In P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO 1984 Tax LR 1197, the Supreme Court has categorically held that mere pendency of proceedings of assessment reassessment under the Act against an assessee is not a bar of initiation of criminal prosecution for the offence punishable under section 276C or section 277. In any criminal case before the prosecution can succeed it has to establish all the ingredients of the offence. No doubt, in case any assessment or reassessment order is passed in favour of the assessee during the criminal proceeding the criminal court has to take note of it and may drop the proceedings. Thus, in the present case initiation of proceedings under section 276C could not be dropped merely because the regular assessment proceedings were pending and had not been finalised or if were finalised in few cases appeals were pending.

Accordingly, the complaint in the instant case, was to be allowed to be proceeded with.

The Supreme Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal [1984] 149 ITR 696 had made it clear that no criminal prosecution can be quashed merely because proceedings under the tax laws are pending. The criminal court is to decide the case on the evidence before it, no doubt giving due weight to findings which could have been rendered by the departmental tribunals and, if need be and if a request is made, to postpone its decision by a short period.

The criminal proceedings, therefore, could not be quashed

If, after the conclusion of the trial and before the pronouncement of the judgment, the petitioner feels that he should make such a request to the trial court not to pronounce the judgment till the departmental proceedings were over, he was free to do so and the Magistrate would deal with that request according to law.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the Revenue.

There is no provision in law which provides that a prosecution for the offences in question cannot be launched until reassessment proceedings initiated against the assessee are completed. Section 279 provides that a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence punishable under section 276C Or section 277 except at the instance of the Commissioner. It further provides that a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence punishable under those provisions in relation to the assessment for an assessment year in respect of which penalty imposed or imposable on him under clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 271 has been reduced or waived by an order under section 273A. The Commissioner has the power either before or after the institution of proceedings to compound any such offence. In this case, it was not claimed that the Commissioner had not initiated the proceedings for instituting the complaints. No other legal bar for the institution of the proceedings was urged except stating that in the event of the petitioner being exonerated in the reassessment proceedings, the prosecutions may have to be dropped.

A mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of the institution of the criminal proceedings under section 276C and section 277. In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The criminal court no doubt has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the criminal court. The criminal court has to judge the case independently on the evidence placed before it. Otherwise there is a danger of a contention being advanced that whenever the assessee or any other person liable under the Act has failed to convince the authorities in the proceedings under the Act that he has not deliberately made any false statement or that he has not fabricated any material evidence, the conviction of such person should invariably follow in the criminal court.

It is only where the Commissioner reduces or waives the penalty imposed or imposable under section 271(1)(iii) in exercise of his discretion under section 273A, section 279(1A) comes into operation and acts as a statutory bar for proceeding with the prosecution under section 276C or section 277. It does not, however, provide that merely because there is a possibility of the Commissioner passing an order under section 273A, the prosecution shall not be instituted.

It may be that in an appropriate case the criminal court may adjourn or postpone the hearing of a criminal case in exercise of its discretionary power under section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the disposal of any proceeding under the Act which has a bearing on the proceedings before it is imminent so that it may take also into consideration the order to be passed therein. Even here the discretion should be exercised judicially and in such a way as not to frustrate the object of the criminal proceedings. There is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a criminal court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of a case before it indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceeding which may have some bearing on it is pending elsewhere. But this, however, has no relevance to the question of maintainability of the prosecution.

Accordingly, notwithstanding the reassessment proceedings started against the petitioner, prosecutions for offences punishable under sections 276C and 277 and under sections 193 and 196 of the Indian Penal Code instituted by the department were maintainable.

Decision of the Madras High Court affirmed.

In the present case, ’T’ was occupying the flat of the company as its employee and it was the case of the company that even after retirement from the service ’T’ had been illegally retaining the same and was not delivering the possession of the same to the company. Such allegation no doubt prima facie made out a case triable under section 630. The mere fact that they had also remedy for possession and damages in civil law and in pursuance of that they had also filed a civil suit for such relief did not make section 630 inoperative in respect of the said matter nor could that be a good ground for staying the proceeding under section 630. The Supreme Court in Atul Mathur v. Atul Kalra, 1989 SCC (Crl.) 761 has held that merely because the accused had schemingly filed a suit in Civil Court, it could never be said that the Civil Court was in seisin of a bona fide dispute between the parties and as such the Criminal Court should have stayed its hands when the company filed a complaint under section 630 and that if such a view was taken, it would not only lead to miscarriage of justice but also render ineffective the salutary provision of section 630. The principle enunciated in the said Supreme Court decision was also applicable in the instant case. However, in the present case, the civil suit that had been filed was that of the company and the civil suit filed by ’T’ was only for his retiral benefit.

Therefore, in the facts and circumstances, prima facie appearing in the case, the company could seek relief both under the civil law as well as under section 630 and there was no bar against the simultaneous continuance of both sorts of proceedings.

In the result, the Court below should proceed with the proceedings under section 630, notwithstanding the pendency and continuance of any civil suit in the matter.

Applying the decision of the Madras High Court in Kamala Ganesan v. ITO [1992] 198 ITR 152 , it was held that the proceedings before the Criminal Court could not be stayed merely because a petition for compounding of the offence was pending before the Commissioner. Accordingly, the instant petition was dismissed. However, in view of the request made by the petitioner that if the criminal case was disposed of expeditiously and subsequently the pending application before the income-tax department was allowed, the relief prayed for would become infructuous. Hence, a direction might be given to the authorities to dispose of the pending petition within a reasonable time to which course the department had no objection.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

Civil Court decision or a decision of the civil proceedings is relevant in a criminal prosecution, but criminal courts are required to reach an independent finding and conclusion. There is no provision in law which provides that the prosecution for the offences cannot be launched until the assessment proceedings initiated against the assessee are completed. Further, a mere expectation of success is some proceedings in appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of the institution of the criminal proceedings under sections 276C and section 277. In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The criminal court, no doubt, has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the Criminal Court. In view of the above opinion expressed by the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO [1984] 149 ITR 696, it could not be said, in the instant case, that merely because a proceeding under the Act was pending, the prosecution under sections 276 and 277 could not be started or that the proceedings in any way deserved to be quashed. Since the two proceedings are different and the standard of proof in both the proceedings are also different, it would not be proper to quash the criminal prosecution, merely because proceedings under the Act in appeal or reference were pending.

Accordingly, the petition was dismissed.

(Criminal Appeal No. 847 of 1999) since reported as 2000 ( ) SCL pendency of proceeding under section 22(1) of SICA alone is not sufficient to get absolved from the liability under section 138 of the NI Act. The contention that if the criminal case was proceeded with and the appellants were convicted and sentenced to fine then it would be necessary to realise the amount of fine from the assets of the company which would be impermissible in view of the provisions of section 22 of the SICA was premature and far-fetched as the occasion to realise fine from the accused company or its directors would arise only in case they were convicted and sentenced or fine was imposed against them. That was not a ground to hold that the criminal proceedings should be foreclosed at the threshold. Another contention that if the Directors of the company on being convicted were arrested and kept in jail the efforts of the BIFR for reconstruction/revival of the company would not be possible and in that event the very purpose of inquiry by the BIFR would be rendered futile was too remote and the apprehension farfetched. Section 22 does not create any legal impediment for instituting and proceeding with a criminal case on the allegations of an offence under section 138 against a company or its Directors. The section only creates an embargo against disposal of assets of the company for recovery of its debts. The purpose of such an embargo is to preserve the assets of the company from being attached or sold for realisation of dues of the creditors. The section does not bar payment of money by the company or its directors to other persons for satisfaction of their legally enforceable dues. The question that remained to be considered was whether section 22A affects a criminal case for an offence under section 138. In the said section provision is made enabling the Board to make an order in writing to direct the sick industrial company not to dispose of, except with the consent of the Board, any of its assets - (a ) during the period of preparation or consideration of the scheme under section 18; and (b) during the period beginning with the recording of opinion by the Board for winding up of the company under sub-section (1) of section 20 and up to commencement of the proceedings relating to the winding up before the concerned High Court. This exercise of the power by the Board is conditioned by the prescription that the Board is of the opinion that such a direction is necessary in the interest of the sick industrial company or its creditors or shareholders or in the public interest. In a case in which the BIFR had submitted its report declaring a company as 'sick' and had also issued a direction under section 22A restraining the company or its directors not to dispose of any of its assets except with consent of the Board then the contention raised on behalf of the appellant that a criminal case for the alleged offence under section 138 could not be instituted during the period in which the restraint order passed by the BIFR remained operative could not be rejected outright. Whether the contention could be accepted or not would depend on the facts and circumstances of the case. Take for instance, before the date on which the cheque was drawn or before expiry of the statutory period of 15 days after notice, a restraint order of the BIFR under section 22A was passed against the company then it could not be said that the offence under section 138 of the NI Act was completed. In such a case it could reasonably be said that the dishonouring of the cheque by the bank and failure to make payment of the amount by the company and/or its Directors was for reasons beyond the control of the accused. It could also be contended that the amount claimed by the complainant was not recoverable from the assets of the company in view of the ban order passed by the BIFR. In such circumstances it would be unjust and unfair and against the intent and purpose of the statute to hold that the Directors should be compelled to face trial in a criminal case.

Except in the circumstances noted above there was no good reason for accepting the contentions raised by the appellant in favour of the prayer for quashing the criminal proceedings or for keeping the proceedings in abeyance. It would be open to the appellant to place relevant materials in this regard before the Magistrate before whom the cases were pending and the Magistrate would examine the matter keeping in mind the discussions made in this judgment. It was clear that the question whether in the facts and circumstances of a particular case section 138 of the NI Act was attracted or not, was a question to be considered by the Court at the appropriate stage of the case in the light of the evidence on record.

The facts on record indicate that the Respondent had admittedly worked intermittently with the Telecommunication Department, Ulhasnagar, from 1980 onwards. His last period of engagement was from 01.08.1990 till 06.12.1992, on the Muster Roll prior to his arrest on allegation of theft. [Para 8]

■

It is undisputed that the Respondent was arrested on 06.12.1992 and he was terminated from service forthwith without any inquiry on the following day, i.e., 07.12.1992. No inquiry was conducted; principles of natural justice were not followed prior to termination. The record reflects that the Respondent workman got bail and gave letters for his reinstatement in 1992 itself, but the Petitioners ignored the same. Thereafter, he was acquitted from the criminal charge by the Competent Court on 28.04.1999 and he once again approached the Petitioners, who ignored him. [Para 9]

■

Despite the Petitioner's contentions, the Tribunal has rightly held that termination without inquiry, especially when allegations are serious and criminal proceedings are pending, is unsustainable. The obligation of the employer to hold a domestic inquiry is not dispensed with merely because a criminal prosecution is launched. The Petitioner has failed to demonstrate any compliance with the procedure under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and no material is placed before the Court to justify non-adherence thereto. [Para 10]

■

The Tribunal has also considered the Petitioner's argument regarding delay and laches. The record shows that the Respondent sent representations immediately after being released on bail and again in 1999 post his acquittal but was intentionally ignored by the Petitioner. The Union took up his cause shortly thereafter. The Court found no gross negligence or inaction on the part of the Respondent to deny relief solely on the ground of delay. On these facts, the grievance of the Petitioner on the ground of delay is unacceptable. [Para 11]

■

The argument that the Respondent was not a member of the Union which raised the dispute is also devoid of merit. It is well settled that a Union may espouse the cause of a workman even without formal membership, if done with his consent or in the larger interest of the workmen. The Tribunal has correctly applied the legal maxim of espousal and its findings are consistent with settled principles of industrial jurisprudence. [Para 12]

■

The Petitioner further contends that acquittal was not on merits but by giving him benefit of doubt, and therefore, reinstatement should not automatically follow. However, in the absence of a departmental inquiry or any evidence on record justifying termination, this Court cannot uphold the punitive action meted out by the Petitioners to the Respondent merely based on a criminal allegation which has not been substantiated. Further, the Respondent stands cleared of all charges. [Para 13]

The submission regarding the Respondent's employment status being "daily-rated" and hence disentitling him to relief is also rejected in view of the aforesaid findings that he admittedly worked from 1980 to 1992 with the Petitioners.
