2.2 Prior Permission for Closure in case of larger undertakings (Section 80) An employer intending to close down an undertaking of an industrial establishment employing 300 or more workers must apply electronically or otherwise in the prescribed manner (As per Draft Rules, 2020, an application for permission must be made in Form X) to the appropriate Government for prior permission at least 90 days before the intended closure.

The application must clearly state the reasons for the intended closure, and a copy of the application must be served simultaneously on representatives of workers in the prescribed manner.

However, this requirement does not apply to undertakings set up for the construction of buildings, bridges, roads, canals, dams or for other construction work.

2.3 Government decision to grant or refuse to grant permission for Closure

The appropriate Government, after making an enquiry as it thinks fit and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the employer, workers, and persons interested in closure, may, by order, grant or refuse to grant permission for closure. A copy of the order must be communicated to the employer and the workers.

If the appropriate Government does not communicate the order granting or refusing permission to the employer within 60 days from the date of application, the permission shall be deemed to have been granted, and the application shall be disposed of accordingly.

Further, the order of the appropriate Government must be final and binding on all the parties and must remain in force for one year from the date of such order.

2.3-1 Whether the power of the Government to deny permission for closure is absolute?

The Supreme Court in Orissa Textile & Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa [2002] 2 SCC 578, held that the Government's power to refuse permission for closure of an undertaking must be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances.

Such refusal is justified only where compelling or overriding reasons exist or where the public interest so demands, for instance, where the establishment is engaged in manufacturing life-saving vaccines or drugs during a prevailing epidemic, or products essential for the defence of India.

2.4 Power of Review or Reference to Tribunal for adjudication

The appropriate Government may, suo motu or on an application by the employer or worker, review its order granting or refusing permission within the prescribed time (As per Draft Rules, 2020, the prescribed time is within 30 days from the date on which the order is made) or refer the matter to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal must pass the award within 30 days from the date of such reference.

2.5 Consequences of Illegal Closure

Where an employer fails to apply for prior permission for closure within the prescribed period or where the permission for closure has been refused, the closure of the undertaking shall be deemed illegal from the date it takes effect. In such circumstances, the workers are entitled to all benefits available under the applicable law as if the undertaking had not been closed down.

2.6 Exemption from Prior Permission Requirement in certain exceptional cases

The appropriate Government may, in certain exceptional cases, such as an accident in the undertaking, the death of the employer, or similar situations, by order direct that no prior permission for the closure of the undertaking is required.

2.7 Compensation payable to workers upon permitted or deemed closure

Where an undertaking is permitted to be closed down or where the permission for closure is deemed to be granted, every worker employed immediately before the date of the application for permission must be entitled to receive compensation.

The compensation payable must be:

(a)

equivalent to 15 days' average pay or

(b)

Average pay of such other number of days as may be notified by the appropriate Government, for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of 6 months.

2.7-1 Whether closure of undertaking amounts to retrenchment of workers?

No, the Supreme Court in S.G. Chemicals & Dyes Trading Employees' Union v. S.G. Chemicals & Dyes Trading Ltd. [1986] 2 SCC 624, clarified that the closure of an undertaking is distinct from retrenchment. Retrenchment means reducing surplus staff in an ongoing business and not ending the entire business.

ATTACHMENT OF CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY TO A CORPORATION

i. Strict Liability

Under this concept, a person shall be made legally responsible for the concerns of his acts even in the absence of guilty mind or criminal intention. Examples of some criminal offences which do not require mens rea are rape, murder, vehicular offences. In US, the rule followed is that whenever a particular legislation does not specify mens rea as an essential, it is deems that mental intent need not be prove in such offence, and hence treated it as strict liability.

In Indianapolis Water Co. v. American Strawboard Co.,27 court held that mere omission, irrespective of mens rea of defaulter, is sufficient to constitute crime.

ii. Vicarious Liability

The maxim qui facit per alium per se explains the concept better, which means, one who does an act through another is deemed to do it by himself. Similarly, under the concept of vicarious liability, one is made responsible for any act or omission of another. The reason here is the presumption that master is aware of what his servant is doing and that the servant is always deemed to act on behalf of and on the directions of the master. In Commonwealth,28 the court made the people acting on behalf of 3 companies liable for its activities by stating that CCL is necessarily vicarious because company is a legal fiction which is comprised of individuals alone.

Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, several minor offences that previously attracted imprisonment or criminal liability have been decriminalized, and certain contraventions can now be compounded in the following manner4:

(a)

For an offence punishable with fine only – The offence may be compounded by payment of 50% of the maximum fine.

(b)

For an offence punishable with imprisonment for up to one year and with fine - The offence may be compounded by payment of 75% of the maximum fine.

Further, once an offence is compounded, no prosecution will be instituted against the offender for that offence.

3.1-2. Whether a lockout is the same as the closure of operations? The Supreme Court in Management of Express Newspapers Ltd. v. Workers & Staff Employed Under it (AIR 1963 SC 569) clarified that a lockout is not the same as a closure. A lockout refers to the temporary closing of the place of employment, the suspension of work, or the employer's refusal to employ workers during an industrial dispute. A closure, on the other hand, refers to the permanent shutdown of business operations. Unlike a lockout, a closure signifies the end of business itself, not just the temporary suspension of operations.

Further, in Management of Kairbetta Estate v. Rajamanickam (AIR 1960 SC 893), the Supreme Court elaborated on the distinction between a lock-out and a lay-off. The Court held that a layoff arises when ongoing operations exist but workers cannot be given work due to reasons beyond the employer's control, while a lockout involves a temporary suspension of operations by the employer. In this case, a justified lockout in response to workers' violence cannot be treated as a layoff, and thus, the workers were not entitled to layoff compensation.

3.2 Prohibition on Strikes and Lockouts:

The provisions relating to the prohibition on strikes and lockouts are as follows:

3.2-1 Prohibition on Strikes

No person employed in an industrial establishment must go on strike, in breach of contract, in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving the employer a notice of strike within 60 days before striking or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of strike specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.2-2 Prohibition on Lockouts

No employer of an industrial establishment must lock out any of his workers in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving a notice of lock-out within 60 days before locking out or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of lock-out specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.3 Exemption from notice requirement in case of existing strike or lockout:

The notice of strike or lockout must not be necessary where a strike or lockout is already in existence. However, the employer must send intimation of such lock-out or strike on the day on which it is declared to such authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government, either generally or for a particular area or for a particular class of services.

3.4 Reporting Requirements for Strikes and Lockout Notices:

If on any day, an employer receives from any person employed by him, any notice or gives to any person employed by him, any notice of strike or lock-out, he must report it within 5 days to the appropriate Government or to such authority as the Government may prescribe and to the conciliation officer, specifying the number of notices received or issued on that day.

3.5 Illegality of Strikes and Lockouts:

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 62 or continued in violation of an order made under Section 42(7) of the Code.

3.5-1. When continuation of a strike or lock-out is not deemed illegal

If a strike or lock-out relating to an industrial dispute has already commenced and is in existence at the time an application is filed before the Tribunal or when the dispute is referred to an arbitrator or the National Industrial Tribunal, its continuance shall not be deemed illegal. The only condition is that the strike or lock-out was legal when it began and has not been prohibited.

3.5-2. Legality of strikes or lock-outs declared in consequence of illegality

A lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out must not be considered illegal.

Intent behind Incorporation of Section 32A of the Code

Insolvency Law committee recommended incorporation of this provision submitted in February 2020.5 It was incorporated keeping in mind the difficulty faced by the successful resolution applicants imposing the restrictions and liabilities on corporate debtor. In is emphasised by the Insolvency Law committee that this provision has been included to absolve the corporate debtor from the offences committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP unless they resolution applicant is also involved or related party to promoter group.

Parliamentary Standing Committee under the chairmanship of by Mr. Jayant Sinha, Former Minister of State of Finance in its report submitted on March 2020.6 The committee rendered its opinion in favour of incorporation of Section 32A into the Code with a view to safeguard the position of the resolution applicant from the offence the former promoters. Such an observation keeping in mind the necessity of cleansed entity where the change in management of the corporate debtor has taken place.

Pre-Condition to the Applicability of Section 32A

In order to discourage the abuse of this provision, safeguard has been introduced by way of pre-condition which need to be satisfied before resorting to Section 32A are:-

The resolution applicant is not involved or related party to promoter group,

The resolution plan results in control of corporate debtor or change in the management.

Liability for the Offence Committed Prior to the Commencement of CIRP

As a result of incorporation of Section 32A of the Code, the corporate debtor shall cease to responsible for the offence committed prior to the commencement of CIRP and the property of corporate debtor which are part of resolution plan, no action can be taken against those property.

However, it is clarified the ambit of the Section 32A is very limited in terms of liability and it doesn't immune or absolve the person who are:-

responsible for the activities of the corporate debtor in conduct of business,

officer in default

directly or indirectly involved in the commission of the offence

All the above mentioned person shall continue to remain liable for the offence committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP. Furthermore there is also no bar against the property other than property of corporate debtor and the person who has acquired that property under the liquidation or CIRP, as the case may be.

Promulgation of Section 32A in the Code has lot of implication and its position is not very in this regard. Various relevant legal issues time and again has come before the Appellate Tribunal and High Courts for consideration and these issues need to be redressed as they core to the application of Section 32A.

The question of interpretation of Section 32A came up before the Appellate tribunal in the case of JSW Steel Ltd. v. However, it wasn't clarified whether it is also applicable to the proceedings which have already been concluded and no adjudication is pending w.r.t. corporate debtor however they satisfies the parameters laid down in the Section 32A of the Code.

In the case of Tata Steel BSL Ltd v. Union of India,8 wherein summon issued before the incorporation of Section32A into the Code by the Investigating officer was under challenge. The Delhi HC ruled that the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under section 32A of the Code as the instant case falls within the clear language used in Section 32A and hence corporate debtor cannot be made responsible for the offence committed prior to commencement of CIRP even when the resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority, when it is expressly prohibited by the provision. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner was upheld and liable to be discharged in the merits of the case.

B. Shanmugam v. Karthik Dasari [2022] SCC OnLine Mad 4417]

The genesis in the cited case rested with the ED registering ECIR on the basis of three (3) FIRs. Out of the three (3) FIRs, one (1) was quashed & the remaining two (2) were stayed till further orders.

Before the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Madras the primary question was about the implication of quashing & staying of FIRs on the proceedings initiated by the ED under the PMLA.

In line with the directions passed in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra), the ED fairly conceded that in so far as the quashed FIR is concerned, the department cannot proceed ahead under the Act. However, it was strenuously contended by them that the accused cannot take benefit of the stayed proceedings and plea before the court that proceedings under PMLA for the remaining two (2) FIRs too be quashed.

On the other hand, the petitioners refuted the said contention of the department, and relied upon the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta in Rashmi Metaliks Ltd. (Supra).

The Division Bench in its judgment discarded the contentions of the Department and answered in negative to the question whether the ECIR, which is also pursuant to the FIRs which have been stayed by the High Court, can be proceeded with or not.

Placing reliance on precedents on 'jurisdictional fact to be taken into account by a Court before assuming jurisdiction over a particular matter', the court opined that the existence of jurisdictional fact is a condition precedent for the exercise of power by a Court of limited jurisdiction. Therefore, in present matter, when there is no cause of action, since the proceeding in one (1) of the cases was quashed, and the proceedings in two (2) other cases have been stayed by the Court, there was no jurisdictional fact or cause of action for the respondent/department to initiate any proceedings during the period of order of stay operating against the two FIRs.

Finally, in its conclusion, the Hon'ble High Court opined that in view of the quashing of the proceedings in one (1) of the FIR and staying of the proceedings in the remaining two (2) FIRs, the scheduled offence was eclipsed, suspended or stop operating during the period of stay. Therefore, the Department has to await the finality of the said proceedings. In case, if the other two (2) remaining FIRs also get quashed pursuant to the orders in the applications filed by the respective accused to quash the proceedings, in which event, the Department cannot step in or initiate any proceedings under the PMLA, as held in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra).

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("IBC") has been amended multiple times since its introduction in 2016to remove difficulties in the corporate insolvency process and streamline the procedure. The latest amendment, The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2020 ("Amended Act"), was introduced in the Lok Sabha, and passed by Rajya Sabha in the budget session and came into force w.e.f 13 March 2020. The Amended Act amends various sections and also introduces a new provision i.e. Section 32A protecting the new management which takes over a Company through an approved resolution plan under Section 31 of IBC.

The newly inserted Section 32A envisages the following; (a) Immunity to the Corporate Debtor as regards any offences committed prior to insolvency commencement date; and (b) Protection as regards any property of the Corporate Debtor in relation to any offence committed prior to commencement of insolvency resolution process where such property is covered under Resolution Plan as approved by the Adjudicating Authority. However, every person who is a designated partner as defined in the Limited Partnership Act or an officer as defined in Clause 60 of Section 2 of the Companies Act 2013 who is in charge of the business of the corporate debtor and is directly or indirectly in the commission of such offence as per report or complaint filed by the investigating authority shall continue to be liable and prosecuted for such offence committed by the corporate debtor notwithstanding that the liability of the corporate debtor has ceased. Accordingly, the newly inserted Section while protecting the new management which takes over a Company under an approved Resolution Plan envisages due continuance of proceedings against others in terms of the applicable provisions of law.

REQUIREMENT AND REASONS FOR PROTECTING CORPORATE DEBTOR AND SUCCESSFUL RESOLUTION APPLICANT

The latest amendment particularly the insertion of Section 32A is a phenomenal step taken by the Government which will enhance the revival of the stressed assets of corporate debtor as it will attract investments from successful bidders for the resolution plan before Adjudicating Authority. Resolution Applicant shall now be secured in as much as in light of Section 32A they shall no longer face further prosecution and threat of dispossession of the assets of the Corporate Debtor on account of prior offences being committed by the erstwhile management/promoter group. The success of any resolution plan was highly dependent on the newly inserted Section since, the uncertainties prevailing prior to the introduction of Section 32A time and again highlighted the need of protecting the corporate debtor as well as the properties belonging to the Corporate Debtor from its prior offence as even after taking over of a Corporate Debtor through a successful resolution plan, a successful bidder faced prosecution and liabilities before courts and tribunals for the prior acts of such corporate debtor.

Such grievance of the Successful Resolution Applicant came to forefront in the matter of Monnet Inspat& Energy which was acquired under CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) jointly by AION and JSW. Similarly in the matter of Bhushan Power Steel Ltd. which is under insolvency resolution process, to be acquired by JSW for over Rs.19,700 crore, the aspect of attachment by the Enforcement Directorate over the assets of Bhushan Power Steel Ltd. on account of alleged offence under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act interdicted the resolution process under the IBC. In the appeal case of Committee of Creditors versus Directorate Enforcement, the apex court stayed the ED attachment order while hearing the petition and the court asked ED to explain whether its money-laundering charges would trump the insolvency proceedings to be heard in forthcoming days.

In addition, we may also say that Section 32A of the IBC shall have a direct implication on the scope and ambit of Section 14 of the IBC, which provides for moratorium period as regards a Company which is undergoing resolution process under the Code. Section 14 lays down that there has to be a mandatory moratorium period provided to the corporate debtor from the insolvency commencement date wherein, inter alia, institution of new suits or continuation of the pending suits, against the corporate debtor, are temporarily suspended until the completion of the CIRP. That this moratorium period will not affect the criminal proceedings against the corporate debtor was made fairly clear in Shah Brothers Ispat (P.) Ltd. v. P. Mohanraj [2018] 97 taxmann.com 233. In this case, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal ("NCLAT") held that Section 14 is not applicable to the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act ("NI Act") as they are criminal proceedings. In crux, the NCLAT held that Section 14 of the IBC does not affect any criminal proceedings. Hence, even during the moratorium, criminal proceedings could be instituted or continued against the corporate debtor.

We hope and trust that the Collector of Custom Bombay shall appropriately revise the said public notice in the light of the observations made herein. If he does not do so, there is a likelihood of the Customs Authorities being themselves made liable for demurrage charges in appropriate cases. 7. So far as this case is concerned, we direct that the detention certificate should be issued without reference to para 4 of the said public notice or any similar public notice. Since the Respondents will not be absolved of the obligation to pay the demurrage charges altogether by reason of the detention certificate the Trustees of the Port of Bombay (Respondent No. 2), are directed to consider sympathetically the request of the respondent No. 1 [M/s. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd., Delhi] for waiver of these demurrage charges."

As can be seen from the highlighted portion, the decision of the Supreme Court referred in Circular No. 967/01/ 2013-CX, dated 1.1.2013 was in a totally different context.

High Court's decision on the same point

4. Further, reference is invited to the recent decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in the case of M/s Siva Sai Constructions, Hyderabad v. Government of India, 2013-TIOL-09-HC-AP-ST. While allowing the petition filed by the assessee, the High Court clearly held that a coercive action under section 87 of the Finance Act, 1994 during the pendency of appeal is not justified. The High Court clearly directed the authorities not to initiate any coercive steps against the assessee or others who owe dues to the petitioner under section 87 or any other appropriate provision. The Court held that such coercive actions should not be taken till disposal of the petitioner's applications for condonation of delay and for grant of interim relief in the appeal preferred by the petitioner to the Tribunal.

Conclusion

5. Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1.1.2013 has completely ignored the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court and will have a devastating effect in case the tax authorities initiate the recovery proceedings. It should be understood that there is a huge pendency of cases before almost all the forums and in such a case, it may become extremely difficult for the stay matter to be heard within the prescribed time-frame.

It is hoped that someone would challenge the validity of the Circular on the grounds of genuine hardship which would be faced by the assessees. Also, if the Circular is implemented, then the assessees will be required to do something which is beyond their control. This is especially in the light of the fact that the statute does not provide a strict time-line for disposal of the stay hearings. There may be situations where department will take adjournments for genuine or unreasonable reasons. Why should assessees suffer if the department takes adjournment? As a corollary, this needs to be addressed at the earliest.

I wish there was someone to do a genuine performance appraisal of the Board based on the quality of clarifications issued !

Investigation - Discover and collect evidence

The word "investigation" is to discover and collect the evidence to prove the charge as a fact or disprove. In criminal case investigation connotes discovery and collection of evidence before charge sheet is filed and based thereon definite charges are framed. Criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings - Objective distinct

In the disciplinary proceedings, the question is whether the employee is guilty of such conduct as would merit his dismissal from service or a lesser punishment, as the case may be, whereas in the criminal proceedings the question is whether the offences registered against him are established and, if established, what sentence should be imposed upon him. Enquiry - Nature determines whether discharge punitive

In order to determine whether the discharge is punitive in nature, it is necessary to ascertain firstly the nature of the enquiry, i.e., whether the termination is preceded by full scale formal enquiry into allegations involving misconduct on the part of the employee, which culminated in the finding of guilt, and secondly, the ‘purpose of enquiry’, i.e., whether the purpose of enquiry is to find out any misconduct on his part or it is aimed at finding out as to the employee being unlikely to prove efficient. Thus, the principle that in order to determine whether the misconduct is motive or foundation of order of termination, the test to be applied is to ask the question as to what was the ‘object of enquiry’. If an enquiry or an assessment is done with the object of finding out any misconduct on the part of the employee and for that reason his services are terminated, then it would be punitive in nature. On the other hand, if such an enquiry or an assessment is aimed at determining the suitability of an employee for a particular job, such termination would be termination simplicitor and not punitive in nature [State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh (2004) 23 ILD 23 (SC)]

30.15 Powers and Duties of Tribunal on presentation of Petition [Sections 443 and 444]

Stay of suits

30.15-1 Earlier, under section 442 power was vested in the High Court to stay suits and proceedings or restrain further proceedings in the suits or proceedings at the instance of any creditor or contributory at any time after presentation of the petition for winding up and before a winding up order is made, only for that interim period, because once the winding up order is made-section 446 providing for same on its making-will become applicable, but with the omission of the section 442 by the Second Amendment Act, 2002 (not yet notified), this power is no longer available to the Tribunal, which means that the suits and proceedings shall continue until making of the winding up order by the Tribunal.

Relief Undertakings Act and Stay

30.15-2 However, it would appear that the stay of proceedings notified in exercise of statutory power under a State legislation like Relief Undertakings Act having overriding efficacy would be effective and the Tribunal would be bound, having regard to the decision in Jaysinth Dyechem v. Mewar Textile Mills Ltd. AIR 1988 Raj. 16, that such a notification is constitutional and not repugnant.

Tribunal’s powers [Sections 443 & 444]

30.15-3 Further, sections 443 and 444 dealing with the powers of Tribunal on hearing petition and its duty to communicate the order when made to the Official Liquidator, have been substituted in their entirety - only to substitute ‘Tribunal’ for ‘Court’ - by the said Act. Accordingly, on hearing a winding up petition, the Tribunal may, at par with the High Court earlier,

u (a ) dismiss the petition with or without costs,

u (b) adjourn the hearing conditionally or unconditionally, (for example, where family disputes over property ownership exist, Shivraj Gupta v. Hansraj Gupta & Co. (P.) Ltd. [1987] 2 Comp. LJ 74 (Delhi),

u (c) make any interim order that it thinks fit (like the appointment of an interim-Administrator to take charge of the company’s affairs pending a decision), or

u (d) make an order for winding up the company with or without costs, or any other order that it thinks fit, such that the Tribunal shall not refuse to make a winding up order on the ground only that the assets of the company have been mortgaged to an amount equal or in excess, or that the company has no assets.

Petition on ‘just & equitable’ ground

30.15-4 In respect of a petition for winding up on the ‘just and equitable’ ground, the Tribunal may refuse to make an order for winding up, if it is of the opinion that some other remedy is available to the petitioners and that they are acting unreasonably in seeking to have the company wound up instead of pursuing that other remedy.

Default of delivering statutory report as a ground

30.15-5 Further, in the case of a petition for winding up on the ground of default in delivering the statutory report to the Registrar, or in holding the statutory meeting, the Tribunal may-instead of making the winding up order-(a) direct that the statutory report shall be delivered or the statutory meeting held, and (b) order the costs to be paid by any persons who, in the opinion of the Tribunal, are responsible for the default.

Workers’ right to present petition for winding up

30.15-6 In National Textile Workers’ Union v. P.R. Ramakrishnan AIR 1983 SC 75, it was held that though the workers have no statutory right to present a winding up petition, they are entitled to be heard of their interest as interveners but not as parties in a winding up petition, and particularly so because the winding up order after it attains finality the workers have no scope to participate in the further proceedings, except by appealing against the winding up order under section 483.

5.14

Case Studies

1. The Company has received a Show Cause Notice during the year 2022-23 from Initiating Officer for holding a benami property and alleging that company is only a shell company and its properties are held by it as benamidar for the real person controlling the company who has channeled his ill gotten funds into the company as share capital through a network of benami shell companies. The alleged benami properties were acquired prior to 25-10-2016. The Company contends that auditor need not report on this as company has sent reply with all details and, in view of Supreme Court judgment in Ganapati Dealcom, the IO will drop proceedings. Proceedings have not been dropped at the time of audit reporting. Company also contends that ARI disclosures are not required in view of the Supreme Court decision. How will you as auditor deal with this?

Auditor is not to sit in judgment on the merits of the case. For auditor, all that matters is that the proceedings are initiated during the year and are pending as of the date of audit report. Therefore, he needs to report the fact of initiation and pendency of the same. Company may disclose its opinion on the merits of the case in notes to financial statements while giving required ARI disclosures.

2. If in Case Study 1, what if, prior to date of audit report, the proceedings are dropped by IO after considering the reply of the Company ?

In that case also, auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings were initiated and subsequently dropped. The wordings in clause 3(i)(e) are "proceedings have been initiated or are pending against the company". Therefore, in view of the word "or" separating the words "initiated" and "are pending", auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings have been initiated during year and dropped after the year-end but prior to date of audit reporting.

3. What if show cause notice dated 1st April 2023 from Initiating Officer is received on 5th April 2023 and audit report is being signed on 30th April 2023? Will auditor have to report it in audit report for FY 2022-23?

No. Auditor will not report this in Audit report for the year under audit i.e. FY 2022-23. Auditor will report it in his report for FY 2023-24.

Audit report for the year is on events during the year. Post-balance sheet date developments in respect of such events which have occurred during the year will be considered. It is one thing that Show Cause Notice is issued during the year and there are further developments after the year-end in the matter which will have to be considered.

It is entirely a different matter that Show Cause Notice is issued and received after the year-end which has nothing to do with conditions existing as at the Balance sheet date. Auditor will not consider such post-balance sheet events in report for the year under audit.

PROTECTION OF EMPLOYEES DURING INVESTIGATION

An employee of company who has disclosed information during investigation is protected against dismissal, discharge or removal or change in terms of his employment to his disadvantage, during investigation, without permission of NCLT [earlier CLB upto 1-6-2016]

Company should give intimation of proposed action to NCLT and if no reply is received within 30 days, proposed action can be taken [section 218(2) of Companies Act, 2013] [corresponding to section 635B(2) of the 1956 Act]

If company is not satisfied with order of NCLT, it can file appeal in NCLAT within 30 days - section 218(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 635B(3) of the 1956 Act]

Such removal or change in terms of employment is subject to other laws also - section 218(5) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 635B(5) of the 1956 Act]

39.5-1 Protection to legal advisers and Bankers

A legal adviser cannot be compelled to supply privileged communication except name and address of his client. A banker has to disclose information about the company or the person under investigation but not of any other customer - section 227 of Companies Act, 2013. [corresponding to section 251 of the 1956 Act].

39.5-2 Freezing of assets of company on inquiry and investigation

Central Government can make application to NCLT for freezing of assets, funds and properties of the company, if there is reasonable ground to believe that removal or transfer or disposal of funds, assets or properties of company is likely to take place in manner prejudicial to interests of company or its shareholders or creditors or in public interest. Such order can be for period upto three years - section 221(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

If despite such order, there is removal or transfer of disposal of assets, company as well as every officer who is in default is liable for punishment of fine and imprisonment - section 221(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

The section 221 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and is effective from 1-6-2016.

39.5-3 Source of information need not be disclosed

Often investigation is carried out on basis of some secret information. To protect the informant, it has been provided that Registrar or officer of Government or any other person shall not be compelled to disclose to Court, Tribunal or other authority, where he got information which has led Central Government to order special audit or order an investigation - section 457 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 635AA of the 1956 Act].

Dilatory part of court procedure is a dampener 1.40-13 In addition to the question on the proper Court of competent jurisdiction discussed above, companies and company affairs that happen to be brought before the courts for adjudication in whatever context are equally subject to the common curse of endemic court delays and related costs largely due to the archaic, outmoded and staid procedural laws made by the imperialist British regime around the 1850’s remaining firm at the core through six decades of India’s Independence to the present electronic era, as a consequence of the law-makers’ choice of creating multiple fast track courts or forums parallelly, to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts which are nearer to people and familiar to them in the view that those courts are super-saturated with other cases and allowing their jurisdiction over company cases to continue would only add to further delays, instead of overhauling the procedural laws to rid them off the dilatory parts for faster disposal of cases by the common law courts and creating more. Unfortunately, seeing the victims sapped by prolonged litigation for years lasting for a generation or over in many cases, there is a misgiving present generally as an aside in the minds of people on ‘who is watching what they do’ about the Judiciary in our system. These factors have contributed to encourage people at large to keep away from approaching the Courts on their disputes with others and swallow the losses unless compelled not for some little money alone as in the case of the common investors, or it forms the lesser evil faced by them, or it found advantageous to show as inescapable and vindicate their own position at any cost to the company or others. Overall, so far as companies are concerned, the combined incidence of these factors has gone in favour of the managements to do what they prefer rather than what they should under the laws in matters of the corporate investors or others.

16.1-2 Private company can prescribe additional disqualifications, but public company cannot

A private company can prescribe additional disqualifications in its Articles - section 164(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 283(3) of the 1956 Act].

Similarly private company can provide grounds in addition to those specified in section 167(1) for vacation of office as director - section 167(4) of Companies Act, 2013.

For example, private company can prescribe disqualification if he joins a rival group or starts a competing business or if he leaves the family of directors etc.

merged.text: It is desirable that if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry is being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending the final disposal of the criminal case. It would be particularly appropriate to adopt such a course where the charge against the workman is of a grave character, because in such a case, it would be unfair to compel the workman to disclose the defence which he may take before the criminal court. But to say that domestic enquiries may be stayed pending criminal trial is very different from anything that if an employer proceeds with the domestic enquiry in spite of the fact that the criminal trial is pending, the enquiry for that reason alone is vitiated and the conclusion reached in such an enquiry is either bad in law or mala fide.

Held, that it was desirable that when the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry was being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending final disposal of the criminal case. In view of the accepted principles of law, in the event thepetitioner was convicted in the criminal trial, he would automatically be dismissed and/or removed from service, without taking recourse to formalities of departmental proceedings and, in the atternative, if the criminal case failed for want of evidence, by an order of discharge and not acquittal, in that event also, the departmental authorities would be entitled to proceed with the departmental enquiry, even after passing of such order of discharge by the criminal court. Therefore, during the pendency of the criminal trial, the employer would be restrained from proceeding further with the departmental enquiry against the petitioner.
Domestic enquiry—Pendency of Criminal case or appeal—Employer need not wait for its decision—Enquiry may be proceeded with.

There is no legal prohibition which prevents the holding of a domestic enquiry into an act of misconduct by a workman just because a criminal case is pending against the workman. The domestic enquiry in which the workman is answerable to his master and which may end in a departmental penalty is entirely different from the criminal proceeding in which the same person in respect of the same act is prosecuted for violation of the penal law of the land, which may end in conviction and sentence.

The decision to hold or not to hold a domestic enquiry, during the pendency of a criminal trial in respect of the same allegation, against a workman, is that of the employer to be taken at his discretion and if the employer decides to hold such enquiry, he cannot be prevented from doing so by the issue of a writ of prohibition.

and again held—

8. Similar view was reiterated by the Supreme Court in Tata Oil Mills’ Co. Ltd. v. The Workmen, 1964 (9) FLR 142 (SC) Jang Bahadur Singh v. Baij Nath Tiwari, 1968 (17) FLR 300 (SC) Kusheshwar Dubey v. M/s Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. and others. 1988 (57) FLR 562 (SC)

In Kushewar Dubey’s case (supra), the Supreme Court held that there was no legal bar to simultaneous proceedings being taken against an employee even though there may be cases where it may be appropriate to defer the disciplinary proceedings awaiting the disposal of the criminal case. The Supreme Court held that it was neither possible nor advisable to evolve a hard and fast straight-jacket formula and that in cases where the charge against the employee was of a grave nature and involved complex questions of law and fact, in that event the disciplinary proceedings could be deferred till the decision of the criminal trial.

In Jang Bahadur Singh v. Baij Nath Tiwari, 1968 (17) FLR 300 (SC) the legal position was summed up by the Supreme Court as under:—

“The issue in the disciplinary proceedings is whether the employee is guilty of the charges on which it is proposed to take action against him. The same issue may arise for decision in a civil or criminal proceeding pending in a Court. But the pendency of the Court proceeding does not bar the taking of disciplinary action. The power of taking such action is vested in the disciplinary authority. The Civil or Criminal Court has no such power. The initiation and continuation of disciplinary proceedings in good faith is not calculated to obstruct or interfere with the course of justice in the pending Court proceeding. The employee is free to move the Court for an order restraining the continuance of the disciplinary proceedings. If he obtains a stay order, a wilful violation of the order would of course amount to contempt of Court. In the absence of a stay order the disciplinary authority is free to exercise its lawful powers.”

In State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Mena and others, 1996 (74) FLR 2550 (SC) the entire case law on this issue was reviewed and the Hon’ble Supreme Court held—

It is not a requirement of the principles of natural justice that an employer should not hold against his employee a departmental enquiry in respect of the very same charges which are pending trial in a criminal court till the termination of such trial and there is no legal right in an aggrieved workman to obtain an order of temporary injunction from the court to restrain the continuation of the departmental proceedings against him. Nor are the courts under any obligation to grant such injunction.
Domestic Enquiry—And criminal trial—Can proceed simultaneously—Decision in criminal case would not materially affect the outcome of domestic enquiry. [Para 5]

It cannot be held as a general rule that whenever a person is acquitted by a criminal court, no further disciplinary action can be taken as the scope, purpose and object of the two enquiries are different and the standards of proof are also different and all depends upon the facts of each case. Where a criminal offence is committed, it is for the management to charge-sheet the employee and conduct a domestic enquiry and if the misconducts are proved, to punish the employee. The management is also free not to conduct the enquiry but to wait for the criminal court judgment.

Kushal Bhan, [1960-61] 19 FJR 183, it is desirable that if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry is being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending the final disposal of the criminal case.”

The question cropped up again with a new angle in Jang Bahadur Singh v. Baij Nath Tiwari, [1969] 36 FJR 128 (SC), as it was contended that initiation of disciplinary proceedings during the pendency of a criminal case on the same facts amounted to contempt of court. This plea was rejected and the court observed as under (page 130) :

“The issue in the disciplinary procedings is whether the employee is guilty of the charges on which it is proposed to take action against him. The same issue may arise for decision in a civil or criminal proceeding pending in a court. But the pendency of the court proceeding does not bar the taking of disciplinary action. The power of taking such action is vested in the disciplinary authority. The civil or criminal court has no such power. The initiation and continuation of disciplinary proceedings in good faith is not calculated to obstruct or interfere with the course of justice in the pending court proceeding. The employee is free to move the court for an order restraining the continuance of the disciplinary proceedings. If he obtains a stay order, a wilful violation of the order would of course amount to contempt of court. In the absence of a stay order the disciplinary authority is free to exercise its lawful powers.”

These decisions indicate that though it would not be wrong in conducting two parallel proceedings, one by way of disciplinary action and the other in the criminal court, still it would be desirable to stay the domestic inquiry if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against the employee in a domestic inquiry is being tried in a criminal court. The case law was reviewed by this court in Kusheshwar Dubey v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd., [1989] 74 FJR 86, and it was laid down as under (page 89) :

“The view expressed in the three cases of this court seem to support the position that while there could be no legal bar for simultaneous proceedings being taken, yet, there may be cases where it would be appropriate to defer disciplinary proceedings awaiting disposal of the criminal case. In the latter class of cases, it would be open to the delinquent employee to seek such an order of stay or injunction from the court. Whether, in the facts and circumstances of a particular case, there should or should not be such simultaneity of the proceedings would then receive judicial consideration and the court will decide in the given circumstances of a particular case as to whether the disciplinary proceedings should be interdicted, pending criminal trial. As we have already stated, it is neither possible nor advisable to evolve a hard and fast, strait-jacket formula valid for all cases and of general application without regard to the particularities of the individual situation. For the disposal of the present case, we do not think it necessary to say anything more, particularly when we do not intend to lay down any general guideline.”

Kushal Bhan ( 1960 (I) L.L.J. 520), the concerned worker had been acquitted by the criminal Court on April 8, 1958 on the ground that the case against him was not free from doubt. The main contention before the Supreme Court was that the company was not bound to wait for the result of the criminal trial and that it would, and did, hold a fair enquiry against the respondent and if the respondent refused to participate in it and left the place where the enquiry was being held, the company could do no more than to complete it and come to such conclusion as was possible on the evidence before it. The Supreme Court said:

“It is true that very often employers stay enquiries pending the decision of the criminal trial Courts and that is fair; but we cannot say that principles of natural justice require that an employer must wait for the decision at least of the criminal trial Court before taking action against an employee. In Bimal Kanta Mukherjee v. Newman’s Printing Works (3), this was the view taken by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. This decision shows that the fact that the criminal Court acquitted the concerned employee after the domestic proceedings were completed does not mean that the order of the tribunal on the basis that the employee was guilty of the departmental delinquency complained of is liable to be set aside.

The criminal proceedings and the domestic proceedings are not based on the same set of facts. Even otherwise, assuming that both the proceedings are based on same sets of fact, in my view, there is no provision of law empowering the Court to stay the departmental proceedings merely because criminal proceedings are pending in a Criminal Court.

Where an employee is alleged to have committed an offence in assaulting an officer, in the proceedings taken by the employer taking disciplinary action against the employee, it is the duty of the employer to accept and treat as conclusive the finding of the Criminal Court which tried the offence. The employer, in such case, of course, need not wait for the decision before taking action; except in grave cases. In simple cases, he can proceed with his own domestic enquiry and decide on the disciplinary action to be taken against the employee. In a case of acquittal of the employee by the Criminal Court, the management must accept the same, otherwise his bona fides will be questioned. In such a case the Industrial Tribunal would be justified in interfering with the order of the employer terminating the services of the employee.

Therefore, the High Court cannot entertain a petition for a writ of prohibition against the employer restraining him from proceeding with a domestic enquiry on the ground that some of the witnesses proposed to be examined were police officers who would be giving evidence against the workman in the criminal case in respect of the same matter.

There is no legal bar for both criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings going on simultaneously against a Government servant. But, in certain situations, it may not be “desirable”, “advisable” or “appropriate” to proceed with the disciplinary enquiry when a criminal case is pending on identical charges. The staying of disciplinary proceedings is a matter to be determined taking into consideration all the facts and circumstances of the particular case and no hard and fast rule can be enunciated in that behalf. The only ground constituting a valid ground for staying the disciplinary proceedings is that the defence of the employee in the criminal case with charges of a grave nature and involving complicated questions of fact and law may not be prejudiced.

The law as enunciated by the Supreme Court leaves no scope for doubt that all said and done, there is no bar for simultaneous proceedings being taken against the delinquent in the form of criminal action and also disciplinary proceedings unless the charges are extremely serious and grave requiring the judicial determination in preference to the verdict in the domestic inquiry proceedings. In the instant case, even though the criminal action and disciplinary proceedings are grounded upon the same sets of fact, in my view, there is no provision of law empowering the Court to stay the departmental proceedings merely because criminal prosecution is pending in the Criminal Court.

It is well settled that criminal and disciplinary proceedings by the department are different and they are not inter-connected. The law is well settled that the inquiry officer can come to a different conclusion than arrived at by a Criminal Court and that it is immaterial whether the charges were identical or the witnesses were the same, as long as the power exercised by the Criminal Court and the inquiry under the relevant law and the service law was distinct and separate. There is no bar for holding a disciplinary proceeding during the pendency of the trial though the basis may be one and the same. It is for the disciplinary authority to decide as to whether in a given case it should keep the domestic inquiry pending till the outcome of the criminal trial or not.

It is now a settled legal principle that the domestic enquiry under the standing order and/or disciplinary proceeding under the service rule qua criminal proceeding on the identical fact situation, there is no embargo of simultaneous proceeding of both the two matters. It is also settled legal position now that the domestic enquiry and/or departmental proceeding relates to adjudication of the conduct of the workman and/or employee concerned upon being charged for misconduct on issue of factual matrix as mentioned in the article of charge, whereas in a criminal proceeding on the identical fact situation, determination and decision of the Court is to find the guilt of the person concerned in terms of the criminal offence either relating to Indian Penal Code or any other penal statute. Furthermore, it is a settled legal principle that proof of fact and the degree of such proof varies in respect of the two proceedings. In a criminal proceeding, charge is required to be proved without any doubt and strictly following the Evidence Act, whereas in a domestic enquiry and/or departmental proceed­ing preponderance of probability would suffice for determining the conduct of the delinquent. Even if in identical fact situation, it is now settled that even after acquittal of an accused from a criminal proceeding, domestic enquiry can be completed and punishment can be imposed. Hence, pendency of a criminal proceeding or adjudication of a criminal proceeding on the identical fact ipso facto will not destroy the findings of the domestic enquiry. In State Bank of India and others v. R.B. Sharma, 2004 (102) FLR 1027 (SC) the Supreme Court held—

“It is fairly well-settled position in law that on basic principles proceedings in criminal case and departmental proceedings can go on simultaneously, except where departmental proceedings and criminal case are based on the same set of facts and the evidence in both the proceedings is common.

The purpose of departmental enquiry and of prosecution are two different and distinct aspects. The criminal prosecution is launched for an offence for violation of a duty, the offender owes to the society, or for breach of which law has provided that the offender shall make satisfaction to the public. So crime is an act of commission in violation of law or omission of public duty. The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. It would, therefore, be expedient that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted and completed as expeditiously as possible. It is not, therefore, desirable to lay down any guidelines as inflexible rules in which the departmental proceedings may or may not be stayed pending trial in criminal case against the delinquent officer. Each case requires to be considered in the backdrop of its own facts and circumstances. There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry and trial of a criminal case unless the charge in the criminal trial is of grave nature involving complicated questions of fact and law. Offence generally implies infringement of public duty, as distinguished from mere private rights punishable under criminal law. When trial for criminal offence is conducted it should be in accordance with proof of the offence as per the evidence defined under the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (in short the ‘Evidence Act’). Converse is the case of departmental enquiry. The enquiry in a departmental proceedings relates to conduct or breach of duty of the delinquent officer to punish him or his misconduct defined under the relevant statutory rules or law. That the strict standard of proof or applicability of the Evidence Act stands excluded is a settled legal position. Under these circumstances, what ZX is required to be seen is whether the department enquiry would seriously prejudice the delinquent in his defence at the trial in a criminal case. It is always a question of fact to be considered in each case depending on its own facts and circumstances.”

May be, in a given case, the court may refuse to stay disciplinary proceedings. It is open to the employer to oppose granting order by a competent court staying disciplinary proceedings on all the grounds available to him. If a work­man is to be denied subsistence allowance at the rate of 75 per cent. under Section 10-A(l)(b), even in a case where he may have a legal right and a good case on merit to get order from a competent court staying domestic inquiry pending criminal trial, he may be forced to suffer in silence. During the period of suspension he has to support his family and survive to fight or defend his case. It appears reference to the delay directly attributable to the conduct of the workman in the said provision is obviously to the one where the workman unjustifiably, deliberately or designedly drags on or prolongs the domestic inquiry. To put it in other way, a workman cannot be permitted to take advantage of delay caused by himself in the absence of any order passed by a court. If such a delay is also to be taken as covered by Section 10-A(l)(b) it may amount to in a way putting restraint or clog on the exer­cise of legal right of a workman to approach a court of law out of fear of losing subsistence allowance at the rate of 75 per cent. It is one thing to say that in a given case there should be no stay of disciplinary proceedings, it is another thing to say that in case stay is granted there will be delay in completion of disciplinary proceedings, which is directly attributable to the conduct of a workman. Merely because legal pro­ceedings will be pending in a court or before other authority and they take sometime for disposal, may be inevitably, that itself cannot be the ground to deny subsistence allowance to a workman against a statutory obligation created on the employer under Section 10-A(l)(b). One must not lose sight of the fact that the Act is beneficial piece of legislation and the provision of subsistence allowance made is intended to serve a definite purpose of sustaining the workman and his family members during the bad time when he is under suspension pending inquiry. This provision is enacted with a view to ensure social welfare and security. Hence, such a beneficial piece of legislation has to be understood and construed in its proper and correct perspective so as to advance the legislative intention underlying its enactment rather than abolish it. Assuming two views are possible, the one, which is in tune with the legislative intention and furthers the same, should be preferred to the one which would frustrate it.

6. Both sides had adverted to decisions of this Court as well as the Supreme Court and I may examine the veracity of the contentions raised with reference to the decided cases.

7. One of the earlier decision, concerning the issue, is the one Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. Kushal Bhan. AIR 1960 SC 806 The Supreme Court had held that in a case where the employer refused to stay the enquiry till a decision of the Court came did not violate the principles of natural justice. It has been pointed out that in a case of grave nature or where questions of fact or law are involved, it would have been advisable for the employer to await the decision of the Trial Court, so that the defence of the employee in the criminal case may not be prejudiced.

8. I find that no absolute prohibition as such has been laid down there. As pointed out by Mr. Sen, the trend has been generally shifting against the principle that domestic enquiry proceedings are to be stayed so long as the criminal proceedings were continuing. It should have been more an exception than the rule. Advertence was made to the decision in State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena. 1996 (74) FLR 2550 (SC) The Court had held then there was no legal bar for both the proceedings to go on simultaneously. However, the desirability and advisability depended on the charges, which were being enquired into. It was further held that not only the charges must be grave, but the case must involve complicated questions of law and fact. In paragraph 14, the Court had explained the principles and had held that “one of the contending consideration is that the disciplinary enquiry cannot be and should not be delayed unduly.” The Court observed that “so far as criminal cases are concerned, it is well known that they drag on endlessly where high officials or persons holding high public offices are involved. They get bogged down on one or the other ground. They hardly ever reach a prompt conclusion.” The ultimate finding was that “stay of disciplinary proceedings cannot be, and should not be, a matter of course”. With regard to the scope of enquiry by the two authorities, light is thrown by the judgment under reference. The approach and objective in the criminal proceedings and the disciplinary proceedings is altogether distinct and different. In the disciplinary proceedings, the question is whether the respondent is guilty of such conduct as would merit his removal from service or a lesser punishment, as the case may be. In criminal proceedings, the question is as to whether in case the crime is established, what sentence should be imposed upon the person. The standard of proof, the mode of enquiry and the rules governing the enquiry and trial are different.

10. In State Bank of India and others v. R.B. Sharma, 2004 (102) FLR 1027 (SC) = 2004 (21) AIC 956 (SC) the Supreme Court held—

“It is fairly well-settled position in law that on basic principles proceedings in criminal case and departmental proceedings can go on simultaneously, except where departmental proceedings and criminal case are based on the same set of facts and the evidence in both the proceedings is common.

The purpose of departmental enquiry and of prosecution are two different and distinct aspects. The criminal prosecution is launched for an offence for violation of a duty the offender owes to the society, or for breach of which law has provided that the offender shall make satisfaction to the public. So crime is an act of commission in violation of law or omission of public duty. The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. It would, therefore, be expedient that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted and completed as expeditiously as possible. It is not, therefore, desirable to lay down any guidelines as inflexible rules in which the departmental proceedings may or may not be stayed pending trial in criminal case against the delinquent officer. Each case requires to be considered in the backdrop of its own facts and circumstances. There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry and trial of a criminal case unless the charge in the criminal trial is of grave nature involving complicated questions of fact and law. Offence generally implies infringement of public duty, as distinguished from mere private rights punishable under criminal law. When trial for criminal offence is conducted it should be in accordance with proof of the offence as per the evidence defined under the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (in short the “Evidence Act’). Converse is the case of departmental enquiry. The enquiry in a departmental proceedings relates to conduct or breach of duty of the delinquent officer to punish him or his misconduct defined under the relevant statutory rules or law. That the strict standard of proof or applicability of the Evidence Act stands excluded is a settled legal position. Under these circumstances, what ZX is required to be seen is whether the department enquiry would seriously prejudice the delinquent in his defence at the trial in a criminal case. It is always a question of fact to be considered in each case depending on its own facts and circumstances.”

11. From the aforesaid it is clear that there is no bar for simultaneous proceedings being taken against the petitioner in the form of criminal action and also the disciplinary proceedings unless the charges are extremely serious requiring judicial determination in preference to the verdict in the domestic proceedings.

12. In my view, in the present case, the criminal proceedings and the domestic proceedings are not based on the same set of facts. Even otherwise, assuming that both the proceedings are based on same sets of fact, in my view, there is no provision of law empowering the Court to stay the departmental proceedings merely because criminal proceedings are pending in a Criminal Court.

13. In my opinion, the purpose of the two proceedings are quite different. The object of the departmental proceedings is to ascertain whether the delinquent is required to be retained in service or not. On the other hand the object of criminal prosecution is to find out whether the offence in the penal statute has been made out or not. Therefore, the area covered by the two proceedings are not identical. The object in both the proceedings are different. Whereas, the departmental proceedings are taken to maintain the discipline and the efficiency in the service, the criminal proceedings are initiated to punish a person for committing an offence violating any public duty.

14. In my view, no complicated questions of fact or law are involved which requires the employee to await the decision of the Criminal Court nor any evidence has been led by the petitioner to show as to how he would be prejudiced in the continuance of the departmental proceedings.

In view of the aforesaid, I do not find it to be a fit case for interference in the domestic inquiry proceedings. Consequently, there is no merit in this petition and is dismissed without any order as to cost.

Apart from this, the Supreme Court in the case of Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., 1999 (82) FLR 627 (SC) held as under:—

“Conclusions which are deducible from various decisions of the Supreme Court (referred to in paras 14 to 22 of the judgment) on this point, are as follows: (i) Departmental proceedings and proceedings in a criminal case can proceed simultaneously as there is no bar in their being conducted simultaneously, though separately; (ii) If the departmental proceedings and the criminal case are based on identical and similar set of facts and the charge in the criminal case against the delinquent employee is of a grave nature which involves complicated questions of law and fact, it would be desirable to stay the departmental proceedings till the conclusion of the criminal case; (iii) Whether the nature of a charge in a criminal case is grave and whether complicated questions of fact and law are involved in that case, will depend upon the nature of offence, the nature of the case launched against the employee on the basis of evidence and material collected against him during investigation or as reflected in the charge-sheet; (iv) The factors mentioned at (ii) and (iii) above cannot be considered in isolation to stay the departmental proceedings but due regard has to be given to the fact that the departmental proceedings cannot be unduly delayed; (v) If the criminal case does not proceed or its disposal is being unduly delayed, the departmental proceedings, even if they were stayed on account of the pendency of the criminal case, can be resumed and proceeded with so as to conclude them at an early date.”

Applying the litmus test laid down by Supreme Court, it is crystal clear that it is not a fit case where the petitioner fulfills the aforesaid requirement. Merely because the petitioner is subjected to a criminal case as well, the department has not committed any error in conducting the departmental enquiry against the petitioner. In the opinion of this Court, there are no complicated questions of fact and law involved and therefore the department was under no obligation to stay their hands in conducting the domestic enquiry. Accordingly, this issue is also decided against the petitioner.

13. Petitioner preferred Annexures P/17 and P/19, which were rejected by the Bank by document Annexure P/20. The request of petitioner to examine the documents by a Government Expert situated at Calcutta was declined by the employer on the ground that there exists an authorised lincensed handwriting expert at Gwalior itself, who can examine the said documents. The said witness Rajiv Verma subsequently entered the witness box and produced the licence and other requisite documents, which enables him to do the same. No rule or provision has been shown by the petitioner which shows that such an action of the Bank either violates the principles of natural justice or any legal, valuable or statutory right of the petitioner is infringed. The petitioner has not assailed the genuineness of the handwriting expert, i.e., his qualification and licence etc. and, therefore, merely because the petitioner’s request for examining the documents by Government authorities is declined, I am unable to hold that the enquiry stands vitiated on this score. Accordingly, this point is also decided against the petitioner.

Mr. Menon’s argument that the Tribunal was justified in considering the merits of the dispute for itself in the present reference proceedings. Since the enquiry has been fairly conducted, and the findings recorded therein are based on evidence which is believed, there would be no justification for the Industrial Tribunal to consider the same facts for itself. Findings properly recorded at such enquiries are binding on the parties, unless, of course, it is known that the said findings are perverse, or are not based on any evidence. There is yet another point which remains to be considered. The industrial Tribunal appears to have taken the view that since criminal proceedings had been started against Raghavan, the domestic enquiry should have been stayed pending the final disposal of the said criminal proceedings. As this Court has held in the Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. Kaushal Bhan ( (1960) 3 S. C. R. 227), it is desirable that if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry is being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending the final disposal of the criminal case. It would be particularly appropriate to adopt such a course where the charge against the workman is of a grave character, because in such a case, it would be unfair to compel the workman to disclose the defence which he may take before the criminal court. But to say that domestic enquiries may be stayed pending criminal trial is very different from anything that if an employer proceeds with the domestic enquiry in spite of the fact that the criminal trial is pending, the enquiry for that reason alone is vitiated and the conclusion reached in such an enquiry is either bad in law or mala fide. In fairness, we ought to add that Mr. Menon did not seek to justify this extreme position. Therefore, we must hold that the Industrial Tribunal was in error when it characterised the result of the domestic enquiry as mala fide partly because the enquiry was not stayed pending the criminal proceedings against Raghavan. We accordingly hold that the domestic enquiry in this case was properly held and fairly conducted and the conclusions of fact reached by the Enquiry Officer are based on evidence which he accepted as true. That being so, it was not open to the Industrial Tribunal to reconsider the same questions of fact and come to a contrary conclusion.

The result is, the appeal is allowed. The order passed by the Industrial Tribunal is set aside and the reference made to it is answered in favour of the appellant. Before we part with this appeal, we ought to add that Mr. Pai for the appellant has fairly offered to pay exgratia Rs. 1,000/- to Raghavan in addition to the amount which has already been paid to him by the appellant in pursuance of the order of this Court granting stay to the appellant pending the final disposal of the present appeal. There would be no order as to costs.

Appeal allowed.

11. In HPCL v. Sarvesh Berry, (2005) 10 SCC 471 the respondent was charged with possessing assets disproportionate to his known sources of income. The question was whether disciplinary proceedings should remain stayed pending a criminal charge being examined by the competent criminal Court. Allowing the appeal of the employer-corporation this Court held:

“A crime is an act of commission in violation of law or of omission of public duty. The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. It would, therefore, be expedient that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted and completed as expeditiously as possible. It is not, therefore, desirable to lay down any guidelines as inflexible rules in which the departmental proceedings may or may not be stayed pending trial in criminal case against the delinquent officer. Each case requires to be considered in the backdrop of its own facts and circumstances. There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry and trial of a criminal case unless the charge in the criminal trial is of a grave nature involving complicated questions of fact and law..... Under these circumstances, what is required to be seen is whether the departmental enquiry would seriously prejudice the delinquent in his defence at the trial in a criminal case. It is always a question of fact to be considered in each case depending on its own facts and circumstances.”

12. It is unnecessary to multiply decisions on the subject for the legal position as emerging from the above pronouncements and the earlier pronouncements of this Court in a large number of similar cases is well settled that disciplinary proceedings and proceedings in a criminal case can proceed simultaneously in the absence of any legal bar to such simultaneity. It is also evident that while seriousness of the charge levelled against the employees is a consideration, the same is not by itself sufficient unless the case also involves complicated questions of law and fact. Even when the charge is found to be serious and complicated questions of fact and law that arise for consideration, the Court will have to keep in mind the fact that departmental proceedings cannot be suspended indefinitely or delayed unduly. In Paul Anthony (supra) this Court went a step further to hold that departmental proceedings can be resumed and proceeded even when they may have been stayed earlier in cases where the criminal trial does not make any headway. To the same effect is the decision of this Court in State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena, 1996 (74) FLR 2550 (SC) where this Court reiterated that there was no legal bar for both proceedings to go on simultaneously unless there is a likelihood of the employee suffering prejudice in the criminal trial. What is significant is that the likelihood of prejudice itself is hedged by providing that not only should the charge be grave but even the case must involve complicated questions of law and fact. Stay of proceedings at any rate cannot and should not be a matter of course. The following passage is in this regard apposite:

Criminal Court cannot be held to be conclusive. The Labour Court is not bound by the judgment of the Criminal Court. The Labour Court is not bound to direct the reinstatement of an employee into service on the sole ground of employee’s acquittal even on merits in the criminal case. It may be one of the factors to be taken into consideration in awarding appropriate punishment in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the Act. The same principle would apply to the proceedings before the disciplinary authorities.” 14. While acquittal of the workman in the criminal case may be one of the factors to be taken into consideration in awarding appropriate punishment in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, Industrial Tribunals/ Labour Courts cannot direct reinstatement solely on the ground of the workman’s acquittal in the criminal case as was done in the present case.
