In the circumstances the word ‘proceedings’ under section 442 could not be interpreted in a manner as to exclude criminal proceedings pending in a Court from its purview.

The question whether in a particular case the proceedings are to be stayed or not to be stayed is to be viewed on merit of each case. Objections to maintainability of application and jurisdiction of the Court were, therefore to be overruled. As section 442 operates during the interregnum period between presen-tation of petition and making of order of winding up and thereafter, provisions of section 446, much wider in their scope, take over undoubtedly lead to conclusion that the object of section 442 is subservient to main object of winding up proceedings, viz., to facilitate protection and realisation of company’s assets for equitable distribution amongst its creditors pari passu, in order of priorities fixed under law. Expeditious disposal of pending proceeding too is in aid of this paramount object.

The criminal proceedings are the proceedings instituted and conducted for the purpose either of preventing the commission of a crime or for fixing the guilt of a crime already committed and punishing the offender, as distinguished from a civil proceeding which is for the redress of a private injury, for the ventilation of a private right and determining the other persons’ liability on their right. If that principle is applied, ordinarily, a criminal proceeding is not one which has a bearing on the company’s civil liability having reference to the object of winding up.

As to the question whether multiple criminal proceedings would continue to be defended by the company which was declared as relief undertaking and would be contrary to the object of declaration, production under the N.I. Act, with respect to proceedings under section 138 thereof has not been provided for recovery of the sum in respect of which the cheque has been returned unpaid. That could only be enforced by pursuing proceeding in the civil court or any other civil proceedings. Thus, the prosecution under the N.I. Act is not for enforcement of liability against the company but is to fulfil the object of statute to lend impetus and credibility to banking system by enhancing acceptability of cheques as payments which is in general interest of trade and industry. Imposing punishment for an offence under section 138 is not so much for failure to pay the debt as is for affecting faith in general acceptability of cheques as mode of transacting payment through bank. In ordinary course, such proceedings cannot be said to have a bearing on the determination of the liabilities of the company nor can they affect protection or realisation of company’s assets in the event of winding up order if it is ultimately passed.

If viewed in the light of object of the BRUA, the result would not be different. The object of the BRUA may be discerned from its preamble. The object is to enable State Government to conduct or to provide loan guarantee of financial assistance for the conduct of industrial undertakings as a measure of preventing unemployment or unemployment relief. The Act is clearly a beneficial piece of legislation to enable State Government in extending temporarily financial assistance to the undertaking for the benefit of industrial workmen, who are likely to face unemployment in case the undertaking is closed, rather than as a measure of revival schemes, as is the case under Sick Industrial Companies (Special provisions) Act, 1976. The object is clearly to provide financial assistance to prevent closure of the undertaking and keep the employment going on.

Keeping in view the objective, direction too has been issued to suspend all rights, privileges, obligations and liabilities and remedies for enforcement thereof, excluding liabilities arising in relation to workers of the undertaking. A continued winding up proceeding which may culminate in closure of the undertaking may rightly come under embargo to continue with the pending proceedings or institution of new proceedings, as it directly affects the continued existence of undertaking and an order of winding up being made may cause unemployment. However, the same cannot be said about continuing with criminal proceedings under the NI Act in general. Continuance of such proceedings against the company or its officers neither affects the continued existence of the undertaking nor the interest of workers against unemployment. Moreover, the notification is only a temporary measure; the obligation and liabilities and remedies are only envisaged to be suspended for a while and not effaced.

Therefore, criminal proceedings, which do not have nexus with the object with which an undertaking is declared as ‘relief undertaking’ under the BRUA, ordinarily are not required to be stayed in aid of such declaration, if the same are not specifically directed to be stayed by the State Government and otherwise do not affect the purpose for which undertaking is declared as ‘relief undertaking’.

In the present case, as noticed above, declaration of undertaking as a relief undertaking was a temporary measure and operated for a limited period. Extension to such declaration is also envisaged only to a limited extent. The uncertainty of continued status of the undertaking as relief undertaking is not in the realm of indefinite (ness). While enforceability of civil liability is kept in abeyance during such period, the conduct of business in regular manner is not suspended. Thus continuing of proceedings in question which arose in ordinary course of conduct of business due to financial stringency, but were absolute in term and not liable to abate on payment, was not likely to affect the conduct of affairs of the company, more particularly, when on their own plea, no relief was sought to stay such proceedings against directors and proceedings against them were otherwise likely to continue.

FACT: Respondent No. 2-complainant had filed the proceedings under section 630 against the applicant/accused, seeking his eviction from the accommodation allotted to him as a condition of his service inasmuch as he was not in its service. The applicant moved an application seeking for discharge of the proceedings on the ground that his ULP complaint against the termination of his service was pending before the Labour Court. His main contention was that the proceedings under section 630 were not tenable inasmuch as a Labour Court proceedings in ULP for setting aside the relevant order of termination issued by the complainant were pending and the applicant/accused therein had claimed reinstatement by seeking quashing of the order of illegal termination. The trial Judge rejected his application, and the said order was confirmed in revision application preferred by him.

On application under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 the applicant contended that it was obligatory on the part of complainant to obtain prior permission of the Labour Court under section 33(1) of the 1947 Act before resorting to filing of the complaint under section 630.

HELD: In the instant case, the applicant/accused was claiming discharge on the ground that his proceeding challenging the termination order was pending before the Labour Court. The condition of the service of the applicant/accused which provided for allotment of quarter was perhaps on consideration of nature of his duties. Once the accused/applicant was terminated and had been issued notice to vacate the quarter, unless the stay was granted by the Labour Court or by the concerned authorities to his termination order, he would not be entitled to retain the accommodation allotted to him by virtue of his service condition. If anybody was appointed by the complainant-company in his place, that person would be entitled to residential accommodation, which obviously could not be allotted to him, had the applicant remained in possession of the same, despite his being not in the service of the company. [Para 7]

It is true that section 33(1) of the 1947 Act requires permission of the concerned Labour Court, before the service conditions of the employee are altered. But in the instant case the service condition of the applicant/accused was not changed, in fact he had been terminated. Therefore, even if it was to be assumed for a moment that he would be reinstated in future if his ULP complaint succeeded, because he was not doing at instant stage any work related to his duties, he would not be able to retain the quarter. At the most if he succeeded, he might be entitled to suitable compensation. Consequently, the proceedings under section 630 would not be bad only because the permission required under section 33(1) of the 1947 Act had not been obtained. [Para 6]

Therefore, the application was to be dismissed. [Para 9]

HELD: ■

The facts on record indicate that the Respondent had admittedly worked intermittently with the Telecommunication Department, Ulhasnagar, from 1980 onwards. His last period of engagement was from 01.08.1990 till 06.12.1992, on the Muster Roll prior to his arrest on allegation of theft. [Para 8]

■ It is undisputed that the Respondent was arrested on 06.12.1992 and he was terminated from service forthwith without any inquiry on the following day, i.e., 07.12.1992. No inquiry was conducted; principles of natural justice were not followed prior to termination. The record reflects that the Respondent workman got bail and gave letters for his reinstatement in 1992 itself, but the Petitioners ignored the same. Thereafter, he was acquitted from the criminal charge by the Competent Court on 28.04.1999 and he once again approached the Petitioners, who ignored him. [Para 9]

■

Despite the Petitioner's contentions, the Tribunal has rightly held that termination without inquiry, especially when allegations are serious and criminal proceedings are pending, is unsustainable. The obligation of the employer to hold a domestic inquiry is not dispensed with merely because a criminal prosecution is launched. The Petitioner has failed to demonstrate any compliance with the procedure under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and no material is placed before the Court to justify non-adherence thereto. [Para 10]

■

The Tribunal has also considered the Petitioner's argument regarding delay and laches. The record shows that the Respondent sent representations immediately after being released on bail and again in 1999 post his acquittal but was intentionally ignored by the Petitioner. The Union took up his cause shortly thereafter. The Court found no gross negligence or inaction on the part of the Respondent to deny relief solely on the ground of delay. On these facts, the grievance of the Petitioner on the ground of delay is unacceptable. [Para 11]

■

The argument that the Respondent was not a member of the Union which raised the dispute is also devoid of merit. It is well settled that a Union may espouse the cause of a workman even without formal membership, if done with his consent or in the larger interest of the workmen. The Tribunal has correctly applied the legal maxim of espousal and its findings are consistent with settled principles of industrial jurisprudence. [Para 12]

■

The Petitioner further contends that acquittal was not on merits but by giving him benefit of doubt, and therefore, reinstatement should not automatically follow. However, in the absence of a departmental inquiry or any evidence on record justifying termination, this Court cannot uphold the punitive action meted out by the Petitioners to the Respondent merely based on a criminal allegation which has not been substantiated. Further, the Respondent stands cleared of all charges. [Para 13]

■

The submission regarding the Respondent's employment status being "daily-rated" and hence disentitling him to relief is also rejected in view of the aforesaid findings that he admittedly worked from 1980 to 1992 with the Petitioners. The Tribunal has taken into account the pattern of the Respondent's employment and found continuity in engagement sufficient to attract the protection of the Industrial Disputes Act, which the Court is unable to dislodge. [Para 14]

■

On the basis of the above, no case is made out to interfere with the well-reasoned and cogent Award passed by the Tribunal. The Writ Petition is devoid of merit and stands dismissed. The Respondent has expired in the interregnum. Hence, under the Award, the dues would have to be paid over to Respondent Nos. 1A to 1F, equally i.e., in equal proportion, forthwith. [Para 15]

The purpose of section 279(1) of Companies Act, 2013 is to protect assets of the company, Criminal proceedings under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act [for dishonour of cheque] has no bearing on proceedings for winding up or the assets of the company. Thus, proceedings under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act cannot be stayed for want of leave of NCLT (that time company court). Criminal proceedings against directors can be launched for bouncing of cheque, even if petition for winding up has been made. - Pankaj Mehra v. State of Maharashtra 2000 AIR SCW 992 = 100 Comp Cas 917 = (2000) 2 Comp LJ 47 = 25 SCL 13 (SC) - followed in Rajiv Gupta v. State (2001) 104 Comp Cas 26 (Del HC).

Section 446 of the 1956 Act [section 279 of Companies Act, 2013] covers criminal proceedings against the company also. However, it does not bar criminal proceedings against employees of the company for criminal offences (of cheating in this case), as the proceedings cannot be said to be against the company - Gain Chand v. Amar Nath (1970) 40 Comp Cas 1158 (P&H).

Criminal proceedings against director of a company under Negotiable Instruments Act (for bouncing of cheque) are purely for punishment of person who issued the cheque. No recovery of any amount can be claimed in respect of dishonoured cheque in the criminal case. The proceedings are not against assets of the company and hence cannot be stayed - K P Devassy v. Official Liquidator (1998) 90 Comp Cas 438 = 1997(2) KLJ 243 (Ker HC) - quoted with approval and followed Jose Antony v. Official Liquidator (1998) 18 SCL 431 = 98 Comp Cas 275 (Ker HC) - confirmed in Jose Antony v. Official Liquidator (2000) 27 SCL 251 = 100 Comp Cas 811 (Ker HC DB). - followed in Rakoor Industries v. R L Bali (2002) 39 SCL 139 = 2001 DLT 478 (Del HC).

In Firth (India) Steel Co. Ltd. In re AIR 1999 Bom 75 also, it was held that criminal proceedings against company and its directors for dishonour of cheque under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act can continue without sanction of Company Court (now NCLT) - same view in Nagarjuna Finance Ltd. v. Kanosika Laboratories Ltd. (1998) 94 Comp Cas 127 (AP HC) = AIR 1998 AP 396 (AP) * GSL (India) Ltd. v. Bayer ABS Ltd. (2000) 25 SCL 285 (Guj HC) * Prehari Mutual Welfare Society (Regd) v. Gurcharan Singh (2008) 142 Comp Cas 772 (P&H HC).

In Piyush Rastogi v. Moulik Finance (2008) 86 SCL 104 (All HC), it has been held that section 446 does not apply to criminal proceedings. Hence, criminal proceedings against company as well as director can continue.

26.12-2 Criminal proceedings against directors under Income Tax Act cannot be stayed

Criminal proceedings against directors under Income Tax Act cannot be stayed under section 446 of the 1956 Act [section 279 of Companies Act, 2013]. - Rakoor Industries v. R L Bali, ITO (2002) 36 SCL 747 = 108 Comp Cas 83 = 122 Taxman 650 = 2001 DLT 478 (Del HC).

In Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. 1999 AIR SCW 4228, it was held that prosecution of directors can be sustained even if company itself is not prosecuted - or cannot be prosecuted as winding up proceedings. However, actual offence should have been committed by the company.

26.12-3 Criminal proceedings against directors under Provident Fund Act can continue

Criminal proceedings against directors and officers of a company (in liquidation) under Employees' Provident Fund Act can continue without sanction of Company Court (now NCLT) - Manekchowk & Ahmedabad Mfg. Co. Ltd., In re (1983) 53 Comp Cas 515 (Guj) * Orr Cee Electronics Ltd. v. Judicial Magistrate (1999) 34 CLA 164 (Kar).

1.40-17 At par with the directors, company employees are eligible for sweat equity shares at a discount or for a consideration other than cash for providing know-how or making available rights in the nature of intellectual property or value addition, under section 79A; and otherwise they are eligible for financial assistance by the company to acquire company’s shares as provided under section 77. The services of employees during investigation under sections 235, 237, 239 and 247 are protected against discharge or punishment by the company under section 635B by an obligation cast on the company to notify the Tribunal by previous intimation in writing for objections, and if none received within thirty days, only then can the company proceed to act as proposed by it against any employee, section 635B. Section 633 provides for relief and presumptive relief against liability for negligence, default, breach of duty, misfeasance or breach of trust when the employees had acted honestly and reasonably, subject to the condition that in a criminal proceeding the Court shall have no power to grant relief from any civil liability due to such negligence etc. The acts of employees done under the Act in good faith are protected under section 635A, and they are immune from being compelled by any Court, tribunal or authority to disclose whence they got the information furnished to the Central Government for any special audit under section 233A or investigation under section 235, 237 or 247, section 635AA, but they are liable to provide information and assistance within their control to the special auditor/inspector. Employees are liable to be prosecuted for defaults and offences against the Act, if they constitute officers who are in default in accordance with the provisions of section 5, particularly, the obligation as to disclosures on unethical market practices indulged in the company to the auditor under section 221(3). From the very beginning till its final conclusion the company court has embarked its journey on the defence taken by the appellant-company in reply to a statutory notice. What has weighed much to a company court is that such defence has been taken at a point of time when legal assistance has been rendered. The company court has proceeded on the ground that the earlier statutory notice upon which the earlier company petition was founded was not replied. It is only after the dismissal of the earlier company petition on a technical ground of service of statutory notice as by that time the advocates have intervened the reply to a subsequent statutory notice has been shown the light of the day. [Para 15]

Admittedly, the petitioning creditor could not annex a sheet of paper evidencing the service of the statutory notice upon the appellant-company in an earlier company petition. The appellant-company has categorically denied to have received any such statutory notice. If it is a specific defence taken by the appellant-company that such statutory notice has not been received and the petitioning creditor could not have proved satisfactorily that such notice has been served, there is no occasion on the part of the appellant-company to have replied to such statutory notice which has not been served upon it. [Para 16]

The company court has further proceeded that the story of issuing the debit note is not probable as audits are done at the interval of every financial year. The company court has put much stress on the fact that once having confirmed the balance, the appellant-company could not have raised any dispute as to the difference in rates of the price of the goods so sold and delivered. It is further recorded that there is no explanation forthcoming as to why such objection was raised after the confirmation of the balance. [Para 17]

Such defence cannot be said to be absolutely irrational and/or illegal and leads to the conviction without any reasonable doubt. The defence may be untenable or may not appeal to the Court as the company court or a civil court proceeds on a preponderance of an evidence unless an evidence so tendered appears to the court to be false to the knowledge of the person adducing it. [Para 18]

Merely that the defence is not found favouabe by the company court does not render such defence in falsity so that it can be tried under the criminal law. The Court must record its reasonableness as to the conviction of an offence committed by the erring litigant and it is expedient in the interest of justice that a cognizance should be taken for such an offence. [Para 26]

The defence which has been taken by the appellant-company is of such nature which makes it expedient in the interest of justice to be referred to for being tired under the criminal law. [Para 27]

The parties have settled their dispute in relation to monitory claim and as such the satisfaction of the petitioning creditor is recorded. [Para 28]

The portion of the order by which the company court directed the Registrar, original side to lodge a complaint for taking cognizance of an offence alleged to have been committed by the appellant-company is to be set aside. [Para 29]

Suspension

86. (1) An employee may be placed under suspension by the competent authority :—

(a) Where a disciplinary proceeding against him is contemplated or is pending ; or

(b) Where a case against him in respect of any criminal offence is under investigation, inquiry or trial.

(2) An employee shall be deemed to have been placed under suspension by an order of the competent authority—

(a) with effect from the date of his detention, if he is detained in custody, whether on a criminal charge or otherwise, for a period exceeding 48 hours ;

(b) with effect from the date of his conviction, if, in the event of a conviction for an offence, he is sentenced to a term of imprisonment and is forthwith not dismissed or removed or compulsorily retired consequent to such conviction.

Explanation : The period of 48 hours referred to in clause (b) of this sub-regulation shall be computed from the commencement of the imprisonment after the conviction and for that purpose, intermittent periods of imprisonment, if any, shall be taken into account.

(3) Where a penalty of dismissal, removal or compulsory retirement from service imposed upon an employee under suspension is set aside in appeal under these regulations and the case is remitted for further enquiry or action or with any other directions, the order of his suspension shall be deemed to have been continued in force on and from the date of original order of dismissal, removal or compulsory retirement and shall remain in force until further orders.

(4) Where a penalty of dismissal or removal or compulsory retirement from service imposed upon an employee is a set aside or declared or rendered void in consequence of or by a decision of a Court of Law and the Competent Authority, on a consideration of a circumstances of the case, decides to hold a further enquiry against him on the allegations on which a penalty of dismissal, removal or compulsory retirement was originally imposed, the employee shall be deemed to have been placed under suspension by the Competent Authority from the date of the original order of dismissal, removal or compulsory retirement and shall continue to remain under suspension until further orders.

(5) Provided that no such further enquiry shall be ordered unless it is intended to meet a situation where the Court has passed an order purely on technical grounds without going into the merits of the case.

Subsistence allowance

(6) An order of suspension made or deemed to have been made under this regulation may at any time be modified or revoked by the Competent Authority which made or is deemed to have made the order.

During such suspension, he shall receive subsistence allowance equal to (i) his substantive pay plus fifty percent of allowances thereon, for the first six months of suspension; and (ii) his substantive pay plus seventy-five per cent of allowances thereon for the period of suspension beyond six months.

Provided that the enhanced rate of subsistence allowance specified under sub-clause (ii) shall be admissible only if the enquiry is not delayed for reasons attributable to the concerned employee or any of his representatives.

Provided further that if no penalty under Regulation 79 is imposed, the employee shall be refunded the difference between the subsistence allowance and the emoluments which he would have received but for such suspension, for the period he was under suspension, and that, if a penalty is imposed on him under Regulation 79, no order shall be passed which shall have the effect of compelling him to refund such subsistence allowance. The period during which an employee is under suspension shall, if he is not dismissed or removed or compulsorily retired from service, be treated as period spent on duty or leave as the Competent Authority who passes the final order may direct.

The respondent-complainant filed a complaint before the Court against the appellant-company, a company under liquidation, for the commission of an offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 alleging that a cheque issued by the company towards discharge of their liability for the works done for them, was dishonoured when presented for encashment. The appellant-company filed an application before the company court requesting that the above proceedings be stayed in view of section 446. The Company court, after hearing the appellant and the official liquidator, held that section 446 could not be attracted in criminal proceedings where the assets of the company were not involved and the proceedings pending against the accused were only in respect of the commission of the offence and the punishment therefor. Accordingly, the petition was dismissed.

The assessee-firm was criminally charged for having allegedly made false entries in account books and improperly verified stocks so as to evade income-tax. The first appellate authority did not accept revenue's allegation regarding improper verification of stock whereupon revenue filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The assessee contended before the trial court that since discrepancies in the stock of assessee on basis of which prosecution was launched against it had been set aside the criminal proceedings were no longer maintainable. The trial court, accepting revenue's contention that matter was sub judice in the Tribunal, held that even if order passed by appellate authority be taken at face value, it did not in any way absolve assessee of its liability under section 276C. The assessee's revision petition against this order was dismissed.

HEADNOTE: Section 10E of the Companies Act, 1956 - Company Law Board - Powers of - Whether proceedings before Company Law Board can continue even when criminal case is pending which might have been filed by either parties against each other - Held, yes - A company petition under section 397/398 was filed against respondents - When pleadings in said petition were completed, petitioners filed a criminal case against respondents and obtained an order of investigation - Respondents filed application for stay of proceedings before CLB on ground that criminal proceedings initiated against them tantamounted to parallel proceedings - Whether since Criminal Court had not taken cognizance of offence alleged to have been committed by respondents but merely had referred complaint to police for investigation and to file a challan/charge sheet if there was evidence, there was no criminal proceeding pending so as to tantamount to a parallel proceeding as contemplated by respondents - Held, yes.

FACT: The petitioners originally filed a company petition under section 397/398 alleging oppression against the respondents. However, when the matter was listed for hearing and the petitioner had concluded his arguments, the petitioner registered a criminal case against the respondents for alleged tampering with shareholding of respondent No. 1-company and obtained an order under section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for investigation. In these circumstances, the respondents filed the instant application for stay of proceedings of the company petition on ground that the party could not adopt parallel proceedings/forum shopping to agitate its grievance. The respondents further contended that the company petition and criminal complaint being based on identical and similar facts and the nature of charge in the criminal case as filed by the petitioners being grave and because it raised complicated questions of facts and law, the company petition ought to be stayed.

HELD: The facts as contended before the CLB dealing with the criminal matter even if similar to some extent would have no bearing on the instant proceedings as the CLB can grant relief keeping the Act in mind while the Court dealing with the criminal proceedings will deal with the matter in the light of the law applicable thereto. The respondents were not entitled to copies of criminal complaint inasmuch as it is only the appropriate Court dealing with the complaint that can pass appropriate orders. In the instant case, only a complaint had been filed against some of the respondents in their individual capacity and not in the capacity as a director. Accordingly, merely for the reason that they were also parties in the present proceedings as respondents, it could not be said that the petition was against the same party or that there were any parallel proceedings. The complaint filed before the Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, was merely an allegation against the accused referred therein under section 126(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate had yet not taken cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused named therein but merely had referred the complaint to the police for investigation and to file a challan/charge sheet if there was evidence. From the above, it was clear that there was no criminal proceeding pending so as to tantamount to a parallel proceeding as contended by the respondents. The application for stay was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. [Paras 14 and 15]

On appeal: HELD: In the case at hand, as was evident, the charges levelled related to the departmental proceeding under the Act as amended from time to time. The said enactment had been enacted to make provisions for the regulation of the profession of Chartered Accountant and for that purpose to establish the Institute of Chartered Accountants. The purpose of enacting such legislation was to authorize the incorporation by a statute of an autonomous professional body. The body has been conferred the certain responsibilities. No member of the institute is entitled to practise unless he has obtained certificate of practice from the council. Certain disqualifications have been stipulated in section 8. The Legislature confers numerous functions on the council. The institute has the power to take disciplinary action against the registered Chartered Accountants. The Act also defines professional or other misconduct to include any act or omission provided in the Schedule to the Act. There is a provision for appeal. If the Act and the Schedule appended thereto are appreciated with studied scrutiny, it is quite evident that a legislative endeavour has been made to ensure high standards, confidence and integrity in the profession. Keeping in view, in fiscal matters, responsibility and sanctity attached to accounts, audit and role of a statutory auditor are the fundamental paradigms. The professional conduct stands on a different footing than a delinquent employee facing a disciplinary enquiry. Keeping the aforesaid in view, it is obligatory on the part of the court to see whether such a proceeding should be interdicted. The submission of the appellant basically conveyed that there was similarity of charges; that there were same witnesses; that the element of prejudice was involved; that if the simultaneous proceedings were continued the appellant accused in criminal trial would be compelled to disclose his defence; that the standard of proof was not the only test; that the impact of verdict in criminal proceeding on the disciplinary authority in case of acquittal would be of great magnitude; and that the direction given by the Supreme Court to conclude the trial by end of July 2011 became an additional reason on the part of the institute not to proceed with the enquiry. The submissions, in oppugnation, by the respondents were that the charges were absolutely different; that the question of fraud and cheating were not involved in the departmental enquiry; that the witnesses were few in number in the departmental proceeding; that there was a violation of accounting standards by the CA which could not be gone into in the criminal trial; that they had not functioned appositely as statutory auditors; that they had not shown due diligence and acted with gross negligence; that they had failed to obtain sufficient information and there had been material departure from the generally accepted procedure of accounting; that the direction for conclusion of trial did not help as there were number of witnesses; that the standard of proof was totally different; and that the conspiracy and other factors were not the matter in the disciplinary proceeding. Quite apart from the above, it was contended that the appellant could not take shelter under the umbrella that he had stopped practising inasmuch as the institute had no power to suspend his registration. Additionally, it was urged by the respondent that the charges levelled against appellant did not involve complex questions of law and fact and, hence, it was not desirable to invite an interdiction in exercise of the inherent jurisdiction of this Court. [Para 28]

On a perusal of the comparative chart of the charges levelled in the disciplinary proceeding and the chargesheet in the criminal proceeding, the list of witnesses, the nature of enquiry, the purpose of enquiry and arraigning the appellant as accused person in the criminal case were on a different base. The theory of prejudice that had been canvassed was not to be routinely inferred. It could not be held in the obtaining factual matrix, that participation of the appellant in the departmental enquiry would seriously prejudice the defence at the trial in the criminal case. That apart, it was not desirable to interdict in the proceeding initiated by the institute as that would be against the public interest since the Act has its rigorous technical norms and the Chartered Accountants registered with it are required to function with statutory responsibility. In addition, the charges levelled against the appellants in the departmental proceeding/the proceeding under the Act did not involve grave and complex questions of law. [Para 29]

At this juncture, a contention was canvassed that the appellant would not be able to participate in the departmental enquiry as the Supreme Court had directed the trial to proceed on day-to-day basis. The respondents fairly stated that enquiry would be fixed on such dates which would be suitable and convenient for the Chartered Accountant-appellant and he would not face any kind of difficulty on that score. [Para 30]

In the year 2000, the firm was appointed as the statutory auditors of SCSL. The statutory audits of SCSL for the years 2001 to March, 2007 were conducted and the reports were signed by the appellant. Subsequently, ‘R’ the Chairman of SCSL, in a communication sent to the Board of Directors, disclosed that the balance sheet of SCSL carried inflated (non-existent) cash and bank balances and the liability was understated. The ICAI corresponded with PW, referring to the letters of ‘R’ the Chairman of SCSL, that the said firm had failed to carry out necessary checks which were required while undertaking the audit of the financial statements and certifying the quarterly results of the company. The ICAI alleged that the firm had violated the accounting principles while auditing and certifying the accounts/quarterly results of SCSL for the aforementioned years and quarters and did not give a true and fair view of the accounts and further did not exercise due diligence and were negligent in their professional duties as statutory auditors. The ICAI treated the newspaper report as information within the meaning of section 21(2) of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 [as amended by the Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2006. Thus, PW was called upon to disclose the name or names of the member or members who was/were answerable to the allegation/s and send a copy of the aforesaid information letter along with its enclosures to the said member/members. After certain correspondence, PW replied to the ICAI stating, inter alia, that the key members included the appellant herein. PW informed that the appellant had been arrested by the local police for committing offences punishable under sections 409, 420, 468, 471, 477A, 201 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. At this juncture, the Director (Discipline) of ICAI placed a prima facie opinion before the disciplinary committee and the committee was of the prima facie view that the said chartered accountants including the appellant were guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of clauses (5), (6), (7), (8) and (9) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Act. A prima facie opinion was also formed that the said chartered accountants were guilty of other misconduct within the meaning of section 22, read with section 21 of the Act. On the basis of the said prima facie opinion, a notice was sent to the chartered accountants enclosing a copy of the prima facie opinion and requiring each of them to send their written statement along with supporting documents. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court contending that disciplinary proceedings against him should be deferred since the alleged acts of commission or omission on the basis of which the disciplinary proceedings had commenced not only formed the basis of a prima facie opinion but also form the basis of various charges against him in the criminal cases and, hence, any disclosure of his explanation or defences until the final conclusion of the criminal trial pending before the Special Court would seriously impact his defence in the criminal trial.

It was further contended before the Single Judge that the charge sheet in the criminal case and the prima facie opinion formed by the Director (Discipline), ICAI were more or less identical and the list of witnesses in both the proceedings were same and if they were allowed to continue simultaneously, serious prejudice would be caused to him as his defence would be disclosed. The Single Judge taking a view that the appellant failed to make out a case for stay of disciplinary proceedings pending the conclusion of the criminal trial, dismissed the petition.

SCC ONLINE SC 1335 regarding 'res judicata' was not applicable, since the Hon'ble Supreme Court was dealing with a situation where the labour Court found the findings of the Industrial Tribunal to be incorrect when the Industrial Tribunal was superior to the labour Court and Industrial Tribunal had decided the application under Section 33 (2) (b) of the Act, whereas the Deputy Commissioner of Labour is only a quasi judicial authority and not superior to the labour Court. [Para 15]

■ The Deputy Commissioner of Labour in a petition filed seeking approval under Section 33 (2) (b) of the Act has discussed in detail the allegations made, nature of evidence adduced and also concluded regarding the facts of the case having discussed the evidence elaborately. However, contrary to the finding of the labour Court in the impugned order, evidence was not adduced. The understanding of the labour Court that both parties have let in evidence before the Deputy Commissioner of Labour is incorrect. There is no provision under the Act which enables the workman or the Management to file an appeal before the Industrial Tribunal questioning the refusal or acceptance of an approval application. However, an Industrial Dispute can be filed by the workman in case of any punishment imposed by employer, including an order of dismissal. The approval granted under 33 (2) (b) of the Act by the Deputy Commissioner would only ensure mandatory compliance of seeking an 'approval', however, such determination will not finally conclude about the validity of the dismissal of the workman. If 'approval' is refused, dismissal would stand ineffective from its inception. As already stated, once the dismissal is approved, workman can approach the labour Court by filing an Industrial Dispute. [Para 16]

■

A common preliminary issue before the labour Court in any Industrial Dispute would be to look into whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper. If the labour Court finds that enquiry was held to be defective, the management/employer should be given an opportunity to adduce evidence before the labour Court to justify the correctness of the domestic enquiry and also the dismissal. [Para 17]

■

A reading of the above state Amendment, Section 4 of the Act and also Rule 64 of the Tamil Nadu Industrial Disputes Rules, 1958, it can be said that a Conciliation Officer while considering the Approval Petition filed under Section 33 (2) (b) of the Act may summon any witness and examine and also compel production of documents. However, in so far as the duty imposed on the Conciliation Officer regarding the Approval Petition made under Section 33 (2) (b) of the Act, powers to examine the witness or cause production of a document can only be confined to the parameters laid down by the Supreme Court in Lalla Ram (supra), as extracted supra. The Conciliation Officer in the present case erred in discussing the evidence and drawing his own conclusion regarding charges on the basis of the evidence. The said procedure adopted is wholly unwarranted and not approved under any Statute. [Para 20]

■

The Conciliation Officer - II, who is an 'authority' to determine "Approval Application" made under Section 33 (2) (b) can only confine his enquiry to examine whether there is legal evidence, whether a prima facie case was made out and whether the employer acted bona fide and there was no victimisation. The Conciliation Officer - II has not recorded any evidence but has re-appreciated the evidence of allegations adduced during the course of domestic enquiry, which approach is incorrect. The labour Court should recognise that the proceedings before the Conciliation Officer - II, though not a judicial proceedings but the Conciliation Officer was exercising a valid statutory jurisdiction to grant or refuse approval. The labour Court is at liberty to disagree with the conclusions drawn in the Approval proceedings however cannot treat such Approval proceedings as being without jurisdiction or as nullity. [Para 21]

■

In view of the discussion made and peculiar circumstances of the present case, the labour Court cannot decide the issue regarding the correctness of domestic enquiry as though sitting in an appeal against the approval by the Conciliation Officer. If the labour Court prima facie finds that prejudice was caused to the employee for the reason of domestic enquiry not being carried out in accordance with law, grant permission to the Management to let in evidence to establish that the domestic enquiry was conducted properly. [Para 22]

■

For the said reason, the impugned order dated 9/10/2024 passed by the Presiding Officer, Second Additional Labour Court, Chennai, is set aside and the writ petition is allowed. The labour Court shall proceed as directed above. No costs. Consequently, connected Miscellaneous Petition is closed. . [Para 23]

■ The Division Bench judgment in Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation v. B.H. Satfale (1980 Mh.L.J. 197) explains that object of Section 33(2)(b) is to shield employee against possible victimisation because he has raised industrial dispute pending before legal forum. Legislature was faced with two realities. On one side, worker should not suffer retaliation because he invoked industrial proceedings. On the other side, employer cannot be rendered helpless even in genuine misconduct cases. Section 33 therefore creates middle path. It does not prohibit dismissal in every case. It regulates it through conditions. [Para 25]

In the present matter, company has contended that once references were settled, insistence upon approval under Section 33(2)(b) would be technical requirement. According to company, if no dispute survived, then no prejudice could be caused to workman and no purpose remains in demanding approval. Statutory consequences cannot be determined merely by convenience of one party. Where Legislature has used defined expressions regarding pendency and conclusion of proceedings, Court must first examine statutory language, scheme and binding precedent. Therefore, contention cannot be accepted merely because it appears pragmatic. [Para 26]

The judgment of Supreme Court in Grindlays Bank Limited v. Central Government Industrial Tribunal (1980 (Supp) SCC 420; 1980 taxmann.com 1237 (SC)) gives authoritative interpretation to Section 20(3) of the Act. It has been held therein that proceedings before Tribunal are deemed to continue until date on which award becomes enforceable under Section 17A. Such enforceability arises after expiry of thirty days from publication of award under Section 17. Till that point, Tribunal retains jurisdiction over dispute and may entertain applications connected with same. This principle clarifies that pendency under Industrial Disputes Act is not exhausted because award is pronounced. The Act creates further statutory period during which proceeding continues. Thus, pendency has wider meaning. [Para 27]

■

Therefore, where award recording settlement, disposal or other closure has been made, legal pendency under Section 20(3) does not vanish because parties may feel that dispute has ended. Once Legislature has said that proceeding shall be deemed to continue till certain stage, Court cannot shorten such period. [Para 28]

Reliance was placed by company upon principle that legal fiction cannot be extended beyond purpose for which it is created, as observed in Sanjay V Redkar v. State of Goa (2020 (4) Mh.L.J. 242). There can be no quarrel with that proposition. It is settled principle that deeming clause must not be enlarged beyond legislative object. Yet, said principle does not advance respondent's case here. In present matter, Court is not stretching fiction. Court is only applying Section 20(3) for purpose for which it was enacted, namely deciding when proceedings commence and when they legally conclude. [Para 29]

Once it is held that proceedings were pending in eye of law on relevant date, compliance with Section 33(2)(b) became obligatory if employer intended to dismiss workman for misconduct not connected with dispute. Requirement of approval allows competent authority to see whether action is bona fide, whether it is colourable exercise of power, whether one month wages are paid, whether procedure is followed, and whether dismissal is being used as weapon against workman. Such scrutiny is part of legislative protection. [Para 30]

The dispute arose from an incident at Borjan Tea Estate in March 2007 when around 1,500 workers gathered at the factory gate; some forcefully entered, damaged office property, pelted stones, and the Manager sustained injuries, following which the Estate remained under lockout for 11 days. Eleven workmen were charge-sheeted for forming an unlawful assembly, instigating violence and damage to garden property, with alleged loss of about Rs. 19.66 lakhs, and were charged with gross misconduct under the Estate Standing Orders. The workmen denied involvement; the gateman stated the gate was broken by some workers after overpowering him. Separate domestic enquiries were conducted against each of the 11 workmen and enquiry reports held them guilty of gross misconduct. The management issued notices seeking representations; after time extension, no representations were submitted, and the workmen were dismissed from service, the Reference later describing dismissal as with effect from 10.09.2007.

■

Following the dismissal, the Government of Assam referred the dispute to the Labour Court, Dibrugarh, on whether the management was justified in dismissing the 11 named workmen and, if not, whether they were entitled to reinstatement with back wages. In its written statement, the management relied on the domestic enquiries as the basis for dismissal and reserved the right to adduce evidence on merits if the enquiries were found violative of natural justice. The workmen, in their written statement, asserted that the enquiries were not impartial, that they were denied opportunity to adduce defence evidence, and that the Presenting Officer for the management also acted as a witness; they denied instigating or participating in the violence.

■

The Labour Court proceeded to record evidence without first framing a preliminary issue on the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries. The proceedings initially went ex parte against the workmen; the management submitted evidence-in-chief and later stated it would not adduce further evidence. Management witnesses were cross-examined and the workmen also adduced evidence. The Enquiry Officer (examined as M.W. 4) stated in cross-examination that although workmen were informed of the enquiry and to participate, he did not inform them that they were required to adduce evidence, stating that the Presenting Officer would inform them. The records of the domestic enquiries were not placed before the Labour Court. The Head Clerk (examined as M.W. 2), whose evidence had formed the basis of the domestic findings, admitted in cross-examination that he did not remember the names of the workers involved in the incident. The enquiry reports recorded that the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt and did not give reasons for proceeding only against these 11 workmen.

■

By Award dated 29.02.2016 in Reference Case No. 02/2009, the Labour Court upheld the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries and, on that basis, upheld the dismissal of the workmen; no separate finding on proportionality of the punishment was recorded.

The law declared in the case of Shambu Nath Goyal v. Bank of Baroda (supra) was affirmed by the Constitution Bench in the case of Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation v. Smt. Lakshmidevamma (supra). The judgment of the Constitution Bench was based upon three opinions of the Hon'ble Judges. One opinion was of His Lordship N. Santosh Hegde, J. (as His Lordship then was) wherein the opinion rendered in Shambu Nath Goyal v. Bank of Baroda (supra) was maintained taking into account that the law as declared by the Supreme Court in the case of Shambu Nath Goyal v. Bank of Baroda (supra) was holding the field for 18 years. However, it is very interesting to take note of that in the opinion rendered by His Lordship N. Santosh Hegde, J., it was observed at paragraph No.17 of the report that the judgment in the case of Shambu Nath Goyal v. Bank of Baroda (supra) need not be varied as it was just and fair in as much as there can be no complaint from the Management side for this procedure because this opportunity of leading evidence is being sought by the Management only as an alternative plea and not as an admission of illegality in the domestic enquiry. [Para 22]

■

In the instant case, as would be seen that it is not the case of the Management of the Respondent No.2 that there was any domestic enquiry carried out. In fact, it is also not the case of the Petitioner that there was any domestic enquiry carried out. Therefore, the question of the Management of the Respondent No.2 to take an alternative plea in the present case do not arise. [Para 23]

■

This Court further finds it pertinent to take note of the concurring opinion of His Lordship Shivaraj V. Patil, J. (as His Lordship then was) wherein it was observed that though the Management has to seek leave of the Court/Tribunal in the written statement itself to lead additional evidence to support its action in the alternative, and without prejudice to its rights and contention, but the said observation so made in the majority opinion opined by His Lordship N. Santosh Hegde J. should not be understood as placing fetters on the powers of the Court or Tribunal requiring or directing the parties to lead additional evidence including production of documents at any stage of the proceedings before they are concluded if on facts and circumstances of this case, it is deemed just necessary in the interest of justice. [Para 24]

■

In the backdrop of the above, if this Court duly takes note of the order dated 19.05.2016 which has been reproduced in the previous segments of the instant judgment, it would be seen that the learned Labour Court had permitted the Management to adduce evidence. Further to that, as there was no reliance on any domestic enquiry being carried out by the Management, the question of seeking leave as an alternative plea to adduce evidence did not arise. [Para 25]

■

From the above law so declared by the Supreme Court and if applied to the facts of the instant case, it would be seen that the principles of law in the case of Shambhu Nath Goyal v. Bank of Baroda (supra) as well as Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation v. Smt. Lakshmidevamma (supra) cannot be applied to the facts of the instant case in as much as the Management of the Respondent No.2 neither relied upon any domestic enquiry nor sought for filing of evidence as an alternative. In this regard, this Court finds it very pertinent to take note of a judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Regional Manager v. Pawan Kumar Dubey (1976) 3 SCC 334 wherein the Supreme Court observed that one additional or a different fact can make a world of a difference between conclusions in two cases even when the same principles are applied in each case to the similar facts. [Para 26]

■

Taking into account the above, this Court is of the opinion that the impugned order dated 25.07.2016 requires no interference, more so in exercise of the certiorari jurisdiction of this Court which can only be exercised when the jurisdiction is being exercised in a palpably erroneous manner or when an authority having no jurisdiction has exercised such jurisdiction, which is not the present case. [Para 27]

In order to arrive at an appropriate conclusion, what is also to be kept in perspective is that undisputedly the parties are already before the Arbitrator in respect of the very same transaction. The legal position, no doubt is clear that if adequate material is available on record to indicate that the respondent company is unable to pay its debts, the winding petition will not be barred merely because of the pendency of any other proceeding. In the instant case, firstly it is a winding up petition filed against the guarantor company and not against the borrower company. Even though, in law the creditor would have the option of proceeding against the guarantor, the question raised is as to the very validity of the guarantee said to have been executed. In fact, that is also an issue raised in the Arbitration proceedings between the same parties, to which the borrower company is also a party. [Para 16]

The claim petition filed before Justice Dr. B.P. Saraf is to the objection statement and the respondents are the respondents Nos. 3 to 5 therein. The same was filed during July 2009. The common written statement is filed by the respondents to the said claim petition. In the said written statement the contention relating to the collusion in bringing about the documents of guarantee has been exhaustively urged. The written statement is dated 11-2-2010. It is true that these winding up petitions have been filed on 5-10-2009, which is marginally prior to the date on which the written statement was filed in the Arbitration case and a stand had been taken before the Arbitrator, but the notice of these petitions was served only during January 2010. The stand taken in the Arbitration case is very proximate to the date when the instant petition was filed and notice was served. Therefore it cannot be concluded that the contention put forth in the objection statement to these petitions has been urged for the first time and in such event the legal notice not being replied along cannot be the basis to raise the presumption of inability to pay the debts in the instant facts.

That apart, though after lapse of sometime, the respondents have initiated criminal complaint and the same has been referred for investigation, the fact which cannot be ignored is that the respondents have not barely raised the defense, but are pursuing their legal remedies before the appropriate forum. [Para 17]

The above noticed aspects will disclose that the defense has not been taken for the sake of defense in the objection statement so as to consider it as moonshine or frivolous defense though the Court at this stage cannot also accept the same to be correct, but there can be no denial of the fact that the issues raised are substantial and would go to the root of the matter in so far as invoking the corporate guarantee. The nature of contentions will indicate that the Court can neither accept nor reject it on the face of it. The resolution of such disputed questions will require adjudication based on evidence, but as held by the Supreme Court, the Court while acting as the Company Court is not expected to hold a full trial of the matter. [Para 18]

In the instant case, in any event the parties are already before the appropriate forum raising the same issues and the adjudication therein will settle these issues, which if held against the respondent company and at that stage if it is shown that they are unable to repay their debts, certainly the petition can be entertained at that stage, but as of now, the substantial issues raised will weigh in favour of the respondent to secure adjudication of the same in the forum where it is pending and that aspect cannot be decided at this stage based on the averments made in the petition and the objection statement. [Para 19]

Hence, at this stage, there is no reason to admit these petitions. The parties would have the liberty of having the dispute relating to the validity of the execution of the guarantee, adjudicated in the pending Arbitration. [Para 20]

Thus, the petitions are dismissed. [Para 21]

[2011] 2 taxmann.com 1125 (Allahabad)[17-02-2011] PURVANCHAL VIDYUT VITRAN NIGAM LTD., VARANASI and another vs. It has been held by the Supreme Court in several authorities including the following that if the only defect in the termination order of a workman is non compliance of section 25-F of Industrial Dispu

Commission passed an order allowing the application to be proceeded with, such prosecution ought to be stayed until such time as a final order was passed by the Settlement Commission under section 245D(4). The question assumes importance for the reason that in such cases, the Settlement Commission has necessary jurisdiction under section 245H to grant immunity to the assessee from prosecution for any offence under the Act or under the Indian Penal Code, 1860 or under any other Central Act for the time being in force. In the light of the judgment of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.N. Bhattachargee [1979] 118 ITR 461/ 1 Taxman 348 , the Settlement Commission is required to exercise its power of immunising against criminal prosecution by using its power only sparingly and in deserving cases. There is, therefore, no ground to believe that if the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with, it shall grant as a matter of course immunity from criminal prosecution to the applicant under section 245H. The power to grant such immunity is dependent upon the satisfaction of the Settlement Commission that the applicant has co-operated with the Settlement Commission in the proceeding before it and has made a full and true disclosure of his income and the manner in which such income has been derived. Thus, a mere expectation of success in some proceeding or appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of institution of criminal proceedings under sections 276C and 277. If a criminal prosecution has been validly instituted, it is in the interest of justice that the trial of the case should be concluded as early as possible. Thus, the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal (First ITO) [1984] 149 ITR 696/19 Taxman 1 after observing that "it may be that in an appropriate case, a criminal court may adjourn or postpone the hearing of a criminal case in exercise of its discretionary power under section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the disposal of any proceeding under the Act which has a bearing on the proceedings before it is imminent so that it may take also into consideration the order to be passed therein," had also taken care to make a further observation that "Even here the discretion should be exercised judicially and in such a way as not to frustrate the object of the criminal proceedings." The Apex Court then went on to emphasise that "There is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a criminal court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of a case before it indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceeding which may have some bearing on it is pending elsewhere. The principle laid down by the Apex Court in P. Jayappan’s case (supra) in another context is also applicable in the matter of staying criminal proceedings pending before the criminal court, which has been validly instituted and where on the application of the assessee, the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with but has not yet passed any final orders including an order granting or refusing immunity from the criminal prosecution. A blanket order staying criminal proceedings only because the Settlement Commission has allowed an application before it to be proceeded with and the Commission has the necessary authority under the Act to grant immunity from criminal prosecution is also not necessary in the interest of justice. If any such proceeding is decided in favour of the applicant and immunity from criminal prosecution is granted, he can take advantage of any such decision even after his conviction before the appellate or the revisional Court or before the Supreme Court in an application under article 136 for special leave to appeal. The process of criminal law including the trial, appeal and revision is a protracted one and it is difficult to visualise a situation where the Settlement Commission in a particular case shall take such a long time for disposing of the application and in granting immunity from criminal prosecution that the accused shall have lost all opportunities to take benefit of such an order granting immunity even before the appellate or the revisional Court.

On overall analysis of the intent of Article 311(2), it is vivid that an employee holding a post in Union or State ought not to be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to the one by which he was appointed. It is further specified that a person shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank after an inquiry supplying the charges if any against him and giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges. The applicability of the said clause is restricted in a situation wherein his conduct led to his conviction of criminal charges or where the authority empowered who dismissed, removed or reduced in rank records reason in writing upon satisfaction that it is not 'reasonably practicable' to hold an enquiry against him. In addition, where such power has been exercised by the President or the Governor it may be in the interest of security of the State or if not expedient to hold such an enquiry, then exceptional power under clause (c) of second proviso to Article 311 ought to be exercised. [Para 40]

■

In case such a decision invoking the extraordinary power is taken by the competent authority in light of the judgment Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel 1985 taxmann.com 1415 (SC)/(1985) 3 SCC 398 within the parameter as discussed, the scope of judicial review is available to the Constitutional Courts wherein the reasons as assigned for satisfaction of the authority must be reasonable, valid, justified and in writing. In addition, the satisfaction as recorded must be the objective satisfaction on the basis of material brought on record which ordinarily the disciplinary authority may take as a prudent person. Otherwise, dispensing with the enquiry is not permissible in law. In the present case, Section 21 of the 1978 Act confers power of punishment and Section 22 prescribes the procedure for awarding such punishment. The procedure as contemplated has been elaborated under the 1980 Rules. In the present case, in the Court’s view, the power exercised by the authority is completely without application of mind, thus, the question of recording of satisfaction as affirmed by the appellate authority, the CAT and the High Court does not arise. Therefore, it can be held that the order dispensing with the regular procedure of inquiry is arbitrary and consequently the order of dismissal of the appellant is liable to be quashed and the orders of the CAT and the High Court affirming the said dismissal order stand set aside. [Para 41]

■

In light of the above discussion, the irresistible conclusion is to set aside the order passed by the CAT and the High Court and to quash the order of dismissal passed by the DCP and confirmed by the appellate authority. In consequence, the appellant shall forthwith be reinstated with continuity of service. He shall be entitled for all consequential benefits notionally. Since, the appellant is found involved in a criminal case, therefore, in the facts of the case, back wages from the date of dismissal till reinstatement are restricted to 50%. [Para 42]

■

The setting aside of the order passed under Article 311(2) proviso (b) of the Constitution and direction for reinstatement shall be without prejudice to the right of the respondent to take recourse as permissible by initiating a departmental enquiry in accordance with law. Accordingly, and with the aforesaid directions, the present appeal stands allowed to the extent indicated. Parties to bear their own costs. [Para 43]

In conclusion, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, provides a clear and workable framework for employers and workers to deal with situations of lay-off, retrenchment, and closure. The Code requires employers to carefully assess applicability thresholds, follow prescribed procedures, obtain prior approvals where mandated, and ensure timely payment of statutory compensation. Any deviation from these requirements can result in the action being treated as illegal, exposing employers to penal consequences.

At the same time, the Code protects workers by ensuring continuity of service during lay-off, fair compensation, advance notice, and safeguards against arbitrary termination or closure. Overall, the Code encourages lawful, disciplined, and balanced handling of workforce adjustments in line with business needs and worker welfare.

4.5 Illegality of Strikes and Lockouts:

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 22 or 23 of the Act.

4.5-1. When continuation of a strike or lock-out is not deemed illegal If a strike or lock-out relating to an industrial dispute has already commenced and is in existence at the time of reference of the dispute to the Board, a labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal, its continuance shall not be deemed illegal. The only condition is that the strike or lock-out was legal when it began and has not been prohibited.

4.5-2. Legality of strikes or lock-outs declared in consequence of illegality

A lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out must not be considered illegal.

4.5-2-1 Whether a lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike is automatically illegal?

The Supreme Court in Indian Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. & Another v. Their Workmen (1958 AIR 130, 1958 SCR 667), noted that a lock-out was declared in consequence of repeated illegal strikes by the workmen. The Supreme Court held that the lockout was lawful and that the lockout notice, stating that employees' services "shall be deemed to be discharged," meant a temporary refusal to employ, not a permanent dismissal.

The intention was not termination, but rather the suspension of services due to work disruption. Workers who reported within an extended period retained the right to resume work unconditionally. Further, the Court emphasised that Industrial Tribunals have limited scope to interfere in disciplinary actions and may intervene only where the action is malafide, constitutes unfair labour practice, violates principles of natural justice or is based on findings not supported by material.

2. Jurisdiction of Writ Courts:

On perusal of the provisions contained in the earlier act, it may be noted that an exemption was granted to cases pending before High Courts or Supreme Court, but no such exemption has been provided for under the IBC. The issue was discussed in Canara Bank v. Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd.9. The appellant (i.e. the creditor) submitted that the adjudicating authority cannot exclude any court from the purview of moratorium for the purpose of recovery of amount or execution of any judgment or decree, including the proceeding, if any, pending before the High Courts and the Supreme Court of India against a corporate debtor.

The NCLAT acknowledged that clause (a) of Section 14(1) specifically does not exclude any Court, including the High Courts or even the Apex Court. However, the Hon'ble Bench there are certain constitutional provisions which must be considered. There is no provision to file any money suit or suit for recovery before the Supreme Court except under Article 131 of the Constitution; some High Courts have original jurisdiction to entertain the suits, which may include money suit or suit for recovery of money. However, the writ jurisdiction conferred on the Supreme Court and the High Court under Article 32 and Article 226 of Constitution of India, being a constitutional power, cannot be curtailed by any provision of an Act or court. Therefore, 'moratorium' will not affect any suit or case pending under Article 32 or 226. However, so far as suit, if filed before any High Court under original jurisdiction which is a money suit or suit for recovery, against the corporate debtor such suit will be covered by the bar imposed under Section 33(5).

3. Criminal Proceedings:

In criminal proceedings, particularly in the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the directors or officers in default, as the case may be, are generally held personally liable, as against the civil liability of the company. The company and its directors cannot shirk their criminal liability merely on the ground that the company was already wound up and the liquidator had taken charge of the affairs of the company.

Upholding the principle laid down by the Kerala High Court in Jose Antony Kakkad v. Official Liquidator10, in Counter Point Advt. P. Ltd., Rep. by its Director, Mr. Naresh Purushotham v. Harita Finance Limited, Rep. by its Special Legal Assistant, Miss. Gulzar Sayeeda [2006] 133 Comp Cas 435 (Mad.)11, the Madras High Court observed that:

"Though the words 'legal proceedings' in Section 446 of the Companies Act is wide enough to be taken in criminal proceedings also, such criminal proceedings must be in relation to the assets of the company. Criminal proceedings which are not in respect of the assets of the company but which end in the conviction or acquittal of the accused, cannot be stayed under Section 446 of the Companies Act. Proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, can end only in the conviction or acquittal of the accused in the case and no recovery of any amount covered by the dishonoured cheques can be made in the criminal proceedings. As the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are not in respect of the assets of the company, the proceedings pending in the criminal Courts cannot be stayed under Section 446 of the Companies Act."

3.5 Whether Criminal Liability can be initiated against the new management for the offence committed by the assessee company

The Madras High Court in Vasan Healthcare (P.) Ltd. v. DIT (Investigation) [2024] 159 taxmann.com 135 has held that where the assessee-company had gone into the hands of new management pursuant to the order passed by NCLT, new management apart from not taking criminal liability could not be made to undergo criminal prosecution for an offence committed by persons who were in charge of company during the relevant point of time

The High Court relied on the Apex Court's judgment in Ajay Kumar Radheyshyam Goenka v. Tourism Finance Corporation of India Ltd. [2023] 148 taxmann.com 280/178 SCL 401 . Held that criminal prosecution cannot be made to the new management

Brief summary of the case

The present quash petitions have been filed by the new management on the grounds that as per 32A of IBC, the liability of A1 company completely gets wiped off after the resolution plan is approved by the NCLT. Therefore, the prosecution as against A1 company cannot be continued. A further stand has been taken to the effect that the criminal prosecution cannot be proceeded against the new management which has taken over A1 company. It is clear from the above that the criminal liability of a company cannot be transferred to another company or the new management ipso facto. the Supreme Court revisited the nature of Section 138 proceedings and questioned the basis of the reasoning adopted in P. Mohanraj (supra). The Court observed the 2 tier aspects of Section 138 proceeding, i.e. (a) compensatory aspect, and (b) a criminal aspect. This led the Court to raise a significant question as to if the moratorium is intended to protect the debtor's assets and therefore affects the recovery aspect, should it also stop the criminal prosecution? It is important to note here that the difference between the two judgments is not about who can be prosecuted. Both judgments recognise that directors and other persons in charge of the company can continue to face proceedings under the NI Act. The real issue is whether the moratorium should stop a Section 138 case against the corporate debtor itself merely because the proceeding also involves recovery of money.

Therefore, the key question before the larger Bench is whether Section 138 proceedings should be stayed completely during the moratorium, as held in P. Mohanraj (supra), or whether only the compensatory aspect should be affected while the criminal prosecution continues, as suggested in Dineshchand Surana (supra).

If the larger Bench agrees with the view expressed in Dineshchand Surana (supra), criminal prosecution under Section 138 may continue against the CD, even during the moratorium, while only the recovery or compensation aspect will be subject to moratorium. Even then, the authors are of the view, given that a corporate entity cannot be imprisoned; the impact would be limited to imposition of fine; and then, it might involve questions surrounding vicarious liability on the directors, etc. and the effect of section 14 on such fines. The decision of the larger Bench will therefore be crucial in determining how the objectives of the IBC will be aligned with the consequences under NI Act.

State [1990] 68 Comp. Cas. 482 (Cal.); T.N.V. Nanjappa Chettiar v. Devi Films (P.) Ltd. [1993] 76 Comp. Cas. 875 (Mad.); Kannankandi Gopal Krishna Nair v. Prakash Chunder Juneja [1994] 81 Comp. Cas. 104 (Bom.). However, the offence under section 630(1)(b) was held to be complete when committed but not a continuing offence for purposes of limitation in B.R. Herman & Mohatta India Ltd. v. Ashok Rai [1984] 55 Comp. Cas. 61 (Delhi); whereas the occupant after committing the offence was held to be a trespasser-in-occupation which is a continuing offence in Beguram v. Jaipur Udyog Ltd. [1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 744 (Raj.), and Petlad Bulakhidas Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat (1998) 31 CLA 45/18 SCL 438 (Guj.). The trial of offence is not a proceeding under the Companies Act, it is a proceeding under the Code of Criminal Procedure, Hindustan Biologicals Ltd. v. Jagat Narain Rohtagi [1953] 23 Comp. Cas. 58 (All.).

26.26-8-2 LIMITATION - The limitation for filing complaint under section 630 is three years - B.R. Herman & Mohatta India Ltd. v. Ashok Rai [1984] 55 Comp. Cas. 61 (Delhi).

26.26-8-3 JURISDICTION - The offence of wrongful withholding of property is committed where premises is situated, and as such the court, within whose jurisdiction the premises is situated falls, is the court having jurisdiction to try the offence, and the situation of head office of the company is not relevant, Vijai Kapur v. Guest Keen Williams Ltd. [1995] 83 Comp. Cas. 339 (Cal.). The place of cause of action must be specifically mentioned in the complaint which alone matters for deciding the jurisdiction of the court and in the event of a failure to do so, the Magistrate has no jurisdiction to try the case, Cap. M. Gopalakrishnan v. Leafin India Ltd. [1995] 83 Comp. Cas. 351 (Mad.). Pendency of conciliation proceedings under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, whether initiated before or after the launch of prosecution under section 630, is no bar to the jurisdiction of the criminal court, Mohd. Zameel Hussain v. Asstt. Labour Commissioner [2000] 27 SCL 343 (MP). Section 41 of Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882 has no application to suits or proceedings for recovery of possession of immovable property to which section 630 applies, Manohar Gunaji Anubhawne v. State of Maharashtra [2004] 52 SCL 536 (Bom.). Civil suit by company is no bar for criminal prosecution under section 630, Maratt Rubber Ltd. v. J.K. Maratukalam [2001] 32 SCL 171 (SC); Manas Kumar Ghosh v. T.T. P. Mahmood [2000] 27 SCL 281 (Cal.).

On a complaint under section 630, it was contended that when the debit note was created by the company, it could not be said that he was withholding the company’s assets: held that lawful possession on issue of the debit note turned into unlawful for non-payment - Satwant Singh v. Bharati Mobinet Ltd. [2004] 55 SCL 667 (Mad.).
