39.3

INVESTIGATION

Investigation of company can be carried out in one of following situations-

Order by Central Government - Central Government may order investigation into affairs of the company in following situations - (a) On receipt of report from Registrar or inspector under section 208 of Companies Act, 2013 (b) On intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company be investigated (c) In public interest - section 210(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 235(1) of the 1956 Act].

Central Government shall order investigation into affairs of the company if order is passed by a Court or NCLT in any proceedings before it - section 210(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Order by NCLT on application from members - Section 213 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and is effective w.e.f. 1-6-2016.

NCLT can order investigation in specified cases.

Such order can be passed by NCLT only after giving reasonable opportunity of being heard to the concerned parties.

Security from applicants - Central Government (presently CLB) may require appellants to provide security upto Rs. 25,000 towards cost of investigation. The security will be refunded if investigation results in prosecution - section 214 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 236 of the 1956 Act]

Applicability of provisions to foreign company - The provisions of investigation apply to foreign company also [section 228 of Companies Act, 2013].

Procedure for making application before NCLT - An application under section 213 of Companies Act, 2013 may be made in Form NCLT.1. The application shall be accompanied with such documents as are mentioned in Annexure B of NCLT Rules - Rule 80 of NCLT Rules, 2016.

39.3-1 Investigation cannot be ordered lightly

In Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. SD Agarwal 39 Comp Cas 781 = AIR 1969 SC 707 = (1969) 1 SCC 325 = (1969) 1 Comp LJ 350 = (1969) 3 SCR 108 (SC 3 member bench), it was held that standard required under section 237(b) is that of an expert and not of an ordinary citizen. An investigation may seriously damage the company and should not be ordered without proper material. Investigation is a serious matter. It should not be ordered except for good and satisfactory grounds. - . - Opinion formed by Government (for ordering investigation) is not amenable to review by Courts, but whether circumstances existed [as prescribed under section 237(b)] can be examined by Court.

39.3-2 Appointment of Inspector

Central Government can appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and report to Central Government - section 210(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 235(1) of the 1956 Act].

If such report is on basis of request of company by special resolution, then security will have to be deposited by company (between Rs 10,000 to Rs 25,000) If investigation results in prosecution, the security will be refunded - Rule 5 of Companies (Inspection, Investigation and Inquiry) Rules, 2014.

Only an individual can be appointed as inspector. A firm or company or association cannot be appointed as inspector - section 215 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 238 of the 1956 Act].

Such inspector may or may not be Government employee.

39.3-3 Investigation once continued cannot be stopped

Once investigation is ordered, the investigation can continue even if (a) special resolution for voluntary winding up is passed or (b) petition for oppression and mismanagement has been made under section 241 of Companies Act, 2013 or (c) any other proceeding for winding up is made before NCLT - section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 250A of the 1956 Act].

If winding up of company is ordered by NCLT, inspector shall inform NCLT about pending investigation - first proviso to section 226 of Companies Act, 2013.

Irrespective of any winding up order, the director or other employee is still required to participate in proceedings before inspector or any liability as a result of findings of the inspector - second proviso to section 226 of Companies Act, 2013.

In conclusion, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, provides a clear and workable framework for employers and workers to deal with situations of lay-off, retrenchment, and closure. The Code requires employers to carefully assess applicability thresholds, follow prescribed procedures, obtain prior approvals where mandated, and ensure timely payment of statutory compensation. Any deviation from these requirements can result in the action being treated as illegal, exposing employers to penal consequences.

From the above case law, it is abundantly clear that the company has to ensure compliance in all stages i.e. right from the incorporation till the company is finally liquidated through the corporate insolvency resolutions process during which time the powers of the board of directors of the company stands suspended and such power is vested with the resolution professional / liquidator. By taking over, they became the officer in default and assumed the responsibility of ensuring compliance. Even though the company has gone into liquidation mode, the earlier management had been relieved from their responsibilities, still, for the non-compliance, the Liquidator and the Resolution Professional both were identified as defaulters for the required compliance of filing annual returns and annual financial statements and accordingly the Registrar of Companies penalized them.

In conclusion, we can say that the company is required to ensure all the required compliance at all stages till it is finally closed down and the person whosoever is responsible including Liquidator and Resolution professional have to ensure absolute compliance at all stages and at all time in order to avoid the penal actions from the regulators.

Enquiry - Nature determines whether discharge punitive

In order to determine whether the discharge is punitive in nature, it is necessary to ascertain firstly the nature of the enquiry, i.e., whether the termination is preceded by full scale formal enquiry into allegations involving misconduct on the part of the employee, which culminated in the finding of guilt, and secondly, the ‘purpose of enquiry’, i.e., whether the purpose of enquiry is to find out any misconduct on his part or it is aimed at finding out as to the employee being unlikely to prove efficient. Thus, the principle that in order to determine whether the misconduct is motive or foundation of order of termination, the test to be applied is to ask the question as to what was the ‘object of enquiry’. If an enquiry or an assessment is done with the object of finding out any misconduct on the part of the employee and for that reason his services are terminated, then it would be punitive in nature. On the other hand, if such an enquiry or an assessment is aimed at determining the suitability of an employee for a particular job, such termination would be termination simplicitor and not punitive in nature [State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh (2004) 23 ILD 23 (SC)]

Abstract

Liability of corporate entities arising from the offence committed by it discourages the bidders and resolution applicant from taking control over the company. It ultimately defeats the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process which aims at reviving the company. It is quintessential to ensure that maximum safeguard are introduced to keep the process viable and not to render hinder the process by any means. This paper attempts to highlight the intent with which Section 32A has been incorporated into the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and the legal and economic issues which flows therefrom.

Introduction

Section 32A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (hereinafter 'the Code') deals with Liability for prior offences creates a statutory fiction which provides immunity to the corporate debtor from any prosecution or any action against the property under the resolution plan under section 31 of the Code or in liquidation on the condition that there is change in the management taking place. Earlier there was no provision in the code which provide for such express immunity, this amendment is introduced into the Code only by way of Second Amendment Bill, 2019.

Background

Initially, Section 32A of the Code was introduced as an ordinance by President of India by exercising the power vested by virtue of Article 123 of the Constitution of India as the Parliament was not in session. Owing to strong objection against the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Second Amendment) Bill, 2019 by the Opposition Party on various grounds like bill was circulated without giving two days' advance notice, lack of information to all the MPs and on the merits of the bill and its aftermath on the economy.

It was referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee headed by Mr. Jayant Sinha, Former Minister of State of Finance and Dr. Manmohan Singh, Former Prime Minister of India to examine and submit its report within period of 3 months. After having introducing the bill in the Winter Session, it was again introduced in the Budget Session of the Parliament along with the report of the committee. The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on Mar 06, 2020 while the Rajya Sabha passed the on Mar 12, 2020 through voice vote. Lastly, Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Second Amendment) Bill, 2019 was incorporated into the Code when it received president's assent and notified in the official gazette on Mar 13, 2020.

Position Prior to Promulgation of the Section 32A

The classical approach which has been followed by various tribunal and court across the country is that the moratorium doesn't affect the on-going criminal proceedings and hence, criminal proceedings can be continued simultaneously with the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (hereinafter 'CIRP'). The researcher believes it is correct approach in light of the purpose with which penal statues are enacted and object which these statues seek to achieve.

In the case of Shah Bros. Ispat (P.) Ltd. v. P. Mohanraj,1 wherein question before tribunal regarding the applicability of Section 14 (Moratorium) of the Code to the criminal proceeding, in particular to the criminal proceeding under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Appellate tribunal took the view that the Moratorium under section 14 wouldn't be applicable to criminal proceeding.

The similar view has been reiterated by the NCLAT in the case of Varrsana Ispat Ltd. v. Dy. Director, Directorate of Enforcement,2 wherein the Appellate tribunal took the view that the Moratorium under section 14 of the Code cannot be said to have made applicable to the penal action or criminal proceeding and even to action pursued are of criminal nature and in essence deals with some crime proceeds. Furthermore, the Appellate Tribunal observed that the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (hereinafter 'PMLA') was enacted with the object of preventing the money laundering and provided for confiscation of the property and matters incidental thereto which reflects that such proceedings is criminal in nature and hence cannot be immuned under section 14 of the Code.

Moreover, even in the case of Rotomac Global (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. Director, Directorate of Enforcement,3 the Appellate tribunal relied on the Varrsana Ispat, took the view that the Moratorium imposed under section 14 of the Code doesn't prohibit or stays the proceedings undertaken by the Directorate Enforcement for it being criminal proceeding in nature.

In this case, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal ("NCLAT") held that Section 14 is not applicable to the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act ("NI Act") as they are criminal proceedings. In crux, the NCLAT held that Section 14 of the IBC does not affect any criminal proceedings. Hence, even during the moratorium, criminal proceedings could be instituted or continued against the corporate debtor. However, the introduction of Section 32A effectively nullifies the exception created for criminal cases under Section 14 of the IBC by Shah Brothers Ispat, as there is a complete cessation of corporate debtor's liability in cases wherein under an approved Resolution Plan, the Corporate Debtor is taken over by a new Company and management. Thus, once the CIRP culminates in an approved resolution plan, there can neither be institution nor continuation of criminal proceedings against the Corporate Debtor for the offences committed by it prior to the commencement of the CIRP.

Conclusion

From the perspective of companies dealing with the takeover of corporate debtors, the amendment is completely secures the Resolution Applicants as it ensures that the previous liability of the Corporate Debtors does not interfere with either the operations or the assets of the Corporate Debtor as taken over by an approved Resolution Plan thereby smoothing the entire takeover process. However, to understand and implement the amended provision in its letter and spirit, it would be pertinent to clarify certain parts in the provision which the amendment brings about. The aim should not be to let off those involved in the offences, but merely to proceed against them in a more just manner, so as to ensure that genuine parties interested in the resolution of the corporate debtor do not face any difficulties that were not envisaged.

The moratorium under the Code also applies to the SARAFESI Act. Thus, if there is any pending matter on enforcement of security interest created upon the Corporate debtor, then that matter has to be suspended during the moratorium period.25 But in the case of Canara Bank v. Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd.26 the said provision has been multiple time questioned. The issue of whether the moratorium granted under Section 14 of the Code extends to proceedings and suits pending before various High Courts and Supreme Court? To answer this question two broad proposition were given. First, the powers of the Supreme Court and High Court cannot be curtailed under Articles 32 and 136 of the Supreme Court and of High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution, by any provision of the Code.27 Second, once the moratorium is declared under this Code than any proceedings or suit in respect to the recovery of assets should be stayed under the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court or High Courts. The allowance to such suits will create hindrances to the reviving process of corporate defaulters and will end up tarnishing the essence of the Code. Furthermore, it is a well settled principle that the meanings of suit and proceeding as per the definition are taken in their general sense. Suit refers to the proceedings which are non-criminal and is only curial in nature28 and for the purpose of stay does not include execution proceedings.29

Thus there is an exception to this rule, which lies in matters of writ petition and criminal matters, as these matters involve criminal actions against the company and its directors and more importantly involve public interest, so such proceedings will not be barred upon commencement of the moratorium period.30 Similarly, a proceeding to assess or determine liability, and a proceeding to recover the assessed or determined liability31 will not be barred under it.

Before the Principle bench of the NCLAT, a very interesting question was raised wherein the bench had to decide whether the proceedings under the Sec. 138of Negotiable Instruments Act, which provides punishment of imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of cheque or with both, be covered under the provisions of the moratorium.32 As the primary objective of the Code is the revival and rejuvenation and the bench had to take into consideration the impact of such fines on the financial stability of the corporate debtor, but the bench considered the impact of criminal actions on the rem and held that "Section 138 is a penal provision, which empowers the court of competent jurisdiction to pass order of imprisonment or fine, which cannot be held to be proceeding or any judgment or decree of money claim. Imposition of fine cannot held to be a money claim or recovery against the Corporate Debtor nor order of imprisonment, if passed by the court of competent jurisdiction on the Directors, they cannot come within the purview of Section 14. In fact, no criminal proceeding is covered under Section 14 of I&B Code."33

Thus, the objective of the moratorium to protect and provide the corporate debtors with a breathing space is only restricted to the scope of civil suits and no such support or protection will be given under the Code, whenever there is any matter of public interest or when the criminal acts of such debtors affect the public at large.

Overriding Clause

Overriding clauses have always been a point of conflict between various provisions and the overriding clause in the Code. Section 238 under the Code is no different and has also been a hot topic as it not only results into a conflict of application of other Laws but is also backed by a moratorium.

In the landmark case of Innoventive Industries v. ICICI Bank,34 the Supreme Court affirmed, that Sec.107 under the Government of India Act, 1935 is in substance reproduction of Article 254 of the Constitution, with one difference that the power of Parliament under Article 254(2) goes to the extent of repealing a State law and affirmed again that under Article 254 of the Constitution of India, the State law in contravention with any Central Law can be repealed.35 Apart from applying the doctrine of repugnancy in the present matter, the Supreme Court highlighted the fact that contours of Section 238 of the Code which is the non-obstante clause are broader than the objective of state legislation.

The same contention was also affirmed in the case of Jotun India Private Ltd. v. Psl Ltd.36 wherein it was held that provisions of the Code will have an overriding effect even over the Companies Act, 2013 and the argument that winding-up petitions were already filed before the High Court does not bar the remedy to file fresh proceedings under the Code, the Hon'ble Court referred to the judgement in Madura Coats Ltd. v. Modi Rubber Ltd. which had held SICA's primacy over the Companies Act37, since the Code has replaced SICA, it will enjoy the same relationship with the Companies Act.

PROBLEMS WITH THE EXISTING JURISPRUDENCE

The most debatable topic since ages is whether a company can be made criminally liable. One might say imposition of fines is way of punishing a corporation, but that hardly resulted in any deterrence in the crimes by corporations. The main problem is the so called statutory inadequacy. And if one says lifting of corporate veil is a solution, there are again difficulties in identifying to whom exactly the evil intent belonged to. And in large companies it is impossible for the shareholders to control the management and directors, and therefore cannot be made liable.

The major problem is, though the definition of a 'person' includes a company, it is not possible to imprison a company being a juristic person. The courts find a dead end in cases where a corporation is charged under provisions providing for mandatory imprisonment as it cannot be imprisoned. The temporary solutions that courts have come up is to make companies liable for greater amounts fines. Also, there are problems in holding the agents liable, such as, identifying who controlling person was; do all the concerned staff have the same state of mind. In Moore v. Bresler Ltd.,34 an employee whose duty was to pay tax had not performed duty resulting in the guilt of the company, wherein the court stated that such act should be attributed to company irrespective of the fact that it was done to conceal his theft from the company. However the appellate court reverse the decision by holding that the sales were not made by them on behalf of the corporation but rather in fraud of the company itself. In India it is considered that knowledge is a pre-requisite before holding a company liable. This shows the attitude of Indian Criminal Law towards corporate crimes.

Another question which arises in the concept of CCL is the punishment. Can a corporation be imprisoned? The punishments which may be imposed to a corporation are imposing fine, forfeiture of its properties and cancelling of its license. In Northern Star Mining Corporation Ltd. case35, a company was prosecuted for manslaughter which was criticized to be inadequate. Again in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. J.B. Company,36 where the court held that company is not an exception to criminal law and that it could be tried for an offence for which imprisonment is the prescribed punishment, but will be fined.

CONCLUSION

Earlier, the concept of a separate legal entity of a company and of corporate veil created by statutory provisions, has been exploited to a great extent by individuals in order to evade personal liability, which lead to a well-established law worldwide, that a company can be made liable for criminal offences irrespective of looking into whether it had an evil intent or not. Though the laws in India are not developed as that of other countries for making a corporation completely liable, but it had to an extent developed the law through its judicial pronouncements. In spite of this, India has not gone beyond imposing of fines and forfeiture of property of a company, which mean that the laws in India are insufficient to deal with the present day cases.

2.2 Prior Permission for Closure in case of larger undertakings (Section 80) An employer intending to close down an undertaking of an industrial establishment employing 300 or more workers must apply electronically or otherwise in the prescribed manner (As per Draft Rules, 2020, an application for permission must be made in Form X) to the appropriate Government for prior permission at least 90 days before the intended closure.

The application must clearly state the reasons for the intended closure, and a copy of the application must be served simultaneously on representatives of workers in the prescribed manner.

However, this requirement does not apply to undertakings set up for the construction of buildings, bridges, roads, canals, dams or for other construction work.

2.3 Government decision to grant or refuse to grant permission for Closure

The appropriate Government, after making an enquiry as it thinks fit and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the employer, workers, and persons interested in closure, may, by order, grant or refuse to grant permission for closure. A copy of the order must be communicated to the employer and the workers.

If the appropriate Government does not communicate the order granting or refusing permission to the employer within 60 days from the date of application, the permission shall be deemed to have been granted, and the application shall be disposed of accordingly.

Further, the order of the appropriate Government must be final and binding on all the parties and must remain in force for one year from the date of such order.

2.3-1 Whether the power of the Government to deny permission for closure is absolute?

The Supreme Court in Orissa Textile & Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa [2002] 2 SCC 578, held that the Government's power to refuse permission for closure of an undertaking must be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances.

Such refusal is justified only where compelling or overriding reasons exist or where the public interest so demands, for instance, where the establishment is engaged in manufacturing life-saving vaccines or drugs during a prevailing epidemic, or products essential for the defence of India.

2.4 Power of Review or Reference to Tribunal for adjudication

The appropriate Government may, suo motu or on an application by the employer or worker, review its order granting or refusing permission within the prescribed time (As per Draft Rules, 2020, the prescribed time is within 30 days from the date on which the order is made) or refer the matter to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal must pass the award within 30 days from the date of such reference.

2.5 Consequences of Illegal Closure

Where an employer fails to apply for prior permission for closure within the prescribed period or where the permission for closure has been refused, the closure of the undertaking shall be deemed illegal from the date it takes effect. In such circumstances, the workers are entitled to all benefits available under the applicable law as if the undertaking had not been closed down.

2.6 Exemption from Prior Permission Requirement in certain exceptional cases

The appropriate Government may, in certain exceptional cases, such as an accident in the undertaking, the death of the employer, or similar situations, by order direct that no prior permission for the closure of the undertaking is required.

2.7 Compensation payable to workers upon permitted or deemed closure

Where an undertaking is permitted to be closed down or where the permission for closure is deemed to be granted, every worker employed immediately before the date of the application for permission must be entitled to receive compensation.

The compensation payable must be:

(a)

equivalent to 15 days' average pay or

(b)

Average pay of such other number of days as may be notified by the appropriate Government, for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of 6 months.

2.7-1 Whether closure of undertaking amounts to retrenchment of workers?

No, the Supreme Court in S.G. Chemicals & Dyes Trading Employees' Union v. S.G. Chemicals & Dyes Trading Ltd. [1986] 2 SCC 624, clarified that the closure of an undertaking is distinct from retrenchment. Retrenchment means reducing surplus staff in an ongoing business and not ending the entire business.

v. Insolvency and Bankruptcy Issues

Recently the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was passed in 2016. So, here the issue is under Section 29A(d) of the code which provides an eligibility criteria for the purpose of the resolution applicant i.e., a "person or a connected persons" for the resolution application should not be convicted for an offence with imprisonment more than 2 years. So, whether the section is applicable to the corporation and can make company criminally liable. The issue was raised in a recent judgment Renaissance steel ltd. v. Electro steel India Ltd26 where the company Vedanta Ltd is a successful bidder in the resolution process of the insolvent company belonged to Electro steels.

The allegations was that the one of the connected persons namely Konala Copper Mines of Vedanta company was imprisoned for more than 3 years under Zambia laws and paid fine of certain amount. The Electro steels approached NCLAT (National Company Law Appellate Tribunal) under Section 29A (d). The tribunal dismissed the appeal upholding that the Section 29A (d) applies only to natural persons and not to legal persons and the conviction talks about the imprisonment where we cannot imprison the company. Hence the court concluded that the body corporate is outside the preview of Section29A (d) of IBC to make them criminally liable.

ATTACHMENT OF CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY TO A CORPORATION

i. Strict Liability

Under this concept, a person shall be made legally responsible for the concerns of his acts even in the absence of guilty mind or criminal intention. Examples of some criminal offences which do not require mens rea are rape, murder, vehicular offences. In US, the rule followed is that whenever a particular legislation does not specify mens rea as an essential, it is deems that mental intent need not be prove in such offence, and hence treated it as strict liability.

In Indianapolis Water Co. v. American Strawboard Co.,27 court held that mere omission, irrespective of mens rea of defaulter, is sufficient to constitute crime.

ii. Vicarious Liability

The maxim qui facit per alium per se explains the concept better, which means, one who does an act through another is deemed to do it by himself. Similarly, under the concept of vicarious liability, one is made responsible for any act or omission of another. The reason here is the presumption that master is aware of what his servant is doing and that the servant is always deemed to act on behalf of and on the directions of the master. In Commonwealth,28 the court made the people acting on behalf of 3 companies liable for its activities by stating that CCL is necessarily vicarious because company is a legal fiction which is comprised of individuals alone.

30.15-1 Earlier, under section 442 power was vested in the High Court to stay suits and proceedings or restrain further proceedings in the suits or proceedings at the instance of any creditor or contributory at any time after presentation of the petition for winding up and before a winding up order is made, only for that interim period, because once the winding up order is made-section 446 providing for same on its making-will become applicable, but with the omission of the section 442 by the Second Amendment Act, 2002 (not yet notified), this power is no longer available to the Tribunal, which means that the suits and proceedings shall continue until making of the winding up order by the Tribunal.

Relief Undertakings Act and Stay

30.15-2 However, it would appear that the stay of proceedings notified in exercise of statutory power under a State legislation like Relief Undertakings Act having overriding efficacy would be effective and the Tribunal would be bound, having regard to the decision in Jaysinth Dyechem v. Mewar Textile Mills Ltd. AIR 1988 Raj. 16, that such a notification is constitutional and not repugnant.

Tribunal’s powers [Sections 443 & 444]

30.15-3 Further, sections 443 and 444 dealing with the powers of Tribunal on hearing petition and its duty to communicate the order when made to the Official Liquidator, have been substituted in their entirety - only to substitute ‘Tribunal’ for ‘Court’ - by the said Act. Accordingly, on hearing a winding up petition, the Tribunal may, at par with the High Court earlier,

u (a ) dismiss the petition with or without costs,

u (b) adjourn the hearing conditionally or unconditionally, (for example, where family disputes over property ownership exist, Shivraj Gupta v. Hansraj Gupta & Co. (P.) Ltd. [1987] 2 Comp. LJ 74 (Delhi),

u (c) make any interim order that it thinks fit (like the appointment of an interim-Administrator to take charge of the company’s affairs pending a decision), or

u (d) make an order for winding up the company with or without costs, or any other order that it thinks fit, such that the Tribunal shall not refuse to make a winding up order on the ground only that the assets of the company have been mortgaged to an amount equal or in excess, or that the company has no assets.

Petition on ‘just & equitable’ ground

30.15-4 In respect of a petition for winding up on the ‘just and equitable’ ground, the Tribunal may refuse to make an order for winding up, if it is of the opinion that some other remedy is available to the petitioners and that they are acting unreasonably in seeking to have the company wound up instead of pursuing that other remedy.

Default of delivering statutory report as a ground

30.15-5 Further, in the case of a petition for winding up on the ground of default in delivering the statutory report to the Registrar, or in holding the statutory meeting, the Tribunal may-instead of making the winding up order-(a) direct that the statutory report shall be delivered or the statutory meeting held, and (b) order the costs to be paid by any persons who, in the opinion of the Tribunal, are responsible for the default.

Workers’ right to present petition for winding up

30.15-6 In National Textile Workers’ Union v. P.R. Ramakrishnan AIR 1983 SC 75, it was held that though the workers have no statutory right to present a winding up petition, they are entitled to be heard of their interest as interveners but not as parties in a winding up petition, and particularly so because the winding up order after it attains finality the workers have no scope to participate in the further proceedings, except by appealing against the winding up order under section 483.

Case Studies

1. The Company has received a Show Cause Notice during the year 2022-23 from Initiating Officer for holding a benami property and alleging that company is only a shell company and its properties are held by it as benamidar for the real person controlling the company who has channeled his ill gotten funds into the company as share capital through a network of benami shell companies. The alleged benami properties were acquired prior to 25-10-2016. The Company contends that auditor need not report on this as company has sent reply with all details and, in view of Supreme Court judgment in Ganapati Dealcom, the IO will drop proceedings. Proceedings have not been dropped at the time of audit reporting. Company also contends that ARI disclosures are not required in view of the Supreme Court decision. How will you as auditor deal with this?

Auditor is not to sit in judgment on the merits of the case. For auditor, all that matters is that the proceedings are initiated during the year and are pending as of the date of audit report. Therefore, he needs to report the fact of initiation and pendency of the same. Company may disclose its opinion on the merits of the case in notes to financial statements while giving required ARI disclosures.

2. If in Case Study 1, what if, prior to date of audit report, the proceedings are dropped by IO after considering the reply of the Company ?

In that case also, auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings were initiated and subsequently dropped. The wordings in clause 3(i)(e) are "proceedings have been initiated or are pending against the company". Therefore, in view of the word "or" separating the words "initiated" and "are pending", auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings have been initiated during year and dropped after the year-end but prior to date of audit reporting.

3. What if show cause notice dated 1st April 2023 from Initiating Officer is received on 5th April 2023 and audit report is being signed on 30th April 2023? Will auditor have to report it in audit report for FY 2022-23?

No. Auditor will not report this in Audit report for the year under audit i.e. FY 2022-23. Auditor will report it in his report for FY 2023-24.

Audit report for the year is on events during the year. Post-balance sheet date developments in respect of such events which have occurred during the year will be considered. It is one thing that Show Cause Notice is issued during the year and there are further developments after the year-end in the matter which will have to be considered.

It is entirely a different matter that Show Cause Notice is issued and received after the year-end which has nothing to do with conditions existing as at the Balance sheet date. Auditor will not consider such post-balance sheet events in report for the year under audit.

PROTECTION OF EMPLOYEES DURING INVESTIGATION

An employee of company who has disclosed information during investigation is protected against dismissal, discharge or removal or change in terms of his employment to his disadvantage, during investigation, without permission of NCLT [earlier CLB upto 1-6-2016]

39.5-1 Protection to legal advisers and Bankers

A legal adviser cannot be compelled to supply privileged communication except name and address of his client. A banker has to disclose information about the company or the person under investigation but not of any other customer - section 227 of Companies Act, 2013. [corresponding to section 251 of the 1956 Act].

39.5-2 Freezing of assets of company on inquiry and investigation

Central Government can make application to NCLT for freezing of assets, funds and properties of the company, if there is reasonable ground to believe that removal or transfer or disposal of funds, assets or properties of company is likely to take place in manner prejudicial to interests of company or its shareholders or creditors or in public interest. Such order can be for period upto three years - section 221(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

If despite such order, there is removal or transfer of disposal of assets, company as well as every officer who is in default is liable for punishment of fine and imprisonment - section 221(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

The section 221 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and is effective from 1-6-2016.

39.5-3 Source of information need not be disclosed

Often investigation is carried out on basis of some secret information. To protect the informant, it has been provided that Registrar or officer of Government or any other person shall not be compelled to disclose to Court, Tribunal or other authority, where he got information which has led Central Government to order special audit or order an investigation - section 457 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 635AA of the 1956 Act].

Court in Crompton Greaves Ltd. v. Workmen (AIR 1978 SC 1489) observed that a strike is a legal weapon available to workers. However, its justification depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The Court clarified that even an illegal strike may be justified in rare situations, while a legal strike may still be unjustified if the conduct of workers is unreasonable.

3.1-2. Whether a lockout is the same as the closure of operations? The Supreme Court in Management of Express Newspapers Ltd. v. Workers & Staff Employed Under it (AIR 1963 SC 569) clarified that a lockout is not the same as a closure. A lockout refers to the temporary closing of the place of employment, the suspension of work, or the employer's refusal to employ workers during an industrial dispute. A closure, on the other hand, refers to the permanent shutdown of business operations. Unlike a lockout, a closure signifies the end of business itself, not just the temporary suspension of operations.

Further, in Management of Kairbetta Estate v. Rajamanickam (AIR 1960 SC 893), the Supreme Court elaborated on the distinction between a lock-out and a lay-off. The Court held that a layoff arises when ongoing operations exist but workers cannot be given work due to reasons beyond the employer's control, while a lockout involves a temporary suspension of operations by the employer. In this case, a justified lockout in response to workers' violence cannot be treated as a layoff, and thus, the workers were not entitled to layoff compensation.

3.2 Prohibition on Strikes and Lockouts:

The provisions relating to the prohibition on strikes and lockouts are as follows:

3.2-1 Prohibition on Strikes

No person employed in an industrial establishment must go on strike, in breach of contract, in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving the employer a notice of strike within 60 days before striking or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of strike specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.2-2 Prohibition on Lockouts

No employer of an industrial establishment must lock out any of his workers in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving a notice of lock-out within 60 days before locking out or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of lock-out specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.3 Exemption from notice requirement in case of existing strike or lockout:

The notice of strike or lockout must not be necessary where a strike or lockout is already in existence. However, the employer must send intimation of such lock-out or strike on the day on which it is declared to such authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government, either generally or for a particular area or for a particular class of services.

3.4 Reporting Requirements for Strikes and Lockout Notices:

If on any day, an employer receives from any person employed by him, any notice or gives to any person employed by him, any notice of strike or lock-out, he must report it within 5 days to the appropriate Government or to such authority as the Government may prescribe and to the conciliation officer, specifying the number of notices received or issued on that day.

3.5 Illegality of Strikes and Lockouts:

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 62 or continued in violation of an order made under Section 42(7) of the Code.

3.5-1. When continuation of a strike or lock-out is not deemed illegal

If a strike or lock-out relating to an industrial dispute has already commenced and is in existence at the time an application is filed before the Tribunal or when the dispute is referred to an arbitrator or the National Industrial Tribunal, its continuance shall not be deemed illegal. The only condition is that the strike or lock-out was legal when it began and has not been prohibited.

3.5-2. Legality of strikes or lock-outs declared in consequence of illegality

A lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out must not be considered illegal.

Intent behind Incorporation of Section 32A of the Code

Insolvency Law committee recommended incorporation of this provision submitted in February 2020.5 It was incorporated keeping in mind the difficulty faced by the successful resolution applicants imposing the restrictions and liabilities on corporate debtor. In is emphasised by the Insolvency Law committee that this provision has been included to absolve the corporate debtor from the offences committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP unless they resolution applicant is also involved or related party to promoter group.

Parliamentary Standing Committee under the chairmanship of by Mr. Jayant Sinha, Former Minister of State of Finance in its report submitted on March 2020.6 The committee rendered its opinion in favour of incorporation of Section 32A into the Code with a view to safeguard the position of the resolution applicant from the offence the former promoters. Such an observation keeping in mind the necessity of cleansed entity where the change in management of the corporate debtor has taken place.

Pre-Condition to the Applicability of Section 32A

In order to discourage the abuse of this provision, safeguard has been introduced by way of pre-condition which need to be satisfied before resorting to Section 32A are:-

The resolution applicant is not involved or related party to promoter group,

The resolution plan results in control of corporate debtor or change in the management.

Liability for the Offence Committed Prior to the Commencement of CIRP

As a result of incorporation of Section 32A of the Code, the corporate debtor shall cease to responsible for the offence committed prior to the commencement of CIRP and the property of corporate debtor which are part of resolution plan, no action can be taken against those property.

However, it is clarified the ambit of the Section 32A is very limited in terms of liability and it doesn't immune or absolve the person who are:-

responsible for the activities of the corporate debtor in conduct of business,

officer in default

directly or indirectly involved in the commission of the offence

All the above mentioned person shall continue to remain liable for the offence committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP. Furthermore there is also no bar against the property other than property of corporate debtor and the person who has acquired that property under the liquidation or CIRP, as the case may be.

Conundrum Continues

Promulgation of Section 32A in the Code has lot of implication and its position is not very in this regard. Various relevant legal issues time and again has come before the Appellate Tribunal and High Courts for consideration and these issues need to be redressed as they core to the application of Section 32A.

The question of interpretation of Section 32A came up before the Appellate tribunal in the case of JSW Steel Ltd. v. Mahendra Kumar Khandelwal., 7 wherein the Appellate tribunal held that the Section 32A is retrospectively applicable and also set aside all the attachments of the corporate debtor made by Enforcement Department under PMLA. However, it wasn't clarified whether it is also applicable to the proceedings which have already been concluded and no adjudication is pending w.r.t. corporate debtor however they satisfies the parameters laid down in the Section 32A of the Code.

In the case of Tata Steel BSL Ltd v. Union of India,8 wherein summon issued before the incorporation of Section32A into the Code by the Investigating officer was under challenge. The Delhi HC ruled that the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under section 32A of the Code as the instant case falls within the clear language used in Section 32A and hence corporate debtor cannot be made responsible for the offence committed prior to commencement of CIRP even when the resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority, when it is expressly prohibited by the provision. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner was upheld and liable to be discharged in the merits of the case.

5. Comparative Study

A comparative overview is as follows:

| S. No. | Key Changes | Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 | Industrial Relations Code, 2020 | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. | Definitions | Section 2(q) defines the term 'Strike' and Section 2(l) defines the term 'Lockout' | Section 2(zk) defines the term 'Strike' and Section 2(u) defines the term 'Lockout' | The Code broadens the concept of strike to cover mass casual leave movements often used to circumvent legal restrictions on strikes. |
| 2. | Notice Period for Strike/Lockout | Section 22(1) – Six weeks' notice required; strike not to commence within 14 days of giving notice Section 22(2) – Similar provisions for lockouts | Section 62(1) & (2) – Notice period extended to 60 days before strike/lockout; cannot commence within 14 days of notice | The extension from 6 weeks to 60 days provides a longer window for conciliation and negotiation, allowing parties and authorities to intervene before a shutdown occurs. |
| 3. | Restrictions during proceedings | Section 23 – Prohibition during pendency of conciliation, arbitration or tribunal proceedings and for 2 months thereafter. | Section 62(d) –(f) – Prohibition continues during pendency and extends for 60 days after conclusion of proceedings. | The Code maintains the spirit of the Industrial Dispute Act but standardises the post-proceeding restriction to 60 days across forums. |
| 4. | Exemption from notice | Section 22(3) - Notice is not required if a strike/lockout already exists; the employer must intimate the Government Authority. | Section 63(2) – Similar provision retained; intimation on the day of declaration to the prescribed authority. | The code clarifies the timing and responsibility of intimation, making it obligatory for employers to report on the day of declaration. |
| 5. | Reporting obligation to Government | Section 22(6) – Employer must report notice of strike/lockout within 5 days to the appropriate Government. | Section 62(6) – Employer must report notice of strike/lockout within 5 days to the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer. | The change broadens the reporting requirement by mandating employers to submit the notice of strike/lockout not only to the appropriate Government but also to the conciliation officer. This enhances transparency and strengthens early dispute-resolution mechanisms. |
| 6. | Illegality of Strikes/Lockouts | Section 24 – A strike or lockout is illegal if commenced in contravention of Section 22 or 23 of the Act or continued despite prohibition orders. | Section 63 – Similar provision; declares a strike/lockout illegal if commenced in violation of Section 62 or continued in contravention of orders under Section 42(7). | The concept of illegality is retained but references are streamlined to new Code framework. The clear cross-linking with Section 42(7) strengthens enforceability by aligning illegality with formal adjudication prohibitions, thereby ensuring that industrial actions cannot continue once legally restrained. |
| 7. | When continuation of strike/lockout is not deemed illegal | Section 24(2) – Continuation of strike/lockout is not deemed illegal if strike/lockout was legal at the time of commencement and dispute can later be referred for adjudication. | Section 63(2) – Similar safeguard retained. | The preservation of this clause upholds the balance between statutory regulation and legitimate right to collective bargaining. It ensures that workers and employers are not penalized for lawful actions that precede a reference to adjudication, thereby maintaining fairness in procedural application. |
| 8. | Legality of consequent strikes/lockouts | Section 24(3) – A strike/lockout declared in consequence of an illegal strike or lockout is not considered illegal. | Section 63(3) – Mirrors this position in the Code. | The continuation of this principle maintains parity in employer-employee rights. It prevents one party from gaining an undue advantage through an initial illegal action and ensures equitable treatment under industrial jurisprudence. |
| 9. | Financial support to illegal strikes/lockouts | Section 25 - No person must knowingly spend or apply any money in direct furtherance or support of any illegal strike or lock-out. | Section 64 – No person must knowingly spend or apply any money in direct furtherance or support of any illegal strike or lock-out. | The provision under the Code retains the same prohibition as the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, reflecting continuity in the law. This indicates that legislative intent remains unchanged, ensuring that no financial support is extended to illegal strikes or lockouts. |
| 10. | Penalties | Sections 26-28 – Provided monetary fines and imprisonment for illegal strikes, lockouts and instigation. | Sections 86-89 – Updated penalty structure with higher fines and graded severity. | The updated penalty structure aligns with current economic realities and acts as a stronger deterrent. It also introduces proportionality – higher penalties for employers or unions depending on the gravity and repetition of offences, ensuring better compliance and enforcement efficiency. |

6. Conclusion

The legal framework governing strikes and lockouts in India aims to balance industrial peace with the genuine rights of workers and employers. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020, is expected to modernize and streamline the law by broadening key definitions, standardizing timelines, strengthening reporting requirements and updating penalties to discourage abrupt shutdowns and encourage negotiations. At the same time, it preserves protections for lawful ongoing strikes and lockouts, ensuring fairness to both parties. Overall, the Code seeks to promote

16.1-2 Private company can prescribe additional disqualifications, but public company cannot

A private company can prescribe additional disqualifications in its Articles - section 164(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 283(3) of the 1956 Act].

Similarly private company can provide grounds in addition to those specified in section 167(1) for vacation of office as director - section 167(4) of Companies Act, 2013.

For example, private company can prescribe disqualification if he joins a rival group or starts a competing business or if he leaves the family of directors etc.

Public company cannot provide any other disqualification - In Cricket Club of India v. Madhav L Apte (1975) 45 Comp Cas 574 (Bom HC), it was held that by necessary implication, a public company cannot provide for any additional disqualification.

B. Shanmugam v. Karthik Dasari [2022] SCC OnLine Mad 4417]

The genesis in the cited case rested with the ED registering ECIR on the basis of three (3) FIRs. Out of the three (3) FIRs, one (1) was quashed & the remaining two (2) were stayed till further orders.

Before the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Madras the primary question was about the implication of quashing & staying of FIRs on the proceedings initiated by the ED under the PMLA.

In line with the directions passed in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra), the ED fairly conceded that in so far as the quashed FIR is concerned, the department cannot proceed ahead under the Act. However, it was strenuously contended by them that the accused cannot take benefit of the stayed proceedings and plea before the court that proceedings under PMLA for the remaining two (2) FIRs too be quashed.

On the other hand, the petitioners refuted the said contention of the department, and relied upon the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta in Rashmi Metaliks Ltd. (Supra).

The Division Bench in its judgment discarded the contentions of the Department and answered in negative to the question whether the ECIR, which is also pursuant to the FIRs which have been stayed by the High Court, can be proceeded with or not.

Placing reliance on precedents on 'jurisdictional fact to be taken into account by a Court before assuming jurisdiction over a particular matter', the court opined that the existence of jurisdictional fact is a condition precedent for the exercise of power by a Court of limited jurisdiction. Therefore, in present matter, when there is no cause of action, since the proceeding in one (1) of the cases was quashed, and the proceedings in two (2) other cases have been stayed by the Court, there was no jurisdictional fact or cause of action for the respondent/department to initiate any proceedings during the period of order of stay operating against the two FIRs.

Finally, in its conclusion, the Hon'ble High Court opined that in view of the quashing of the proceedings in one (1) of the FIR and staying of the proceedings in the remaining two (2) FIRs, the scheduled offence was eclipsed, suspended or stop operating during the period of stay. Therefore, the Department has to await the finality of the said proceedings. In case, if the other two (2) remaining FIRs also get quashed pursuant to the orders in the applications filed by the respective accused to quash the proceedings, in which event, the Department cannot step in or initiate any proceedings under the PMLA, as held in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra).

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("IBC") has been amended multiple times since its introduction in 2016to remove difficulties in the corporate insolvency process and streamline the procedure. The latest amendment, The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2020 ("Amended Act"), was introduced in the Lok Sabha, and passed by Rajya Sabha in the budget session and came into force w.e.f 13 March 2020. The Amended Act amends various sections and also introduces a new provision i.e. Section 32A protecting the new management which takes over a Company through an approved resolution plan under Section 31 of IBC.

The newly inserted Section 32A envisages the following; (a) Immunity to the Corporate Debtor as regards any offences committed prior to insolvency commencement date; and (b) Protection as regards any property of the Corporate Debtor in relation to any offence committed prior to commencement of insolvency resolution process where such property is covered under Resolution Plan as approved by the Adjudicating Authority. However, every person who is a designated partner as defined in the Limited Partnership Act or an officer as defined in Clause 60 of Section 2 of the Companies Act 2013 who is in charge of the business of the corporate debtor and is directly or indirectly in the commission of such offence as per report or complaint filed by the investigating authority shall continue to be liable and prosecuted for such offence committed by the corporate debtor notwithstanding that the liability of the corporate debtor has ceased. Accordingly, the newly inserted Section while protecting the new management which takes over a Company under an approved Resolution Plan envisages due continuance of proceedings against others in terms of the applicable provisions of law.

REQUIREMENT AND REASONS FOR PROTECTING CORPORATE DEBTOR AND SUCCESSFUL RESOLUTION APPLICANT

The latest amendment particularly the insertion of Section 32A is a phenomenal step taken by the Government which will enhance the revival of the stressed assets of corporate debtor as it will attract investments from successful bidders for the resolution plan before Adjudicating Authority. Resolution Applicant shall now be secured in as much as in light of Section 32A they shall no longer face further prosecution and threat of dispossession of the assets of the Corporate Debtor on account of prior offences being committed by the erstwhile management/promoter group. The success of any resolution plan was highly dependent on the newly inserted Section since, the uncertainties prevailing prior to the introduction of Section 32A time and again highlighted the need of protecting the corporate debtor as well as the properties belonging to the Corporate Debtor from its prior offence as even after taking over of a Corporate Debtor through a successful resolution plan, a successful bidder faced prosecution and liabilities before courts and tribunals for the prior acts of such corporate debtor.

Such grievance of the Successful Resolution Applicant came to forefront in the matter of Monnet Inspat& Energy which was acquired under CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) jointly by AION and JSW. Similarly in the matter of Bhushan Power Steel Ltd. which is under insolvency resolution process, to be acquired by JSW for over Rs.19,700 crore, the aspect of attachment by the Enforcement Directorate over the assets of Bhushan Power Steel Ltd. on account of alleged offence under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act interdicted the resolution process under the IBC. In the appeal case of Committee of Creditors versus Directorate Enforcement, the apex court stayed the ED attachment order while hearing the petition and the court asked ED to explain whether its money-laundering charges would trump the insolvency proceedings to be heard in forthcoming days.

In addition, we may also say that Section 32A of the IBC shall have a direct implication on the scope and ambit of Section 14 of the IBC, which provides for moratorium period as regards a Company which is undergoing resolution process under the Code. Section 14 lays down that there has to be a mandatory moratorium period provided to the corporate debtor from the insolvency commencement date wherein, inter alia, institution of new suits or continuation of the pending suits, against the corporate debtor, are temporarily suspended until the completion of the CIRP. That this moratorium period will not affect the criminal proceedings against the corporate debtor was made fairly clear in Shah Brothers Ispat (P.) Ltd. v. P. Mohanraj [2018] 97 taxmann.com 233. In this case, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal ("NCLAT") held that Section 14 is not applicable to the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act ("NI Act") as they are criminal proceedings. In crux, the NCLAT held that Section 14 of the IBC does not affect any criminal proceedings. Hence, even during the moratorium, criminal proceedings could be instituted or continued against the corporate debtor.

iii. Environmental Issues

The industrial corporations are one of the main reason for the environmental degradation. Many countries tried to make corporation liable for the environment crimes. So, who will be liable for the environmental crimes was still a question for many jurists. Different countries followed different procedure to make corporation liable for environmental issues17. In India, there are sufficient laws to make corporation liable for environment crimes. Under Indian Penal Code, Sections 27718 and 27819 talks about the offences relating to environment. But the scope of Sec 277 is limited and it only talks about use of the water and not the consequences of such utilization of water. Also under IPC, Section 95 is an exception that if it is a slight harm due to negligence or recklessness will be exempted from the offence but even such slight harm damages and effects the environment in a larger way.

Under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 Section 41 provides an Industry without the consent of the state board, concerned in an industrial operation, then the industry said to be committed an offence. Further, such important legislation is Environment Protection Act, 1986 which aims to deter and protect the environment by imposing fines. Sections 7 and 15 of the Act talks about the same. Also many rules was framed under Environment Protection Act, 1986 to deter the environment crimes. As sanction is imposed, who is responsibility to compensate the same, is it all the members of the company or the person who involved in the environment crime on behalf of the company. It is unjust to make company liable if the members of it commit crimes. The case of Oleum gas leakage20 is a classic example in the development of the criminal liability of the companies. M.C. Mehta case21 also paves the foundation for the development of criminal liability in Indian jurisprudence. The subsidiary company alone will be liable if there is any environmental crime committed by subsidiary irrespective of the parent company22. What kind of criminal sanctions can be imposed upon the corporation? It is impossible to imprison it. So, the only remedy is imposing fines on them. Section 15 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974and Sec 26 of the NGT Act, 2010 imposes heavy fines on industries if it violates any such laws. Under Cr.P.C, a new chapter XXIA is introduced for the purpose of plea bargaining to the person who commit the offences. Minimum Advance Notice Requirement: The notice of retrenchment must be sent to the Central Government and a copy to the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) at least one month before such date.

7.2 Re-Employment to Retrenched Workers The employer must prepare a list of total workers in the particular category from which retrenchment is considered and arrange them according to the seniority of their service. A copy of this list is required to be clearly and visibly pasted on the notice board of the establishment at least seven days before the actual retrenchment.

When any vacancy occurs in an industrial establishment, the employer must, within fifteen days, prominently display the notice on the notice board and inform all eligible retrenched workers of the vacancy by email or speed post.

However, if the vacancy duration is less than one month, the employer is not obligated to inform the retrenched workers of the vacancy.

7.3 Service of Notice for Intended Closure:

If an employer intends to close down an industrial establishment, they must give notice in Form XIII to the central government at least 60 days in advance. They must also send a copy to the concerned Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (central) and the authorised representatives of the workers.

7.4 Special Provisions Relating to Lay-offs, Retrenchment and Closure

Chapter X of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, governs special provisions relating to ‘Lay-offs, Retrenchment and Closure’. The provisions of this Chapter shall apply to an industrial establishment in which 300 or more workers or such higher number of workers as may be notified by the appropriate Government18, were employed on an average per working day in the preceding 12 months.

7.4-1 Application for Permission

As per the rules, the employer must submit applications for permission for Lay-offs, retrenchment, and Closure in Form-XIV.

7.4-2 Service and Display of Application

A copy of the application must be served simultaneously to the workers electronically, in person, or by registered or speed post. The application must also be displayed by the employer on the notice board or on the electronic board at the main entrance of the industrial establishment.

7.4-3 Review of Orders by the Central Government

The Central Government may, either on its own motion or on an application made by the employer or any worker, review its order granting or refusing permission for lay-off, retrenchment, or closure of an industrial establishment.

7.5 Worker Re- Skilling Fund ( Rule 37)

As per the rules, every employer who has retrenched a worker in an industrial establishment is required to transfer, within 10 days from the date of retrenchment, an amount electronically equivalent to 15 days of the last drawn wages of such retrenched worker or workers into the fund.

7.5-1 Maintenance of Fund

The fund must be maintained by the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central)/Office of the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central)/Office of the Regional Labour Commissioner (Central)/Office of the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) as required.

7.5-2 Transfer of Funds to Retrenched Workers within 45 days

Further, the funds so received must be transferred by the office of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) or the office of the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) or the office of the Regional Labour Commissioner (Central) or the office of the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), electronically to each of the retrenched worker account within 45 days of retrenchment to enable them to utilise that amount for his re-skilling.

8 Maintenance of Records, Registers, Forms, Notices, and Display Board ( Rule 47)

Rule 47 sets out provisions for the maintenance of records, registers, forms, notices, and display boards. As per the rules, all records, registers, forms, notices, display boards, and other documents required to be maintained under these rules shall be maintained electronically in the required format or containing the required information.

The records and other documents must be produced or shown as and when required by the concerned authority specified in this behalf under the Code.

9 Compounding of Offences ( Rule 38)

Rule 38 specifies the manner of composition of the offence. As per the rules, the officer notified by the Central Government for compounding of offences, must send a notice to the accused in Form XV through the designated portal of the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

9.1 Application for Compounding

The accused to whom the notice is served may send the duly filled-up application electronically in Part III of Form XV to the compounding officer and deposit the compounding amount electronically within 15 days of the receipt of notice.

9.2 Composition of Offence

Further, where the prosecution has already been instituted against the accused in the court of competent jurisdiction, the accused may apply to such court to allow the composition of the offence against him.

The Court may, after considering the application, allow composition of the offence by the compounding officer in accordance with the provisions of section 89 and the procedure specified in this rule.

reranked.text: There is no legal prohibition which prevents the holding of a domestic enquiry into an act of misconduct by a workman just because a criminal case is pending against the workman. The domestic enquiry in which the workman is answerable to his master and which may end in a departmental penalty is entirely different from the criminal proceeding in which the same person in respect of the same act is prosecuted for violation of the penal law of the land, which may end in conviction and sentence.

Held, that it was desirable that when the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry was being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending final disposal of the criminal case. In view of the accepted principles of law, in the event thepetitioner was convicted in the criminal trial, he would automatically be dismissed and/or removed from service, without taking recourse to formalities of departmental proceedings and, in the atternative, if the criminal case failed for want of evidence, by an order of discharge and not acquittal, in that event also, the departmental authorities would be entitled to proceed with the departmental enquiry, even after passing of such order of discharge by the criminal court. Therefore, during the pendency of the criminal trial, the employer would be restrained from proceeding further with the departmental enquiry against the petitioner.

It is desirable that if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry is being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending the final disposal of the criminal case. It would be particularly appropriate to adopt such a course where the charge against the workman is of a grave character, because in such a case, it would be unfair to compel the workman to disclose the defence which he may take before the criminal court. But to say that domestic enquiries may be stayed pending criminal trial is very different from anything that if an employer proceeds with the domestic enquiry in spite of the fact that the criminal trial is pending, the enquiry for that reason alone is vitiated and the conclusion reached in such an enquiry is either bad in law or mala fide.

The decision to hold or not to hold a domestic enquiry, during the pendency of a criminal trial in respect of the same allegation, against a workman, is that of the employer to be taken at his discretion and if the employer decides to hold such enquiry, he cannot be prevented from doing so by the issue of a writ of prohibition.

There is no legal prohibition for the holding of disciplinary proceedings just because a criminal case is pending. It is also well settled that a writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of a domestic enquiry can issue only when there is total lack of jurisdiction and no such infirmity exists in this case.

In the instant case it was held that the Industrial Tribunal was in error when it characterised the result of the domestic enquiry as mala fide partly because the enquiry was not stayed pending the criminal proceedings against the concerned workman.

A writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of a domestic enquiry by an employer into alleged acts of misconduct by a workman can be issued only if there was total lack of jurisdiction in the authority holding the enquiry. No such writ can be issued preventing an authority having jurisdiction to hold the enquiry, even if criminal proceedings are pending in respect of the same matter.

Therefore, the High Court cannot entertain a petition for a writ of prohibition against the employer restraining him from proceeding with a domestic enquiry on the ground that some of the witnesses proposed to be examined were police officers who would be giving evidence against the workman in the criminal case in respect of the same matter.

Disciplinary proceedings have been instituted against the petitioner in respect of the charge levelled against him in the charge-sheet dated 14th August, 1983 (Annexure-A). The said inquiry is in progress. At this stage, the petitioner has presented this writ petition seeking for the issue of a writ of prohibition restraining the respondents from proceeding with the domestic inquiry on the ground that some of the witnesses now proposed to be examined are police officers, who would be giving evidence against him in a criminal case registered against him in respect of which charge-sheet is yet to be filed. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of this case, learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the management should be prevented from holding the domestic inquiry.

In support of his contention, learned counsel for the petitioner, relies on the observations of the Supreme Court in Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. Kushal Bhan, [1960] 19 FJR 183; AIR 1960 SC 806. A similar question was considered by this Court in the case of Balaiah v. Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, [1981] 1 LLN 789. In the said case, after considering the observations of the Supreme Court in Delhi Cloth and General Mills’ case, [1960] 19 FJR 183; AIR 1960 SC 806, as also the Division Bench decision of this Court in Sri Rama v. Superintendent of Police, [1967] 1 Mys LJ 12, it was held that a master cannot be prevented from holding domestic inquiry even if criminal proceedings were pending in respect of the same act. In the said decision, it was pointed out that as a writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of an enquiry could be issued if only there was total lack of jurisdiction in the authority holding the inquiry for no such writ could be issued preventing an authority having jurisdiction to hold the inquiry, from holding the inquiry. The said decision fully covers the present case.

Sri A. G. Holla, learned counsel appearing for the BEL, also submitted that the Supreme Court has referred to the judgment in Delhi Cloth and General Mills’ case [1960] 19 FJR 183; AIR 1960 SC 806, in Tata Oil Mills Co. Ltd. v. Their Workmen, [1965] 26 FJR 199; AIR 1965 SC 155, and has reiterated that there was no lack of jurisdiction on the part of a master to commence and conclude a domestic inquiry against his servant when a criminal trial was pending against him.

Learned counsel for the petitioner, however, maintained that the ratio of the decision in Balaiah’s case is not applicable to a case in which the charges framed were serious and the employee concerned would be compelled to disclose his defence at the domestic inquiry and if such disclosure was likely to cause prejudice to him in the criminal trial and that the present one was such a case. I see no force in the submission. The decision to hold or not to hold a domestic inquiry, during the pendency of a criminal trial in respect of the same allegation, against an employee, is that of the master to be taken at his discretion and if the master decides to hold such inquiry, he cannot be prevented from doing so by the issue of a writ of prohibition.

In the circumstances, I decline to entertain this petition.

The writ petition is rejected leaving all other contentions open.

The question cropped up again with a new angle in Jang Bahadur Singh v. Baij Nath Tiwari, [1969] 36 FJR 128 (SC), as it was contended that initiation of disciplinary proceedings during the pendency of a criminal case on the same facts amounted to contempt of court. This plea was rejected and the court observed as under (page 130) :

“The issue in the disciplinary procedings is whether the employee is guilty of the charges on which it is proposed to take action against him. The same issue may arise for decision in a civil or criminal proceeding pending in a court. But the pendency of the court proceeding does not bar the taking of disciplinary action. The power of taking such action is vested in the disciplinary authority. The civil or criminal court has no such power. The initiation and continuation of disciplinary proceedings in good faith is not calculated to obstruct or interfere with the course of justice in the pending court proceeding. The employee is free to move the court for an order restraining the continuance of the disciplinary proceedings. If he obtains a stay order, a wilful violation of the order would of course amount to contempt of court. In the absence of a stay order the disciplinary authority is free to exercise its lawful powers.”

These decisions indicate that though it would not be wrong in conducting two parallel proceedings, one by way of disciplinary action and the other in the criminal court, still it would be desirable to stay the domestic inquiry if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against the employee in a domestic inquiry is being tried in a criminal court. The case law was reviewed by this court in Kusheshwar Dubey v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd., [1989] 74 FJR 86, and it was laid down as under (page 89) :

“The view expressed in the three cases of this court seem to support the position that while there could be no legal bar for simultaneous proceedings being taken, yet, there may be cases where it would be appropriate to defer disciplinary proceedings awaiting disposal of the criminal case. In the latter class of cases, it would be open to the delinquent employee to seek such an order of stay or injunction from the court. Whether, in the facts and circumstances of a particular case, there should or should not be such simultaneity of the proceedings would then receive judicial consideration and the court will decide in the given circumstances of a particular case as to whether the disciplinary proceedings should be interdicted, pending criminal trial. As we have already stated, it is neither possible nor advisable to evolve a hard and fast, strait-jacket formula valid for all cases and of general application without regard to the particularities of the individual situation. For the disposal of the present case, we do not think it necessary to say anything more, particularly when we do not intend to lay down any general guideline.”

The court further observed as under (page 89) :
The principles of natural justice do not require that the employer must wait for the decision of a criminal case or an appeal before proceeding with a domestic enquiry. 1960(1) L.L.J. 520, Approved.
