In the instant case, only a complaint had been filed against some of the respondents in their individual capacity and not in the capacity as a director. Accordingly, merely for the reason that they were also parties in the present proceedings as respondents, it could not be said that the petition was against the same party or that there were any parallel proceedings. From the above, it was clear that there was no criminal proceeding pending so as to tantamount to a parallel proceeding as contended by the respondents. The application for stay was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. [Paras 14 and 15]

No prejudice was likely to affect them. Moreover, the CLB has consistently taken a view that if both the parties on similar grounds have filed another civil case, the CLB would not encourage parallel proceedings. There was nothing to prevent the CLB to proceed with the instant case when the criminal complaint filed was only at stage of investigation by the police. Relying on the judgment of the Supreme Court in Karamchand Ganga Pershad v. Union of India [1970] 3 SCC 694, it can be said that the proceedings before the CLB can continue even when criminal case is pending which may have been filed by either parties against each other. The matters before the CLB are to be decided in summary proceedings on the basis of evidence by way of affidavits filed by the parties. The overall assessment of the case led to the conclusion that the CLB could proceed with the case when criminal proceedings were pending. However, there was no need to proceed in the instant case for the reasons that the whole issue was evolving around the question of 55,005 shares held by the petitioner which had been fraudulently and by tampering certain documents allegedly were reduced to 405 shares. There is no provision in law which provides that a prosecution for the offences in question cannot be launched until reassessment proceedings initiated against the assessee are completed. Section 279 provides that a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence punishable under section 276C Or section 277 except at the instance of the Commissioner. It further provides that a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence punishable under those provisions in relation to the assessment for an assessment year in respect of which penalty imposed or imposable on him under clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 271 has been reduced or waived by an order under section 273A. The Commissioner has the power either before or after the institution of proceedings to compound any such offence. In this case, it was not claimed that the Commissioner had not initiated the proceedings for instituting the complaints. No other legal bar for the institution of the proceedings was urged except stating that in the event of the petitioner being exonerated in the reassessment proceedings, the prosecutions may have to be dropped.

A mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of the institution of the criminal proceedings under section 276C and section 277. In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The criminal court no doubt has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the criminal court. The criminal court has to judge the case independently on the evidence placed before it. Otherwise there is a danger of a contention being advanced that whenever the assessee or any other person liable under the Act has failed to convince the authorities in the proceedings under the Act that he has not deliberately made any false statement or that he has not fabricated any material evidence, the conviction of such person should invariably follow in the criminal court.

It is only where the Commissioner reduces or waives the penalty imposed or imposable under section 271(1)(iii) in exercise of his discretion under section 273A, section 279(1A) comes into operation and acts as a statutory bar for proceeding with the prosecution under section 276C or section 277. It does not, however, provide that merely because there is a possibility of the Commissioner passing an order under section 273A, the prosecution shall not be instituted.

It may be that in an appropriate case the criminal court may adjourn or postpone the hearing of a criminal case in exercise of its discretionary power under section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the disposal of any proceeding under the Act which has a bearing on the proceedings before it is imminent so that it may take also into consideration the order to be passed therein. Even here the discretion should be exercised judicially and in such a way as not to frustrate the object of the criminal proceedings. There is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a criminal court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of a case before it indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceeding which may have some bearing on it is pending elsewhere. But this, however, has no relevance to the question of maintainability of the prosecution.

Accordingly, notwithstanding the reassessment proceedings started against the petitioner, prosecutions for offences punishable under sections 276C and 277 and under sections 193 and 196 of the Indian Penal Code instituted by the department were maintainable.

Decision of the Madras High Court affirmed.

The petitioner then filed a case before the present High Court and requested that even the provisions lying under sec. 14 of IBC would not expressly bar the prosecution of a criminal case in opposition to a corporation that has filed for insolvency according to sec. 10 of IBC. The NCLT, according to the clause, also forbids the establishment or completion of any proceedings, although that provision doesn't expressly forbid the continuity of a criminal case. While the verdict in Indorama perceives the provisions of sub-sec. (1) of sec. 446 of the Companies Act, the grounds as well as the reasoning used in that is for concluding that another provision doesn't dissuade the initiation of a criminal case quite visibly determines the rule and could be pursued here also.

What's visible from Clause (a) of sub-sec. (1) of sec. 14 of IBC, until the authorized officer has declared a moratorium on the prohibition of lawsuits or the continuity of existing claims or proceedings in opposition to the corporate debtor such as the application of any judgement, decree, or order before the judiciary, arbitral panel, or other such panels, the full focus of the side's claims in the case is on the terms 'proceedings,' 'order' and 'in any court of law.'

It's already argued right here that such terms do not specifically limit its application to civil courts alone. Terms are omnibus & sometimes also requiring a criminal case, such as a court matter under sec. 138 of the NI Act, 1881 and a criminal review resulting after that. The court was asked by them for an injunction and that the cheque-bounce case isn't legally viable and can be rescinded and put down.

Respondents 2 to 7 requested also that ruling in the context of Indorama would not apply to the circumstances here. Under that situation, the provisions of sub-sec. (1) of sec. 446 of the Companies Act is at issue, while the provisions of sec. 14 of IBC are at issue here.

The object of preventing the prosecution will be annulled if a case under sec. 138 of the NI Act, 1881 were permitted to be pursued. Now, in the Calcutta HC case of M/s. MBL Infrastructure Ltd. v. Starting with the ordinance passed for the moratorium to what's given under Sec. 14 of the IBC, it may be stated that the announcement of the moratorium does not apply to criminal proceedings. In this case, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal ("NCLAT") held that Section 14 is not applicable to the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act ("NI Act") as they are criminal proceedings. In crux, the NCLAT held that Section 14 of the IBC does not affect any criminal proceedings. Hence, even during the moratorium, criminal proceedings could be instituted or continued against the corporate debtor. However, the introduction of Section 32A effectively nullifies the exception created for criminal cases under Section 14 of the IBC by Shah Brothers Ispat, as there is a complete cessation of corporate debtor's liability in cases wherein under an approved Resolution Plan, the Corporate Debtor is taken over by a new Company and management. Thus, once the CIRP culminates in an approved resolution plan, there can neither be institution nor continuation of criminal proceedings against the Corporate Debtor for the offences committed by it prior to the commencement of the CIRP.

Conclusion

From the perspective of companies dealing with the takeover of corporate debtors, the amendment is completely secures the Resolution Applicants as it ensures that the previous liability of the Corporate Debtors does not interfere with either the operations or the assets of the Corporate Debtor as taken over by an approved Resolution Plan thereby smoothing the entire takeover process. However, to understand and implement the amended provision in its letter and spirit, it would be pertinent to clarify certain parts in the provision which the amendment brings about. The aim should not be to let off those involved in the offences, but merely to proceed against them in a more just manner, so as to ensure that genuine parties interested in the resolution of the corporate debtor do not face any difficulties that were not envisaged.

The liquidator under section 537, if he feels the need, can apply to the company court to intervene and the company court can always grant or refuse sanction.

With this background the question of granting permission to prosecute or staying proceedings under section 138, read with section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act can be considered. In so far as directors are concerned, the question of granting sanction to prosecute or staying proceedings does not arise at all. The only question is whether in so far as the company is concerned, the proceedings can be stayed as section 141 makes the company also liable. The language of the section is clear. The expression used is ‘every person who was in charge of the company’ when the offence was committed. Can the normal process of proceeding with the criminal complaint be stayed because a winding up process has been initiated ? Does the criminal law set in motion for an offence come to a halt, or can it be proceeded with only with the permission of the company court? Merely because a fine may be imposed which will have to be paid from the assets of the company can the Company Court intervene? A complaint in such a case can only be at the instance of a payee or the holder in due course. Such a complainant, of course, is also entitled to file his claim as a creditor. If this is accepted, the easiest way out for a company, which is deemed to have committed an offence, will be to sponsor a petition and then apply for stay of proceedings under section 442. The Company Court itself under section 446 cannot try the complaint. Realisation of such fine under the provisions of the Land Revenue Code would be ‘other legal proceedings’. Sale and attachment of the property of the company is subject to section 537. Thus, it is these other legal proceedings which the company court could look into as it would have a bearing on the assets of the company. Therefore, construing the judgment of the Apex Court in the case of S.V. Kondaskar, Official Liquidator & Liquidator of the Colaba Land & Mills Co. Ltd. v. V.M. Deshpande, ITO [1972] 42 Comp. Cas. 168, it is impossible to contend that the company court in winding up would have jurisdiction to stay the criminal prosecution or that permission of the company court is required to prosecute the company for offences committed before a provisional liquidator is appointed or an order of winding up is made. In a rare case if the liquidator himself is to be held liable for the acts of the company, there are always powers in him to seek permission of the company court to prosecute or defend such prosecution. The expression ‘legal proceeding’ or ‘other legal proceeding’ for the purpose of sections 442 and 446 must be read ejusdem generis with the expression ‘suit’ and can mean only civil proceedings which have a bearing in so far as the winding up is concerned, namely, realisation of the assets and discharge of liabilities of the company.

Thus, the expression ‘suit or other legal proceeding’ in section 446(1) and the expression ‘suit or proceeding’ in section 442 do not include criminal complaints filed under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

(4) Where a penalty of dismissal or removal or compulsory retirement from service imposed upon an employee is set aside or declared or rendered void in consequence of or by a decision of a Court of Law and the Competent Authority, on a consideration of circumstances of the case, decides to hold a further enquiry against him on the allegations on which a penalty of dismissal, removal or compulsory retirement was originally imposed, the employee shall be deemed to have been placed under suspension by the Competent Authority from the date of the original order of dismissal, removal or compulsory retirement and shall continue to remain under suspension until further orders.

(6) During such suspension, he shall receive subsistence allowance equal to:

(i)

fifty per cent of his substantive pay plus allowances thereon, for the first six months of suspension; and

(ii)

seventy-five per cent of his substantive pay plus allowances thereon for the period of suspension beyond six months.

2. Jurisdiction of Writ Courts:

On perusal of the provisions contained in the earlier act, it may be noted that an exemption was granted to cases pending before High Courts or Supreme Court, but no such exemption has been provided for under the IBC. The issue was discussed in Canara Bank v. Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd.9. The appellant (i.e. the creditor) submitted that the adjudicating authority cannot exclude any court from the purview of moratorium for the purpose of recovery of amount or execution of any judgment or decree, including the proceeding, if any, pending before the High Courts and the Supreme Court of India against a corporate debtor.

The NCLAT acknowledged that clause (a) of Section 14(1) specifically does not exclude any Court, including the High Courts or even the Apex Court. However, the Hon'ble Bench there are certain constitutional provisions which must be considered. There is no provision to file any money suit or suit for recovery before the Supreme Court except under Article 131 of the Constitution; some High Courts have original jurisdiction to entertain the suits, which may include money suit or suit for recovery of money. However, the writ jurisdiction conferred on the Supreme Court and the High Court under Article 32 and Article 226 of Constitution of India, being a constitutional power, cannot be curtailed by any provision of an Act or court. Therefore, 'moratorium' will not affect any suit or case pending under Article 32 or 226. However, so far as suit, if filed before any High Court under original jurisdiction which is a money suit or suit for recovery, against the corporate debtor such suit will be covered by the bar imposed under Section 33(5).

3. Criminal Proceedings:

In criminal proceedings, particularly in the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the directors or officers in default, as the case may be, are generally held personally liable, as against the civil liability of the company. The company and its directors cannot shirk their criminal liability merely on the ground that the company was already wound up and the liquidator had taken charge of the affairs of the company.

Upholding the principle laid down by the Kerala High Court in Jose Antony Kakkad v. Official Liquidator10, in Counter Point Advt. P. Ltd., Rep. by its Director, Mr. Naresh Purushotham v. Harita Finance Limited, Rep. by its Special Legal Assistant, Miss. Gulzar Sayeeda [2006] 133 Comp Cas 435 (Mad.)11, the Madras High Court observed that:

"Though the words 'legal proceedings' in Section 446 of the Companies Act is wide enough to be taken in criminal proceedings also, such criminal proceedings must be in relation to the assets of the company. Criminal proceedings which are not in respect of the assets of the company but which end in the conviction or acquittal of the accused, cannot be stayed under Section 446 of the Companies Act. Proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, can end only in the conviction or acquittal of the accused in the case and no recovery of any amount covered by the dishonoured cheques can be made in the criminal proceedings. As the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are not in respect of the assets of the company, the proceedings pending in the criminal Courts cannot be stayed under Section 446 of the Companies Act."

HEADNOTE: Section 630 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Offences - Penalty for wrongful withholding of property - One ‘T’, occupying company’s flat as employee, failed to vacate it even after retirement - Company initiated criminal proceedings under section 630 as well as filed a civil suit - Whether pendency of civil suit filed by company for possession of flat and for damages debarred criminal proceedings or necessitated stay of same till disposal of civil suit - Held, no

FACT: ’T’, an employee of the petitioner-company, failed to vacate the company’s flat after retirement, in spite of demand, and a complaint was filed against him under section 630. While the criminal proceedings were in progress, the company also filed a civil suit for recovery of possession of the flat for damages. ’T’ filed an application before the Trial Court for staying the criminal proceedings on the ground of the pendency of the civil suit. When this was rejected, he filed a revisional application. The Sessions Judge ordered that the judgment in the case under section 630 should not be delivered till the disposal of the civil suit.

On revision petition :

HELD: In the present case, ’T’ was occupying the flat of the company as its employee and it was the case of the company that even after retirement from the service ’T’ had been illegally retaining the same and was not delivering the possession of the same to the company. Such allegation no doubt prima facie made out a case triable under section 630. The mere fact that they had also remedy for possession and damages in civil law and in pursuance of that they had also filed a civil suit for such relief did not make section 630 inoperative in respect of the said matter nor could that be a good ground for staying the proceeding under section 630. The Supreme Court in Atul Mathur v. Atul Kalra, 1989 SCC (Crl.) 761 has held that merely because the accused had schemingly filed a suit in Civil Court, it could never be said that the Civil Court was in seisin of a bona fide dispute between the parties and as such the Criminal Court should have stayed its hands when the company filed a complaint under section 630 and that if such a view was taken, it would not only lead to miscarriage of justice but also render ineffective the salutary provision of section 630. The principle enunciated in the said Supreme Court decision was also applicable in the instant case. However, in the present case, the civil suit that had been filed was that of the company and the civil suit filed by ’T’ was only for his retiral benefit.

Therefore, in the facts and circumstances, prima facie appearing in the case, the company could seek relief both under the civil law as well as under section 630 and there was no bar against the simultaneous continuance of both sorts of proceedings.

In the result, the Court below should proceed with the proceedings under section 630, notwithstanding the pendency and continuance of any civil suit in the matter.

2) of the Code, the duration of moratorium can be extended if resolution professional files an application to Adjudicating Authority.23 But the moratorium will be extended only if the application is filed before the expiry of 180 days.24

The moratorium under the Code also applies to the SARAFESI Act. Thus, if there is any pending matter on enforcement of security interest created upon the Corporate debtor, then that matter has to be suspended during the moratorium period.25 But in the case of Canara Bank v. Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd.26 the said provision has been multiple time questioned. The issue of whether the moratorium granted under Section 14 of the Code extends to proceedings and suits pending before various High Courts and Supreme Court? To answer this question two broad proposition were given. First, the powers of the Supreme Court and High Court cannot be curtailed under Articles 32 and 136 of the Supreme Court and of High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution, by any provision of the Code.27 Second, once the moratorium is declared under this Code than any proceedings or suit in respect to the recovery of assets should be stayed under the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court or High Courts. The allowance to such suits will create hindrances to the reviving process of corporate defaulters and will end up tarnishing the essence of the Code. Furthermore, it is a well settled principle that the meanings of suit and proceeding as per the definition are taken in their general sense. Suit refers to the proceedings which are non-criminal and is only curial in nature28 and for the purpose of stay does not include execution proceedings.29

Thus there is an exception to this rule, which lies in matters of writ petition and criminal matters, as these matters involve criminal actions against the company and its directors and more importantly involve public interest, so such proceedings will not be barred upon commencement of the moratorium period.30 Similarly, a proceeding to assess or determine liability, and a proceeding to recover the assessed or determined liability31 will not be barred under it.

Before the Principle bench of the NCLAT, a very interesting question was raised wherein the bench had to decide whether the proceedings under the Sec. 138of Negotiable Instruments Act, which provides punishment of imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of cheque or with both, be covered under the provisions of the moratorium.32 As the primary objective of the Code is the revival and rejuvenation and the bench had to take into consideration the impact of such fines on the financial stability of the corporate debtor, but the bench considered the impact of criminal actions on the rem and held that "Section 138 is a penal provision, which empowers the court of competent jurisdiction to pass order of imprisonment or fine, which cannot be held to be proceeding or any judgment or decree of money claim. Imposition of fine cannot held to be a money claim or recovery against the Corporate Debtor nor order of imprisonment, if passed by the court of competent jurisdiction on the Directors, they cannot come within the purview of Section 14. In fact, no criminal proceeding is covered under Section 14 of I&B Code."33

Thus, the objective of the moratorium to protect and provide the corporate debtors with a breathing space is only restricted to the scope of civil suits and no such support or protection will be given under the Code, whenever there is any matter of public interest or when the criminal acts of such debtors affect the public at large.

Overriding Clause

Overriding clauses have always been a point of conflict between various provisions and the overriding clause in the Code. Section 238 under the Code is no different and has also been a hot topic as it not only results into a conflict of application of other Laws but is also backed by a moratorium.

In the landmark case of Innoventive Industries v. ICICI Bank,34 the Supreme Court affirmed, that Sec.107 under the Government of India Act, 1935 is in substance reproduction of Article 254 of the Constitution, with one difference that the power of Parliament under Article 254(2) goes to the extent of repealing a State law and affirmed again that under Article 254 of the Constitution of India, the State law in contravention with any Central Law can be repealed.35 Apart from applying the doctrine of repugnancy in the present matter, the Supreme Court highlighted the fact that contours of Section 238 of the Code which is the non-obstante clause are broader than the objective of state legislation.

The same contention was also affirmed in the case of Jotun India Private Ltd. v. Psl Ltd.36 wherein it was held that provisions of the Code will have an overriding effect even over the Companies Act, 2013 and the argument that winding-up petitions were already filed before the High Court does not bar the remedy to file fresh proceedings under the Code, the Hon'ble Court referred to the judgement in Madura Coats Ltd. v. In the case of Damodar Das [1985] 57 Comp. Cas. 115 (Bom), the title of the company to the property was in challenge and there was a genuine bona fide dispute being raised regarding the title and thus it was opined that the more appropriate forum for deciding such a disputed bona fide dispute with regard to title would be the civil court. Learned counsel for the respondent has placed reliance on the case of Damodar Das [1985] 57 Comp. Cas. 115 (Bom) in support of his contentions and it appears that the lower courts were also persuaded to go by the ratio laid down in case of Damodar Das [1985] 57 Comp. Cas. 115 (Bom) and also by this court in the case of Smt. Raminder Kaur Bedi (supra) for passing the impugned orders.

In Amritlal Chum v. Devoprasad Dutta Roy [1988] 63 Comp. Cas. 839 ; AIR 1988 SC 733, it has been clearly laid down by the Supreme Court that the words "any property of a company" would also refer to the residential premises allotted to an employee who fails to vacate the premises after termination of his employment and section 630 of the Companies Act would become applicable.

Reference was also made to Bush India Ltd. v. Lekhraj [1984] Crl. LJ 346. In the said case, it was found that the questions raised in the criminal proceedings and the civil suit being the same and the dispute essentially being of civil nature, the criminal case should be stayed. The facts in that, case were totally different from the facts in the present case. There were business dealings between the complainant and the accused in the said case and disputes arose from the said business dealings and thus it was held by the Bombay High Court that the appropriate forum for deciding such a dispute is the civil court and the criminal case was directed to be stayed. I do not understand how anything said in this judgment is of any help to the respondents in the present case.

Learned counsel for the respondents also cited Ram Sumer Puri v. State of U.P., AIR 1985 SC 472. That case was decided on its own facts. In the said case, parallel proceedings under section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code had been brought while the civil court was already seized of the matter. The Supreme Court held that there is no scope to doubt or dispute the position that the decree of the civil court is binding on the criminal court and as the civil court was already seized of the matter and the question of title was to be decided which has been ultimately decided by the civil court, the question of resort to proceedings under section 145, Criminal Procedure Code was misconceived. It was observed that when a civil litigation is pending for a property wherein the question of possession is involved and has been adjudicated, there is hardly any justification for initiating parallel criminal proceedings under section 145 of the Code. That is not the situation here.

In Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. Kushal Bhan, AIR 1960 SC 806, the Supreme Court observed that though very often employers stay enquiries into the misconduct of employees pending the decision of the criminal trial courts dealing with the same facts and that is fair, it cannot be said that the principles of natural justice require that an employer must wait for the decision at least of the criminal trial court before taking action against an employee. However, if the case is of a grave nature or involves questions of fact or law which are not simple, it would be advisable for the employer to await the decision of the trial court so that the defence of the. employee in the criminal case may not be prejudiced. This case pertains to different facts and thus it cannot be of any guide in resolving the issue arising in this petition.

Learning counsel for the petitioner has made a reference to Kishindas Tekchand v. State, AIR 1956 Bom 423. However, this case is also distinguishable on facts. In the said case, the party was not seriously prosecuting the civil suit and the Bombay High Court held that the criminal case could not be stayed till the disposal of the civil suit. There is no allegation in the present case that the respondent is not pursuing his civil suit diligently.

The purpose of enacting section 630 is to provide speedy relief to a company when the property is wrongfully withheld. The Magistrate's jurisdiction under section 630 can extend only to those cases where there is either no dispute or, in any event, no bona fide dispute that the property involved was the property of the company. In cases where there is such a dispute involving complicated questions of title to the property, it would be purely of civil nature and the civil court would be the more appropriate forum for the purpose of adjudicating it and the Magistrate cannot and should not venture to determine the same in a summary proceeding as envisaged under section 630. Every dispute would not become a bona fide dispute merely because the company's claim to possession is refuted by its ex-employee. Merely because a suit has been filed raising some dispute it cannot be said that the civil court is in seisin of a bona fide dispute and that the Criminal Court should have stayed its hands when the company filed a complaint under section 630. There is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a Criminal Court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of the case indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceedings which may have some bearing on the points raised in the criminal proceedings are pending elsewhere.

In the instant case, absolutely no question of title in respect of the flat concerned was involved in the criminal proceedings because there was no dispute that the flat had all along been and was still the property of the company. The only question to be decided in the criminal proceeding was whether the said property was being wrongfully withheld by 'A', the ex-employee of the company and, after his death, by his wife and son, that is, the petitioners. This was not at all a complicated question which could not be conveniently determined by a Criminal Court even in a summary proceeding under section 630. The alleged oral agreement between the parties constituted the only defence of the petitioners in the criminal proceeding and the cause of action for the civil suit was also based on the said agreement. The company had denied the alleged agreement. Such an agreement would at best create a personal obligation of the company under section 40 of the Transfer of Property Act to be enforced in the civil suit. The temporary injunction as prayed for prima facie appeared to be outside the scope of the suit for specific performance. There was no scope for arguing that the possession of the flat by the petitioners or by their predecessor-in-interest, 'A' was lawful, requiring protection from a Court of law at anytime after the expiry of the period allowed by the company. The ex parte ad interim injunction which was in favour of the petitioners and against the company would also be of no avail to them in withholding the possession of the flat. If 'A' was in wrongful possession of the flat after expiry of the period allowed by the company, the petitioners would be as much in wrongful possession of the flat in their capacity as heirs and legal representatives as their predecessor-in-interest. Mere pendency of a suit or operation of an ex parte ad interim injunction could not ipso facto make a dispute bona fide if the dispute was otherwise not so. On a scrutiny of the particular dispute involved in the civil suit in the instant case, it could not be held that it was a bona fide dispute which fell within the exclusive jurisdiction of the civil court and should be decided by the civil court and not the Criminal Court. It could not also be understood how there could be any likelihood of any embarrassment being caused to the petitioners or to the civil court in case the criminal proceedings were allowed to continue to their logical conclusion. The offence under section 630 is a continuing offence and unless and until the alleged agreement was specifically performed by the company by virtue of the decree that might be passed in the civil suit, the question of getting any right to possess the flat by the petitioners would not arise and even if there be any direction by the Criminal Court for delivery of possession of flat, there would be no likelihood of any embarrassment being caused either to the civil court or to the petitioners. The company in that case would get back the possession of the flat to which it was legally entitled and if the conveyance was finally executed in execution of the decree that might be passed in the civil suit, there would be no impediment to the petitioners getting possession from the company at that point of time. It was only if the civil suit reached its concluding stage and the petitioners became successful in getting the possession of the flat in execution of the decree before the criminal case reached its concluding stage that there would be no occasion then for the Criminal Court to direct delivery of possession of the flat in favour of the company. But even in such an eventuality the prosecution under section 630(1) could continue till its logical end without any impediment. Therefore, the instant case was not at all a fit and proper case for staying the criminal proceedings.

The Supreme Court of India has consistently held that if the Management is represented by a legally qualified and trained person, notwithstanding any Rules to the contrary, the workmen would be entitled to be represented by a Lawyer. There is a huge difference between the expressions ''legally qualified'' and ''legally trained''. The expression ''legally trained'' would possibly attract the dicta of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay v. Dilipkumar Raghavendranath Nadkarni and others reported in (1983) 1 SCC 124. [Para 12]

■

However a legally qualified person may not be legally trained. Every other Personnel Officer in the Industrial Department or the Personnel Department of any public or private sector would invariably have a LLB Degree. Such degrees are until recently available easily and obtained by serving personnel in public sector by undergoing evening classes/part time courses. That by itself would not amount to being legally trained which only a practicing Lawyer would acquire. Long experience in the Industrial or Personnel Department, could obviously give more training to a person representing the Management engaged thereat. Using such person with a mere degree of law, as Presenting Officer, would not ipso facto, therefore, entitle a workman in a domestic enquiry to the services of a Lawyer. [Para 13]

■

In the instant case, the workmen had in extensio cross-examined the Management witnesses. He had also re-examined himself. The tenor of cross-examination scrutinized invariably indicates, an experienced and seasoned hand in defending domestic enquiries against the workmen and the employees. [Para 14]

■

i. Tort Issues Corporate liability was first recognized in the case of the public nuisance and breach of the statutory duty11. Later the scope of making corporation liable was widened and extended to nonfeasance and misfeasance acts. The three landmark judgments12 in 1944 discussed about the liability of the corporation in U.K. The liability of the corporation further extended to the offences which do not require criminal intent. In Queen v. Great northern of England co.13 The courts made corporation criminally liable for the misfeasance. From then, the courts went ahead and made company liable to the crimes which also requires intent, reflected in the case, New York central v. Hudson River Railway co.14, from public nuisance to till now, one can observe how the courts have interpreted the criminal liability of the companies.

ii. Manslaughter and Homicide

In U.K, the Corporate Manslaughter and Homicide Act, 2007 makes companies liable for manslaughter and there are many cases where the courts in UK held companies liable under this Act. Before the act came in to existence, the court in Northern Star Mining Corporation Ltd. case15 held that, a company was prosecuted for manslaughter which was criticized to be inadequate. Again in case of R v. HM Coroner ex parte Spooner16, while making the company liable for manslaughter, one has to see the mens rea and actus reus of such offence should be recognized against those who were identified as the mind and will of the company. However, due to lack of proper law with regard to company's liability in manslaughter and homicide crimes, the U.K. government passed an Act in 2007.

iii. Environmental Issues

The industrial corporations are one of the main reason for the environmental degradation. Many countries tried to make corporation liable for the environment crimes. So, who will be liable for the environmental crimes was still a question for many jurists. Different countries followed different procedure to make corporation liable for environmental issues17. In India, there are sufficient laws to make corporation liable for environment crimes. Under Indian Penal Code, Sections 27718 and 27819 talks about the offences relating to environment. But the scope of Sec 277 is limited and it only talks about use of the water and not the consequences of such utilization of water. Also under IPC, Section 95 is an exception that if it is a slight harm due to negligence or recklessness will be exempted from the offence but even such slight harm damages and effects the environment in a larger way.

Under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 Section 41 provides an Industry without the consent of the state board, concerned in an industrial operation, then the industry said to be committed an offence. Further, such important legislation is Environment Protection Act, 1986 which aims to deter and protect the environment by imposing fines. Sections 7 and 15 of the Act talks about the same. Also many rules was framed under Environment Protection Act, 1986 to deter the environment crimes. As sanction is imposed, who is responsibility to compensate the same, is it all the members of the company or the person who involved in the environment crime on behalf of the company. It is unjust to make company liable if the members of it commit crimes. The case of Oleum gas leakage20 is a classic example in the development of the criminal liability of the companies. M.C. Mehta case21 also paves the foundation for the development of criminal liability in Indian jurisprudence. The subsidiary company alone will be liable if there is any environmental crime committed by subsidiary irrespective of the parent company22. Under Section 48 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974the department of the Government will be held liable if it commits any environmental crimes.

What kind of criminal sanctions can be imposed upon the corporation? It is impossible to imprison it. So, the only remedy is imposing fines on them. Section 15 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974and Sec 26 of the NGT Act, 2010 imposes heavy fines on industries if it violates any such laws. Under Cr.P.C, a new chapter XXIA is introduced for the purpose of plea bargaining to the person who commit the offences. But the plea bargaining is not allowed in the environment issues, however, the plea in Bhopal gas disaster Union Carbide Corpn.23 made many victims left uncompensated.

Similarly, under the concept of vicarious liability, one is made responsible for any act or omission of another. The reason here is the presumption that master is aware of what his servant is doing and that the servant is always deemed to act on behalf of and on the directions of the master. In Commonwealth,28 the court made the people acting on behalf of 3 companies liable for its activities by stating that CCL is necessarily vicarious because company is a legal fiction which is comprised of individuals alone. In State v. Great Works Milling Co.,29 court refused to hold the corporation guilty for blocking a river, because it would merely result in holding liable the innocent stockholders, which was not what this court desired. In King v. Central Supply Ass'n, Ltd.,30 it was stated that generally criminal conspiracy includes mens rea as an essential, nevertheless companies are made liable as conspirators, by imputing intent of its employees to that of the corporation.31 A Minnesota court, in US v. Trans-Missouri Freight Ass'n, 32emphasizes that mens rea is not a necessary element in prosecution. In State v. Passaic County Agricultural Society,33 the company was held liable for public nuisance for maintaining a disorderly house, court stated that malice may be imputed to companies in criminal proceedings.

PROBLEMS WITH THE EXISTING JURISPRUDENCE

The most debatable topic since ages is whether a company can be made criminally liable. One might say imposition of fines is way of punishing a corporation, but that hardly resulted in any deterrence in the crimes by corporations. The main problem is the so called statutory inadequacy. And if one says lifting of corporate veil is a solution, there are again difficulties in identifying to whom exactly the evil intent belonged to. And in large companies it is impossible for the shareholders to control the management and directors, and therefore cannot be made liable.

The major problem is, though the definition of a 'person' includes a company, it is not possible to imprison a company being a juristic person. The courts find a dead end in cases where a corporation is charged under provisions providing for mandatory imprisonment as it cannot be imprisoned. The temporary solutions that courts have come up is to make companies liable for greater amounts fines. Also, there are problems in holding the agents liable, such as, identifying who controlling person was; do all the concerned staff have the same state of mind. In Moore v. Bresler Ltd.,34 an employee whose duty was to pay tax had not performed duty resulting in the guilt of the company, wherein the court stated that such act should be attributed to company irrespective of the fact that it was done to conceal his theft from the company. However the appellate court reverse the decision by holding that the sales were not made by them on behalf of the corporation but rather in fraud of the company itself. In India it is considered that knowledge is a pre-requisite before holding a company liable. This shows the attitude of Indian Criminal Law towards corporate crimes.

Another question which arises in the concept of CCL is the punishment. Can a corporation be imprisoned? The punishments which may be imposed to a corporation are imposing fine, forfeiture of its properties and cancelling of its license. In Northern Star Mining Corporation Ltd. case35, a company was prosecuted for manslaughter which was criticized to be inadequate. Again in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. J.B. Company,36 where the court held that company is not an exception to criminal law and that it could be tried for an offence for which imprisonment is the prescribed punishment, but will be fined.

CONCLUSION

Earlier, the concept of a separate legal entity of a company and of corporate veil created by statutory provisions, has been exploited to a great extent by individuals in order to evade personal liability, which lead to a well-established law worldwide, that a company can be made liable for criminal offences irrespective of looking into whether it had an evil intent or not. Though the laws in India are not developed as that of other countries for making a corporation completely liable, but it had to an extent developed the law through its judicial pronouncements. In spite of this, India has not gone beyond imposing of fines and forfeiture of property of a company, which mean that the laws in India are insufficient to deal with the present day cases.

The question assumes importance for the reason that in such cases, the Settlement Commission has necessary jurisdiction under section 245H to grant immunity to the assessee from prosecution for any offence under the Act or under the Indian Penal Code, 1860 or under any other Central Act for the time being in force. In the light of the judgment of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.N. Bhattachargee [1979] 118 ITR 461/ 1 Taxman 348 , the Settlement Commission is required to exercise its power of immunising against criminal prosecution by using its power only sparingly and in deserving cases. There is, therefore, no ground to believe that if the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with, it shall grant as a matter of course immunity from criminal prosecution to the applicant under section 245H. The power to grant such immunity is dependent upon the satisfaction of the Settlement Commission that the applicant has co-operated with the Settlement Commission in the proceeding before it and has made a full and true disclosure of his income and the manner in which such income has been derived. Thus, a mere expectation of success in some proceeding or appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of institution of criminal proceedings under sections 276C and 277. If a criminal prosecution has been validly instituted, it is in the interest of justice that the trial of the case should be concluded as early as possible. Thus, the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal (First ITO) [1984] 149 ITR 696/19 Taxman 1 after observing that "it may be that in an appropriate case, a criminal court may adjourn or postpone the hearing of a criminal case in exercise of its discretionary power under section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the disposal of any proceeding under the Act which has a bearing on the proceedings before it is imminent so that it may take also into consideration the order to be passed therein," had also taken care to make a further observation that "Even here the discretion should be exercised judicially and in such a way as not to frustrate the object of the criminal proceedings." The Apex Court then went on to emphasise that "There is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a criminal court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of a case before it indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceeding which may have some bearing on it is pending elsewhere. The principle laid down by the Apex Court in P. Jayappan’s case (supra) in another context is also applicable in the matter of staying criminal proceedings pending before the criminal court, which has been validly instituted and where on the application of the assessee, the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with but has not yet passed any final orders including an order granting or refusing immunity from the criminal prosecution. A blanket order staying criminal proceedings only because the Settlement Commission has allowed an application before it to be proceeded with and the Commission has the necessary authority under the Act to grant immunity from criminal prosecution is also not necessary in the interest of justice. If any such proceeding is decided in favour of the applicant and immunity from criminal prosecution is granted, he can take advantage of any such decision even after his conviction before the appellate or the revisional Court or before the Supreme Court in an application under article 136 for special leave to appeal. The process of criminal law including the trial, appeal and revision is a protracted one and it is difficult to visualise a situation where the Settlement Commission in a particular case shall take such a long time for disposing of the application and in granting immunity from criminal prosecution that the accused shall have lost all opportunities to take benefit of such an order granting immunity even before the appellate or the revisional Court.

the Supreme Court revisited the nature of Section 138 proceedings and questioned the basis of the reasoning adopted in P. Mohanraj (supra). The Court observed the 2 tier aspects of Section 138 proceeding, i.e. (a) compensatory aspect, and (b) a criminal aspect. This led the Court to raise a significant question as to if the moratorium is intended to protect the debtor's assets and therefore affects the recovery aspect, should it also stop the criminal prosecution? It is important to note here that the difference between the two judgments is not about who can be prosecuted. Both judgments recognise that directors and other persons in charge of the company can continue to face proceedings under the NI Act. The real issue is whether the moratorium should stop a Section 138 case against the corporate debtor itself merely because the proceeding also involves recovery of money.

Therefore, the key question before the larger Bench is whether Section 138 proceedings should be stayed completely during the moratorium, as held in P. Mohanraj (supra), or whether only the compensatory aspect should be affected while the criminal prosecution continues, as suggested in Dineshchand Surana (supra).

If the larger Bench agrees with the view expressed in Dineshchand Surana (supra), criminal prosecution under Section 138 may continue against the CD, even during the moratorium, while only the recovery or compensation aspect will be subject to moratorium. Even then, the authors are of the view, given that a corporate entity cannot be imprisoned; the impact would be limited to imposition of fine; and then, it might involve questions surrounding vicarious liability on the directors, etc. and the effect of section 14 on such fines. The decision of the larger Bench will therefore be crucial in determining how the objectives of the IBC will be aligned with the consequences under NI Act.

The dispute arose from an incident at Borjan Tea Estate in March 2007 when around 1,500 workers gathered at the factory gate; some forcefully entered, damaged office property, pelted stones, and the Manager sustained injuries, following which the Estate remained under lockout for 11 days. Eleven workmen were charge-sheeted for forming an unlawful assembly, instigating violence and damage to garden property, with alleged loss of about Rs. 19.66 lakhs, and were charged with gross misconduct under the Estate Standing Orders. The workmen denied involvement; the gateman stated the gate was broken by some workers after overpowering him. Separate domestic enquiries were conducted against each of the 11 workmen and enquiry reports held them guilty of gross misconduct. The management issued notices seeking representations; after time extension, no representations were submitted, and the workmen were dismissed from service, the Reference later describing dismissal as with effect from 10.09.2007.

■

Following the dismissal, the Government of Assam referred the dispute to the Labour Court, Dibrugarh, on whether the management was justified in dismissing the 11 named workmen and, if not, whether they were entitled to reinstatement with back wages. In its written statement, the management relied on the domestic enquiries as the basis for dismissal and reserved the right to adduce evidence on merits if the enquiries were found violative of natural justice. The workmen, in their written statement, asserted that the enquiries were not impartial, that they were denied opportunity to adduce defence evidence, and that the Presenting Officer for the management also acted as a witness; they denied instigating or participating in the violence.

■

The Labour Court proceeded to record evidence without first framing a preliminary issue on the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries. The proceedings initially went ex parte against the workmen; the management submitted evidence-in-chief and later stated it would not adduce further evidence. Management witnesses were cross-examined and the workmen also adduced evidence. The Enquiry Officer (examined as M.W. 4) stated in cross-examination that although workmen were informed of the enquiry and to participate, he did not inform them that they were required to adduce evidence, stating that the Presenting Officer would inform them. The records of the domestic enquiries were not placed before the Labour Court. The Head Clerk (examined as M.W. 2), whose evidence had formed the basis of the domestic findings, admitted in cross-examination that he did not remember the names of the workers involved in the incident. The enquiry reports recorded that the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt and did not give reasons for proceeding only against these 11 workmen.

■

By Award dated 29.02.2016 in Reference Case No. 02/2009, the Labour Court upheld the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries and, on that basis, upheld the dismissal of the workmen; no separate finding on proportionality of the punishment was recorded.

Subsequent to imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) on the assessee, the department initiated criminal proceedings under section 276C, read with section 278B, against the assessee. The assessee filed discharge petition on ground that the Tribunal had deleted the penalty sought to be imposed on the assessee under section 271(1)(c). The trial court, however, rejected said application on ground that income-tax authorities had preferred an appeal before the High Court and, therefore, the penalty proceedings under the provisions of section 271(1)(c) had not attained finality. On revision, the Additional Sessions Judge observing that the fate of the application for discharge was dependent upon the order to be passed by the High Court in the Income-tax Appeal, set aside the order of the trial court and remanded the matter to the trial court for a decision afresh after the appeal filed by the department was decided by the High Court.

In revision petition, the department contended that the said order was not tenable in law inasmuch as penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and the criminal proceedings under section 276C, read with section 278B, were independent and the pendency of the proceedings under section 271(1)(c) could not be taken as a ground to stay the proceedings under section 276C, read with section 278B.

Complaints were filed against the petitioners seeking their prosecution for an offence under section 138. On revision, the petitioner claimed that a reference had been made in respect of the petitioner-companies to the BIFR under section 15 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 for determining the company as a sick industry and that, as a consequence, an enquiry under section 16 was pending. It was, therefore, contended that the proceedings to prosecute these companies could not be continued in view of section 22.

Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act contemplates alteration of conditions during the pendency of any conciliation proceeding before a conciliation officer or a Board. In the instant case, the quarter had been allotted to the petitioner by virtue of his employment and the petitioner was not entitled to retain the same on termination thereof. A Division Bench of Madhya Pradesh High Court in L.S. Nair v. Hindustan Steel Ltd. AIR 1980 MP 106 has held that there is nothing to indicate that the Estate Officer will have no jurisdiction to evict a person from a quarter until the dispute relating to termination of services is finally decided by the Labour Court. It was opined that the order of termination could not be ignored as void and inoperative and the termination was to be treated as valid and effective until it was set aside. It was held that the petitioner had, therefore, no authority to occupy that quarter till the order of termination was in force.

In the instant case also, the position was no different except that the proceedings had been initiated by the respondents under the provisions of section 630. Section 630 is a penal provision for a wrongful act of obtaining possession, or wrongfully withholding any property. Sub-section (2) creates an independent offence if the direction of the court to deliver the property is not obeyed. Pendency of conciliation proceeding under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, much less the proceedings which were initiated after the initiation of proceedings under section 630, did not, therefore, create a bar to the jurisdiction of the court to deal with the complaint under section 630. The Bombay High Court in Chandragupta Gupta v. Padmanabha Subramani [1989] 65 Comp. Cas. 190 has observed that the fact that there is a dispute between the petitioner and the company as to whether the services have been properly terminated, will not in any way affect the continuation of the trial and decision of the criminal case. It, therefore, clearly follows that pendency of conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer cannot arrest or suspend the jurisdiction of the court to deal with the complaint under section 630.

The court by the impugned order had exercised the jurisdiction under section 630(2) and the jurisdiction was not taken away by the pendency of the proceedings before the Assistant Labour Commissioner. The petition had, therefore, no merit, and was to be dismissed.

The petitioners argued that effective adjudication of the issue involved could only be done by the civil court, that criminal proceedings were an abuse of the process of the Court and were liable to be quashed. The petitioners prayed for staying the criminal proceedings till the disposal of the petition for temporary injunction filed in the civil suit.

FACT: ■

The petitioner–Management had initiated disciplinary action against the respondent–workman following a complaint that he used abusive language and physically attacked a co-employee, who underwent hospital treatment and lodged an FIR. The respondent was suspended pending enquiry. A charge memo with four charges of assault, intimidation, and use of abusive language was issued. His explanation was found unsatisfactory; an external Enquiry Officer conducted a domestic enquiry, examined witnesses, issued findings, which were forwarded for show cause; thereafter, the Management terminated his services. The respondent consistently denied the charges and alleged that the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper.

■

The Management filed an application under Section 33(2)(b) seeking approval of the termination and paid approximately Rs. 0.52 lakhs towards final settlement along with one month’s wages. The Deputy Commissioner of Labour (Conciliation II) approved the termination. It was recorded that no evidence was adduced before the approving authority, though the approval order discussed the allegations, material from the domestic enquiry, and recorded conclusions on the facts.

■

Challenging the termination, the respondent invoked Section 2A. As no order was passed within 45 days, the dispute was filed before the Additional Labour Court as O.P. No. 145 of 2023. The respondent filed a memo seeking a preliminary decision on the fairness of the domestic enquiry. By order dated 9/10/2024, the Labour Court treated the approving authority as a quasi-judicial authority not superior to the Labour Court, noted that parties had let in evidence and were cross-examined before the approving authority, treated the approving authority’s finding on the correctness of the domestic enquiry as beyond jurisdiction and a nullity, and directed the Management to adduce evidence afresh on the preliminary issue of fairness of the domestic enquiry.

At this juncture, it is relevant to notice the ratio in Radheshyam Kejriwal (supra), where the Act, 1973 expressly provided simultaneous prosecution. Paragraph No.38 of the said judgment reads as under: " (vi) The finding in the adjudication proceedings in favour of the person facing trial for identical violation will depend upon the nature of finding. " [Para 24]

■

The ratio is laid down in the context of Act, 1973. Section 56 of said Act, 1973 which provides for simultaneous criminal prosecution and uses the expression "without prejudice to any award of penalty by the adjudicating officer under the Act.'" [Para 25]

■

Even though the Act, 1973, provides for simultaneous criminal prosecution, in addition to penalty by the adjudicating authority, the Apex Court in paragraph No. 38(vi) of the aforementioned judgement has held that, where the person is exonerated on merits, criminal prosecution is unwarranted. [Para 26]

■

This Court is dealing with Section 34. As already noticed, there is no provision in the Act which expressly provides for simultaneous criminal prosecution or expressly bars simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication of an industrial dispute. [Para 27]

■

In the instant case the adjudication under Section 10 is not yet over and is still pending consideration. [Para 28]

■

It is true that the expression "without prejudice to any award of penalty by the adjudicating officer under the Act, found in the Act, 1973 or any other similar expression conveying similar meaning is not used in Section 34. However, as already noticed, the provision if analysed under the scheme of the Act, is there to provide an additional remedy to an aggrieved party to initiate a criminal prosecution (after obtaining authorisation), in the event of violation of the provisions of the Act which attract penal consequences. At the same time, one should not lose sight of the fact that the Act also aims at securing industrial peace over unrest and confrontation. [Para 29]

■

Precisely for these reasons, though the application under Section 34, to seek authorisation to prosecute the person who violates the provisions of the Act, which attract penal consequences is maintainable, sufficient safeguard is also built in the provision to prevent indiscriminate criminal prosecution and the abuse of the said provision. The aforesaid view is evident from the manner in which Section 34 is couched, where there is a requirement to obtain authorisation to lodge the complaint. [Para 30]

■

The appropriate Government acting under Section 34, is required to apply its mind before passing any order on the application under Section 34 and in this behalf the law is well settled. [Para 31]

■

The appropriate Government has to apply its mind to ascertain whether a prima facie case is made out alleging violation of the provision of the Act which attracts penal consequence under Section 34. [Para 32]

Cases where the violation is prima facie established, or not established, or, where the alleged violation is doubtful and requires a finding by the adjudicatory authority, cannot be enlisted exhaustively. ■ In the case of Reena Rani v. State of Haryana (2012) 10 SCC 215 this Court has again applied the law laid down in the judgment of Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel 1985 taxmann.com 1415 (SC)/(1985) 3 SCC 398 and Jaswant Singh v. State of Punjab (1991) 1 SCC 362 and held that the order of dismissal did not disclose the reasons explaining why it was not reasonably practicable to hold a regular departmental enquiry and applicability of the proviso in such a case is not justified. [Para 39]

■

On overall analysis of the intent of Article 311(2), it is vivid that an employee holding a post in Union or State ought not to be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to the one by which he was appointed. It is further specified that a person shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank after an inquiry supplying the charges if any against him and giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges. The applicability of the said clause is restricted in a situation wherein his conduct led to his conviction of criminal charges or where the authority empowered who dismissed, removed or reduced in rank records reason in writing upon satisfaction that it is not 'reasonably practicable' to hold an enquiry against him. In addition, where such power has been exercised by the President or the Governor it may be in the interest of security of the State or if not expedient to hold such an enquiry, then exceptional power under clause (c) of second proviso to Article 311 ought to be exercised. [Para 40]

■

In case such a decision invoking the extraordinary power is taken by the competent authority in light of the judgment Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel 1985 taxmann.com 1415 (SC)/(1985) 3 SCC 398 within the parameter as discussed, the scope of judicial review is available to the Constitutional Courts wherein the reasons as assigned for satisfaction of the authority must be reasonable, valid, justified and in writing. In addition, the satisfaction as recorded must be the objective satisfaction on the basis of material brought on record which ordinarily the disciplinary authority may take as a prudent person. Otherwise, dispensing with the enquiry is not permissible in law. In the present case, Section 21 of the 1978 Act confers power of punishment and Section 22 prescribes the procedure for awarding such punishment. The procedure as contemplated has been elaborated under the 1980 Rules. In the present case, in the Court’s view, the power exercised by the authority is completely without application of mind, thus, the question of recording of satisfaction as affirmed by the appellate authority, the CAT and the High Court does not arise. Therefore, it can be held that the order dispensing with the regular procedure of inquiry is arbitrary and consequently the order of dismissal of the appellant is liable to be quashed and the orders of the CAT and the High Court affirming the said dismissal order stand set aside. [Para 41]

■

In light of the above discussion, the irresistible conclusion is to set aside the order passed by the CAT and the High Court and to quash the order of dismissal passed by the DCP and confirmed by the appellate authority. In consequence, the appellant shall forthwith be reinstated with continuity of service. He shall be entitled for all consequential benefits notionally. Since, the appellant is found involved in a criminal case, therefore, in the facts of the case, back wages from the date of dismissal till reinstatement are restricted to 50%. [Para 42]

■

The setting aside of the order passed under Article 311(2) proviso (b) of the Constitution and direction for reinstatement shall be without prejudice to the right of the respondent to take recourse as permissible by initiating a departmental enquiry in accordance with law. Accordingly, and with the aforesaid directions, the present appeal stands allowed to the extent indicated. Parties to bear their own costs. [Para 43]

On petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898:

The Indian criminal justice system recognizes that not all disputes are criminal at their core. Many arise from financial, commercial, or civil transactions that spiral into criminal litigation due to overlapping allegations of fraud or breach of trust. The recent judgment of the Supreme Court in Suresh C. Singal v. State of Gujarat (AIR 2025 SC 1909) has once again emphasized that when such disputes are settled amicably, and the aggrieved party has no subsisting grievance, criminal proceedings may be quashed to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice.

Factual Background

In the Singal case, the appellants were directors of companies that had availed credit facilities from the Bank of Maharashtra between 1998 and 2005. Due to adverse market conditions and the 2004 Surat floods, the accounts were declared Non-Performing Assetsd (NPAs), leading to proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). While these proceedings were pending, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) registered an FIR under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120B of the IPC and under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, alleging conspiracy and forgery in obtaining letters of credit.

During the pendency of the case, the appellants and the Bank entered into a One-Time Settlement (OTS), the Bank received full repayment, and a No Dues Certificate was issued by the Bank. Despite this settlement, CBI filed a charge sheet, and subsequent attempts by the appellants for discharge and quashing were rejected by the Sessions Court and High Court. The matter eventually reached the Supreme Court.

Criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings - Objective distinct

The objective in the criminal proceedings and the disciplinary proceedings is distinct and different. In the disciplinary proceedings, the question is whether the employee is guilty of such conduct as would merit his dismissal from service or a lesser punishment, as the case may be, whereas in the criminal proceedings the question is whether the offences registered against him are established and, if established, what sentence should be imposed upon him. The standard of proof, the mode of enquiry and the rules governing the enquiry and trial in both cases are entirely distinct and different (State of Rajasthan v. B. K. Meena [1996] 6 SCC 417)

IBC: Where corporate debtor's dispute was that claim made by operational creditor was barred by limitation, pendency of criminal proceeding initiated by operational creditor against corporate debtor was to be considered as an explanation for delay

In the present case, ’T’ was occupying the flat of the company as its employee and it was the case of the company that even after retirement from the service ’T’ had been illegally retaining the same and was not delivering the possession of the same to the company. Such allegation no doubt prima facie made out a case triable under section 630. The mere fact that they had also remedy for possession and damages in civil law and in pursuance of that they had also filed a civil suit for such relief did not make section 630 inoperative in respect of the said matter nor could that be a good ground for staying the proceeding under section 630. The Supreme Court in Atul Mathur v. Atul Kalra, 1989 SCC (Crl.) 761 has held that merely because the accused had schemingly filed a suit in Civil Court, it could never be said that the Civil Court was in seisin of a bona fide dispute between the parties and as such the Criminal Court should have stayed its hands when the company filed a complaint under section 630 and that if such a view was taken, it would not only lead to miscarriage of justice but also render ineffective the salutary provision of section 630. The principle enunciated in the said Supreme Court decision was also applicable in the instant case. However, in the present case, the civil suit that had been filed was that of the company and the civil suit filed by ’T’ was only for his retiral benefit.

Therefore, in the facts and circumstances, prima facie appearing in the case, the company could seek relief both under the civil law as well as under section 630 and there was no bar against the simultaneous continuance of both sorts of proceedings.

In the result, the Court below should proceed with the proceedings under section 630, notwithstanding the pendency and continuance of any civil suit in the matter.

Intent behind Incorporation of Section 32A of the Code

Insolvency Law committee recommended incorporation of this provision submitted in February 2020.5 It was incorporated keeping in mind the difficulty faced by the successful resolution applicants imposing the restrictions and liabilities on corporate debtor. In is emphasised by the Insolvency Law committee that this provision has been included to absolve the corporate debtor from the offences committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP unless they resolution applicant is also involved or related party to promoter group.

Parliamentary Standing Committee under the chairmanship of by Mr. Jayant Sinha, Former Minister of State of Finance in its report submitted on March 2020.6 The committee rendered its opinion in favour of incorporation of Section 32A into the Code with a view to safeguard the position of the resolution applicant from the offence the former promoters. Such an observation keeping in mind the necessity of cleansed entity where the change in management of the corporate debtor has taken place.

Pre-Condition to the Applicability of Section 32A

In order to discourage the abuse of this provision, safeguard has been introduced by way of pre-condition which need to be satisfied before resorting to Section 32A are:-

The resolution applicant is not involved or related party to promoter group,

The resolution plan results in control of corporate debtor or change in the management.

Liability for the Offence Committed Prior to the Commencement of CIRP

As a result of incorporation of Section 32A of the Code, the corporate debtor shall cease to responsible for the offence committed prior to the commencement of CIRP and the property of corporate debtor which are part of resolution plan, no action can be taken against those property.

However, it is clarified the ambit of the Section 32A is very limited in terms of liability and it doesn't immune or absolve the person who are:-

responsible for the activities of the corporate debtor in conduct of business,

officer in default

directly or indirectly involved in the commission of the offence

All the above mentioned person shall continue to remain liable for the offence committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP. Furthermore there is also no bar against the property other than property of corporate debtor and the person who has acquired that property under the liquidation or CIRP, as the case may be.

Conundrum Continues

Promulgation of Section 32A in the Code has lot of implication and its position is not very in this regard. Various relevant legal issues time and again has come before the Appellate Tribunal and High Courts for consideration and these issues need to be redressed as they core to the application of Section 32A.

The question of interpretation of Section 32A came up before the Appellate tribunal in the case of JSW Steel Ltd. v. Mahendra Kumar Khandelwal., 7 wherein the Appellate tribunal held that the Section 32A is retrospectively applicable and also set aside all the attachments of the corporate debtor made by Enforcement Department under PMLA. However, it wasn't clarified whether it is also applicable to the proceedings which have already been concluded and no adjudication is pending w.r.t. corporate debtor however they satisfies the parameters laid down in the Section 32A of the Code.

In the case of Tata Steel BSL Ltd v. Union of India,8 wherein summon issued before the incorporation of Section32A into the Code by the Investigating officer was under challenge. The Delhi HC ruled that the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under section 32A of the Code as the instant case falls within the clear language used in Section 32A and hence corporate debtor cannot be made responsible for the offence committed prior to commencement of CIRP even when the resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority, when it is expressly prohibited by the provision. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner was upheld and liable to be discharged in the merits of the case.
