26.5-6 Tax assessment can continue but recovery proceedings cannot continue without leave of NCLT

Proceedings for recovery of income tax dues cannot continue without leave of Court (now NCLT) - National Conduits P Ltd., In re (1974) 94 ITR 378 (Del) * Asia Pacific Investment v. Shaw Wallace & Co Ltd. (2002) 37 SCL 122 = 110 Comp Cas 58 (AP HC). Tax assessments can continue, but NCLT can scrutinise claim of department - Income Tax assessment of the company under winding up can continue without leave of liquidation Court (now NCLT). The Court (now NCLT) cannot stop assessment proceedings, but has full powers to scrutinise claim of revenue after income tax is assessed and payment is demanded by department from liquidator. It would be open to the liquidation court (now NCLT) to decide how far under the law the amount of income tax determined by the department should be accepted as lawful liability of the company. At the time of winding up, Court (now NCLT) can fully safeguard interest of the company and its creditors - S V Kondaskar, Official Liquidator v. V M Deshpande, ITO AIR 1972 SC 878 = (1972) 42 Comp Cas 168 (SC).

26.5-7 Rent controller cannot fix rent

If Rent Controller has fixed fair rent of property as per provisions of Rent Control Act, Company Court (now NCLT) has jurisdiction to get into correctness of decision of Rent Controller - Official Liquidator v. Tamil Nadu Handloom Weavers' Coop Soc. Ltd. (2009) 96 SCL 25 (Mad HC).

26.5-8 Arbitration proceedings cannot be initiated without leave of NCLT

If leave of Court (now NCLT) is not taken before commencing proceedings of arbitration by giving a notice to company in liquidation, the proceedings will be invalid. - British India Corporation v. Star Spin and Twist Machinery (2001) 106 Comp Cas 467 = 34 SCL 694 (Karn HC).

26.5-9 Industrial dispute cannot continue before labour court

Proceedings under section 33C(2) of Industrial Disputes Act cannot continue without leave of Court (now NCLT), even if initiated prior to winding up order. These are covered under 'other legal proceedings' stated in section 446 of Companies Act. - Basavaiah v. Sri Krishna Rajendra Mills (2001) 106 Comp Cas 366 = 34 SCL 741 (Karn HC DB).

26.5-10 Leave of NCLT required even for suit against directors if company is main defendant

Permission of Court (now NCLT) under section 446 of the 1956 Act (section 279(1) of Companies Act, 2013) is required even for suit against directors, if company is main defendant - Deutsche Bank v. S P Kala (1992) 74 Comp Cas 577 (Bom HC DB) - quoted and followed in CCE v. Indian Magnetic Ltd. (2014) 44 GST 187 = 43 taxmann.com 4 (HP HC DB).

However, if company is not defendant, then suit can continue.

26.6 Can Criminal proceedings by or against company continue?

In Pennar Paterson v. Shikshak Sahakari Bank (2008) 85 SCL 22 (SC), it was held that section 279(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [parallel section 446(1) of the 1956 Act] covers criminal proceedings also.

However, this judgment was delivered when winding up petitions were handled by High Court, which is a judicial authority. However, NCLT is a quasi judicial authority and hence cannot decide on criminal liability.

Hence, in my view, criminal proceedings by or against company will continue. In any case, section 279 applies to legal proceedings by or against company. Thus, legal proceedings against directors or employees cannot be stayed [see case law discussed later in this Chapter].

26.7 Extending period of limitation when company is petitioner, when stay is operative

Period of limitation prescribed in Indian Limitation Act or in any other law in force, remains suspended for any suit by or application in the name and on behalf of a company which is being wound up by the company.

The period of suspension is for the period commencing from date of commencement of winding and upto the date in which winding up order is made plus a period of one year - section 358 of Companies Act, 2013.

This relaxation and extension is only in favour of the company, i.e. it is only in respect of suit or application in the name and on behalf of the company, i.e. it is not applicable to suits filed against the company.

In order to arrive at an appropriate conclusion, what is also to be kept in perspective is that undisputedly the parties are already before the Arbitrator in respect of the very same transaction. The legal position, no doubt is clear that if adequate material is available on record to indicate that the respondent company is unable to pay its debts, the winding petition will not be barred merely because of the pendency of any other proceeding. In the instant case, firstly it is a winding up petition filed against the guarantor company and not against the borrower company. Even though, in law the creditor would have the option of proceeding against the guarantor, the question raised is as to the very validity of the guarantee said to have been executed. In fact, that is also an issue raised in the Arbitration proceedings between the same parties, to which the borrower company is also a party. [Para 16]

The claim petition filed before Justice Dr. B.P. Saraf is to the objection statement and the respondents are the respondents Nos. 3 to 5 therein. The same was filed during July 2009. The common written statement is filed by the respondents to the said claim petition. In the said written statement the contention relating to the collusion in bringing about the documents of guarantee has been exhaustively urged. The written statement is dated 11-2-2010. It is true that these winding up petitions have been filed on 5-10-2009, which is marginally prior to the date on which the written statement was filed in the Arbitration case and a stand had been taken before the Arbitrator, but the notice of these petitions was served only during January 2010. The stand taken in the Arbitration case is very proximate to the date when the instant petition was filed and notice was served. Therefore it cannot be concluded that the contention put forth in the objection statement to these petitions has been urged for the first time and in such event the legal notice not being replied along cannot be the basis to raise the presumption of inability to pay the debts in the instant facts.

That apart, though after lapse of sometime, the respondents have initiated criminal complaint and the same has been referred for investigation, the fact which cannot be ignored is that the respondents have not barely raised the defense, but are pursuing their legal remedies before the appropriate forum. [Para 17]

The above noticed aspects will disclose that the defense has not been taken for the sake of defense in the objection statement so as to consider it as moonshine or frivolous defense though the Court at this stage cannot also accept the same to be correct, but there can be no denial of the fact that the issues raised are substantial and would go to the root of the matter in so far as invoking the corporate guarantee. The nature of contentions will indicate that the Court can neither accept nor reject it on the face of it. The resolution of such disputed questions will require adjudication based on evidence, but as held by the Supreme Court, the Court while acting as the Company Court is not expected to hold a full trial of the matter. [Para 18]

In the instant case, in any event the parties are already before the appropriate forum raising the same issues and the adjudication therein will settle these issues, which if held against the respondent company and at that stage if it is shown that they are unable to repay their debts, certainly the petition can be entertained at that stage, but as of now, the substantial issues raised will weigh in favour of the respondent to secure adjudication of the same in the forum where it is pending and that aspect cannot be decided at this stage based on the averments made in the petition and the objection statement. [Para 19]

Hence, at this stage, there is no reason to admit these petitions. The parties would have the liberty of having the dispute relating to the validity of the execution of the guarantee, adjudicated in the pending Arbitration. [Para 20]

Thus, the petitions are dismissed. [Para 21]

Rashmi Metaliks Limited v. Enforcement Directorate [2022] SCC OnLine Cal 2316]

A Single Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta came to the rescue of the Accused and stayed the two orders of freezing of the accounts of the accused dated July 13, 2022.

The ED had claimed that the company made a wrongful declaration to avail benefits of the Indian Railways' dual freight policy of 2009. The Accused's challenge to the Show cause notice issued by the Railways & Civil Suit filed by the Union of India against the accused was stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2015.

With freezing orders passed by ED in 2022, i.e. after seven (7) years from the date on which all pending proceedings were stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, and also the summons under the Act were issued prior to the stay order, it was held that the ED could not have initiated any action against the petitioners during the subsistence of the order of stay of the pending proceedings against the accused by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2015.

Taking consideartion of the exception carved out in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra) for a person named in the criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence being absolved by a Court of competent jurisdiction, interestingly, the Court has drawn an analogy to the present facts where the proceedings have only been stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court & no discharge or no acquittal have been made while restraining the ED from proceeding ahead with its action against the accused.

B. Shanmugam v. Karthik Dasari [2022] SCC OnLine Mad 4417]

The genesis in the cited case rested with the ED registering ECIR on the basis of three (3) FIRs. Out of the three (3) FIRs, one (1) was quashed & the remaining two (2) were stayed till further orders.

Before the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Madras the primary question was about the implication of quashing & staying of FIRs on the proceedings initiated by the ED under the PMLA.

In line with the directions passed in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra), the ED fairly conceded that in so far as the quashed FIR is concerned, the department cannot proceed ahead under the Act. However, it was strenuously contended by them that the accused cannot take benefit of the stayed proceedings and plea before the court that proceedings under PMLA for the remaining two (2) FIRs too be quashed.

On the other hand, the petitioners refuted the said contention of the department, and relied upon the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta in Rashmi Metaliks Ltd. (Supra).

The Division Bench in its judgment discarded the contentions of the Department and answered in negative to the question whether the ECIR, which is also pursuant to the FIRs which have been stayed by the High Court, can be proceeded with or not.

Placing reliance on precedents on 'jurisdictional fact to be taken into account by a Court before assuming jurisdiction over a particular matter', the court opined that the existence of jurisdictional fact is a condition precedent for the exercise of power by a Court of limited jurisdiction. Therefore, in present matter, when there is no cause of action, since the proceeding in one (1) of the cases was quashed, and the proceedings in two (2) other cases have been stayed by the Court, there was no jurisdictional fact or cause of action for the respondent/department to initiate any proceedings during the period of order of stay operating against the two FIRs.

Finally, in its conclusion, the Hon'ble High Court opined that in view of the quashing of the proceedings in one (1) of the FIR and staying of the proceedings in the remaining two (2) FIRs, the scheduled offence was eclipsed, suspended or stop operating during the period of stay. Therefore, the Department has to await the finality of the said proceedings. In case, if the other two (2) remaining FIRs also get quashed pursuant to the orders in the applications filed by the respective accused to quash the proceedings, in which event, the Department cannot step in or initiate any proceedings under the PMLA, as held in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra).

Abstract

Liability of corporate entities arising from the offence committed by it discourages the bidders and resolution applicant from taking control over the company. It ultimately defeats the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process which aims at reviving the company. It is quintessential to ensure that maximum safeguard are introduced to keep the process viable and not to render hinder the process by any means. This paper attempts to highlight the intent with which Section 32A has been incorporated into the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and the legal and economic issues which flows therefrom.

Introduction

Section 32A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (hereinafter 'the Code') deals with Liability for prior offences creates a statutory fiction which provides immunity to the corporate debtor from any prosecution or any action against the property under the resolution plan under section 31 of the Code or in liquidation on the condition that there is change in the management taking place. Earlier there was no provision in the code which provide for such express immunity, this amendment is introduced into the Code only by way of Second Amendment Bill, 2019.

Background

Initially, Section 32A of the Code was introduced as an ordinance by President of India by exercising the power vested by virtue of Article 123 of the Constitution of India as the Parliament was not in session. Owing to strong objection against the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Second Amendment) Bill, 2019 by the Opposition Party on various grounds like bill was circulated without giving two days' advance notice, lack of information to all the MPs and on the merits of the bill and its aftermath on the economy.

It was referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee headed by Mr. Jayant Sinha, Former Minister of State of Finance and Dr. Manmohan Singh, Former Prime Minister of India to examine and submit its report within period of 3 months. After having introducing the bill in the Winter Session, it was again introduced in the Budget Session of the Parliament along with the report of the committee. The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on Mar 06, 2020 while the Rajya Sabha passed the on Mar 12, 2020 through voice vote. Lastly, Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Second Amendment) Bill, 2019 was incorporated into the Code when it received president's assent and notified in the official gazette on Mar 13, 2020.

ATTACHMENT OF CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY TO A CORPORATION

i. Strict Liability

Under this concept, a person shall be made legally responsible for the concerns of his acts even in the absence of guilty mind or criminal intention. Examples of some criminal offences which do not require mens rea are rape, murder, vehicular offences. In US, the rule followed is that whenever a particular legislation does not specify mens rea as an essential, it is deems that mental intent need not be prove in such offence, and hence treated it as strict liability.

In Indianapolis Water Co. v. American Strawboard Co.,27 court held that mere omission, irrespective of mens rea of defaulter, is sufficient to constitute crime.

ii. Vicarious Liability

The maxim qui facit per alium per se explains the concept better, which means, one who does an act through another is deemed to do it by himself. Similarly, under the concept of vicarious liability, one is made responsible for any act or omission of another. The reason here is the presumption that master is aware of what his servant is doing and that the servant is always deemed to act on behalf of and on the directions of the master. In Commonwealth,28 the court made the people acting on behalf of 3 companies liable for its activities by stating that CCL is necessarily vicarious because company is a legal fiction which is comprised of individuals alone.

During suspension, relationship of master and servant continues between the employer and the employee. However, the employee is forbidden to perform his official duties. Thus, suspension order does not put an end to the service. Suspension means the action of debarring for the time being from a function or privilege or temporary deprivation of working in the office. In certain cases, suspension may cause stigma even after exoneration in the departmental proceedings or acquittal by the Criminal Court, but it cannot be treated as a punishment even by any stretch of imagination in strict legal sense. [Para 7]

The power of suspension should not be exercised in an arbitrary manner and without any reasonable ground or as vindictive misuse of power. Suspension should be made only in a case where there is a strong prima facie case against the delinquent employee and the allegations involving moral turpitude, grave misconduct or indiscipline or refusal to carry out the orders of superior authority are there, or there is a strong prima facie case against him, if proved, would ordinarily result in reduction in rank, removal or dismissal from service. The authority should also take into account all the available material as to whether in a given case, it is advisable to allow the delinquent to continue to perform his duties in the office or his retention in office is likely to hamper or frustrate the inquiry. [Para 9]

In view of the above, the law on the issue can be summarised to the effect that suspension order can be passed by the competent authority considering the gravity of the alleged misconduct i.e., serious act of omission or commission and the nature of evidence available. It cannot be actuated by mala fide, arbitrariness, or for ulterior purpose. Effect on public interest due to the employee's continuation in office is also a relevant and determining factor. The facts of each case have to be taken into consideration as no formula of universal application can be laid down in this regard. However, suspension order should be passed only where there is a strong prima facie case against the delinquent, and if the charges stand proved, would ordinarily warrant imposition of major punishment i.e., removal or dismissal from service, or reduction in rank etc. [Para 10]

Long period of suspension does not make the order of suspension invalid. However, in State of H.P. v. B.C. Thakur [1994] SCC (L & S) 835, the Supreme Court held that where for any reason it is not possible to proceed with the domestic enquiry the delinquent may not be kept under suspension. [Para 12]

There cannot be any doubt that the Rules 1965 are a self contained code and the order of suspension can be examined in the light of the statutory provisions to determine as to whether the suspension order was justified. Undoubtedly, the delinquent cannot be considered to be any better off after the charge sheet has been filed against him in the court on conclusion of the investigation than his position during the investigation of the case itself. [Para 13]

Suspension is a device to keep the delinquent out of the mischief range. The purpose is to complete the proceedings unhindered. Suspension is an interim measure in aid of disciplinary proceedings so that the delinquent may not gain custody or control of papers or take any advantage of his position. More so, at this stage, it is not desirable that the Court may find out as which version is true when there are claims and counter claims on factual issues. The Court cannot act as if it an appellate forum de hors the powers of judicial review. [Para 14]

Case Studies

1. The Company has received a Show Cause Notice during the year 2022-23 from Initiating Officer for holding a benami property and alleging that company is only a shell company and its properties are held by it as benamidar for the real person controlling the company who has channeled his ill gotten funds into the company as share capital through a network of benami shell companies. The alleged benami properties were acquired prior to 25-10-2016. The Company contends that auditor need not report on this as company has sent reply with all details and, in view of Supreme Court judgment in Ganapati Dealcom, the IO will drop proceedings. Proceedings have not been dropped at the time of audit reporting. Company also contends that ARI disclosures are not required in view of the Supreme Court decision. How will you as auditor deal with this?

Auditor is not to sit in judgment on the merits of the case. For auditor, all that matters is that the proceedings are initiated during the year and are pending as of the date of audit report. Therefore, he needs to report the fact of initiation and pendency of the same. Company may disclose its opinion on the merits of the case in notes to financial statements while giving required ARI disclosures.

2. If in Case Study 1, what if, prior to date of audit report, the proceedings are dropped by IO after considering the reply of the Company ?

In that case also, auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings were initiated and subsequently dropped. The wordings in clause 3(i)(e) are "proceedings have been initiated or are pending against the company". Therefore, in view of the word "or" separating the words "initiated" and "are pending", auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings have been initiated during year and dropped after the year-end but prior to date of audit reporting.

3. What if show cause notice dated 1st April 2023 from Initiating Officer is received on 5th April 2023 and audit report is being signed on 30th April 2023? Will auditor have to report it in audit report for FY 2022-23?

No. Auditor will not report this in Audit report for the year under audit i.e. FY 2022-23. Auditor will report it in his report for FY 2023-24.

Audit report for the year is on events during the year. Post-balance sheet date developments in respect of such events which have occurred during the year will be considered. It is one thing that Show Cause Notice is issued during the year and there are further developments after the year-end in the matter which will have to be considered.

It is entirely a different matter that Show Cause Notice is issued and received after the year-end which has nothing to do with conditions existing as at the Balance sheet date. Auditor will not consider such post-balance sheet events in report for the year under audit.

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("IBC") has been amended multiple times since its introduction in 2016to remove difficulties in the corporate insolvency process and streamline the procedure. The latest amendment, The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2020 ("Amended Act"), was introduced in the Lok Sabha, and passed by Rajya Sabha in the budget session and came into force w.e.f 13 March 2020. The Amended Act amends various sections and also introduces a new provision i.e. Section 32A protecting the new management which takes over a Company through an approved resolution plan under Section 31 of IBC.

The newly inserted Section 32A envisages the following; (a) Immunity to the Corporate Debtor as regards any offences committed prior to insolvency commencement date; and (b) Protection as regards any property of the Corporate Debtor in relation to any offence committed prior to commencement of insolvency resolution process where such property is covered under Resolution Plan as approved by the Adjudicating Authority. However, every person who is a designated partner as defined in the Limited Partnership Act or an officer as defined in Clause 60 of Section 2 of the Companies Act 2013 who is in charge of the business of the corporate debtor and is directly or indirectly in the commission of such offence as per report or complaint filed by the investigating authority shall continue to be liable and prosecuted for such offence committed by the corporate debtor notwithstanding that the liability of the corporate debtor has ceased. Accordingly, the newly inserted Section while protecting the new management which takes over a Company under an approved Resolution Plan envisages due continuance of proceedings against others in terms of the applicable provisions of law.

REQUIREMENT AND REASONS FOR PROTECTING CORPORATE DEBTOR AND SUCCESSFUL RESOLUTION APPLICANT

The latest amendment particularly the insertion of Section 32A is a phenomenal step taken by the Government which will enhance the revival of the stressed assets of corporate debtor as it will attract investments from successful bidders for the resolution plan before Adjudicating Authority. Resolution Applicant shall now be secured in as much as in light of Section 32A they shall no longer face further prosecution and threat of dispossession of the assets of the Corporate Debtor on account of prior offences being committed by the erstwhile management/promoter group. The success of any resolution plan was highly dependent on the newly inserted Section since, the uncertainties prevailing prior to the introduction of Section 32A time and again highlighted the need of protecting the corporate debtor as well as the properties belonging to the Corporate Debtor from its prior offence as even after taking over of a Corporate Debtor through a successful resolution plan, a successful bidder faced prosecution and liabilities before courts and tribunals for the prior acts of such corporate debtor.

Such grievance of the Successful Resolution Applicant came to forefront in the matter of Monnet Inspat& Energy which was acquired under CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) jointly by AION and JSW. Similarly in the matter of Bhushan Power Steel Ltd. which is under insolvency resolution process, to be acquired by JSW for over Rs.19,700 crore, the aspect of attachment by the Enforcement Directorate over the assets of Bhushan Power Steel Ltd. on account of alleged offence under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act interdicted the resolution process under the IBC. In the appeal case of Committee of Creditors versus Directorate Enforcement, the apex court stayed the ED attachment order while hearing the petition and the court asked ED to explain whether its money-laundering charges would trump the insolvency proceedings to be heard in forthcoming days.

In addition, we may also say that Section 32A of the IBC shall have a direct implication on the scope and ambit of Section 14 of the IBC, which provides for moratorium period as regards a Company which is undergoing resolution process under the Code. Section 14 lays down that there has to be a mandatory moratorium period provided to the corporate debtor from the insolvency commencement date wherein, inter alia, institution of new suits or continuation of the pending suits, against the corporate debtor, are temporarily suspended until the completion of the CIRP. That this moratorium period will not affect the criminal proceedings against the corporate debtor was made fairly clear in Shah Brothers Ispat (P.) Ltd. v. P. Mohanraj [2018] 97 taxmann.com 233. In this case, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal ("NCLAT") held that Section 14 is not applicable to the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act ("NI Act") as they are criminal proceedings. In crux, the NCLAT held that Section 14 of the IBC does not affect any criminal proceedings. Hence, even during the moratorium, criminal proceedings could be instituted or continued against the corporate debtor.

evidence providing the delivery of articles of charge under sub-regulation (2);

submit a list of documents and witness that he wants for the inquiry;

give a notice within ten days of the order or within such further time not exceeding ten days as the inquiring officer may allow for the discovery or production of the documents referred to in sub-clause (b).

25ZA. Conditions for termination of workman.—(1) No workman employed in any industry who has been in conditions continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be for terminated (otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary termination action) by that employer until—

(a) the workman has been given one month's notice in writing and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been offered in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the notice;

(b) the workman has been paid compensation equivalent to forty-five days salary for every completed year of continuous service in such manner as may be prescribed.

■ The petitioner, during all this while, was incarcerated in a jail in the State of Himachal Pradesh, facing trial in the criminal case under the NDPS Act brought against him by the NCB. One fails to understand how service of notice upon the petitioner at his residential address would be any good service. In paragraph No.21 of the writ petition, there is a specific case pleaded to the effect that the factum of the petitioner's arrest was well within the knowledge of the petitioner (an obvious erroneous reference to the respondent) and it is further asserted that intimation of the fact had been duly given to the Authorities of the Bank by the petitioner's family members. In answering paragraph No.21 of the writ petition, vide paragraph No.10 of the counter affidavit, where paragraph Nos.18 to 32 of the writ petition have been answered, the fact that the respondents were intimated by the petitioner's family members that he had been arrested, has not been denied. The assertions, therefore, in paragraph No.21 of the writ petition, stand admitted by non-traverse. If the respondents were aware of the fact that the petitioner had been arrested, it was their duty to find out the circumstances of his arrest and the place of incarceration. The notices that were sent to the petitioner at the pre-inquiry stage of proceedings, or those asking him to join duties or the charge-sheet they sent at his residential address, should all have been served upon the petitioner through the jailer of the prison, where he was incarcerated. He should then have been given opportunity with permission of the jail authorities, if their rules permitted and the jurisdiction to grant such permission was exercised. If not, the disciplinary proceedings against the petitioner ought have been deferred for a reasonable period of time. The departmental proceedings against the petitioner, including services of all notices, service of charge-sheet and the show-cause notice, seem to have proceeded 'turning a Nelson's eye' to the fact that the petitioner was suffering incarceration all along in a prison in Himachal Pradesh, pending trial. [Para 14]

■

Therefore, to impute to the petitioner the failure to answer notices to join the inquiry and defend himself, is a view of the matter that is clearly perverse. [Para 15]

■

That apart, on the merits of the charges as well, the entire gamut of allegations, comprising the two charges against the petitioner is about his unauthorized absence from 06.09.2021 until the conclusion of inquiry against him, the report whereof was first considered in the meeting of the Committee of Management of the Bank on 17.01.2023. The petitioner was released from prison on 28.06.2024. The order of dismissal had been passed on 28.12.2023. The very terms of the charge, imputing unauthorized absence to the petitioner, when there is judicial record to show that he was in judicial custody pending trial from 06.09.2021 until 28.06.2024, that is, when acquitted, knocks out the bottom of the charge about unauthorized absence. The findings of the Inquiry Officer and the Disciplinary Authority, ignoring from consideration the fact that during the entire period of absence, the petitioner was in judicial custody, and, a fortiori, not in a position to attend duties, renders the findings of the Inquiry Officer as well as the Disciplinary Authority, perverse. [Para 16]

■

The fact, that the petitioner was in jail and subsequently acquitted, has not been denied. What is of utmost importance is the event in the trial on criminal charges, in connection with which the petitioner spent time in jail from 06.09.2021 to 28.06.2024. It is not just the event in the trial that ended in a judgment of acquittal in his favour, but the findings of the learned Special Judge, acquitting him. The relevant findings of the learned Special Judge, carried in his judgment NCB v. Prashant Kumar @ Pankaj and another (Case No. 14 (24) of 2022, dated 28-6-2024), are of prime importance. These read: "In the ultimate analysis, the only inference which can be drawn in the case at hand, is that the prosecution has utterly failed to establish the charge against the accused, as portrayed in the chargesheet, and it would be highly unsafe to return findings of guilt against the accused, on the basis of the highly discrepant evidence led by the prosecution." [Para 17]

16.1-1 Disqualification of un-discharged insolvent as director

16.1-2 Private company can prescribe additional disqualifications, but public company cannot

A private company can prescribe additional disqualifications in its Articles - section 164(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 283(3) of the 1956 Act].

Similarly private company can provide grounds in addition to those specified in section 167(1) for vacation of office as director - section 167(4) of Companies Act, 2013.

For example, private company can prescribe disqualification if he joins a rival group or starts a competing business or if he leaves the family of directors etc.

Public company cannot provide any other disqualification - In Cricket Club of India v. Madhav L Apte (1975) 45 Comp Cas 574 (Bom HC), it was held that by necessary implication, a public company cannot provide for any additional disqualification.

Disqualification can be provided in other Acts - In Ketan Harkishan Marvadi v. Saurashtra-Kutch Stock Exchange (2000) 38 CLA 176 (Guj HC), it was held that such disqualification can be provided in provision of other special Act. [Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 in this case].

16.1-3 Director not disqualified if appeal is filed

Section 164(1)(d), 164(1)(e) and 164(1)(g) of Companies Act, 2013 provide for disqualification in case of conviction of offence or disqualified by NCLT/Court.

The clauses (d), (e) and (g) refer to disqualifications on account of conviction of offences of moral turpitude, disqualification by Court or Tribunal and conviction for offences relating to related party transactions prohibited under section 188.

As per the proviso to section 164(3) inserted w.e.f. 7-5-2018, the disqualification will apply even if appeal has been filed.

Enquiry - Nature determines whether discharge punitive

In order to determine whether the discharge is punitive in nature, it is necessary to ascertain firstly the nature of the enquiry, i.e., whether the termination is preceded by full scale formal enquiry into allegations involving misconduct on the part of the employee, which culminated in the finding of guilt, and secondly, the ‘purpose of enquiry’, i.e., whether the purpose of enquiry is to find out any misconduct on his part or it is aimed at finding out as to the employee being unlikely to prove efficient. Thus, the principle that in order to determine whether the misconduct is motive or foundation of order of termination, the test to be applied is to ask the question as to what was the ‘object of enquiry’. If an enquiry or an assessment is done with the object of finding out any misconduct on the part of the employee and for that reason his services are terminated, then it would be punitive in nature. On the other hand, if such an enquiry or an assessment is aimed at determining the suitability of an employee for a particular job, such termination would be termination simplicitor and not punitive in nature [State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh (2004) 23 ILD 23 (SC)]

HEADNOTE: Section 630 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with section 33(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Penalty - For wrongful withholding of property - Respondent-complainant had filed proceedings under section 630 against applicant-accused seeking his eviction from accommodation allotted to him as a condition of his service inasmuch as he was not in its service - Applicant claimed discharge of proceedings on ground that his proceeding challenging termination order was pending before Labour Court - Whether since condition of service of applicant which provided for allotment of quarter was on consideration of nature of his duties, once applicant was terminated and was issued notice to vacate quarter, unless stay was granted by Labour Court or by concerned authorities to his termination order, he would not be entitled to retain accommodation allotted to him by virtue of his service condition - Held, yes - Whether since service condition of applicant was not changed but he had been terminated, it was not obligatory on part of complainant to obtain prior permission of Labour Court under section 33(1) of 1947 Act, before resorting to file complaint under section 630 - Held, yes

FACT: Respondent No. 2-complainant had filed the proceedings under section 630 against the applicant/accused, seeking his eviction from the accommodation allotted to him as a condition of his service inasmuch as he was not in its service. The applicant moved an application seeking for discharge of the proceedings on the ground that his ULP complaint against the termination of his service was pending before the Labour Court. His main contention was that the proceedings under section 630 were not tenable inasmuch as a Labour Court proceedings in ULP for setting aside the relevant order of termination issued by the complainant were pending and the applicant/accused therein had claimed reinstatement by seeking quashing of the order of illegal termination. The trial Judge rejected his application, and the said order was confirmed in revision application preferred by him.

On application under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 the applicant contended that it was obligatory on the part of complainant to obtain prior permission of the Labour Court under section 33(1) of the 1947 Act before resorting to filing of the complaint under section 630.

HELD: In the instant case, the applicant/accused was claiming discharge on the ground that his proceeding challenging the termination order was pending before the Labour Court. The condition of the service of the applicant/accused which provided for allotment of quarter was perhaps on consideration of nature of his duties. Once the accused/applicant was terminated and had been issued notice to vacate the quarter, unless the stay was granted by the Labour Court or by the concerned authorities to his termination order, he would not be entitled to retain the accommodation allotted to him by virtue of his service condition. If anybody was appointed by the complainant-company in his place, that person would be entitled to residential accommodation, which obviously could not be allotted to him, had the applicant remained in possession of the same, despite his being not in the service of the company. [Para 7]

It is true that section 33(1) of the 1947 Act requires permission of the concerned Labour Court, before the service conditions of the employee are altered. But in the instant case the service condition of the applicant/accused was not changed, in fact he had been terminated. Therefore, even if it was to be assumed for a moment that he would be reinstated in future if his ULP complaint succeeded, because he was not doing at instant stage any work related to his duties, he would not be able to retain the quarter. At the most if he succeeded, he might be entitled to suitable compensation. Consequently, the proceedings under section 630 would not be bad only because the permission required under section 33(1) of the 1947 Act had not been obtained. [Para 6]

Therefore, the application was to be dismissed. [Para 9]

4.5 Illegality of Strikes and Lockouts:

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 22 or 23 of the Act.

4.5-1. When continuation of a strike or lock-out is not deemed illegal If a strike or lock-out relating to an industrial dispute has already commenced and is in existence at the time of reference of the dispute to the Board, a labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal, its continuance shall not be deemed illegal. The only condition is that the strike or lock-out was legal when it began and has not been prohibited.

4.5-2. Legality of strikes or lock-outs declared in consequence of illegality

A lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out must not be considered illegal.

4.5-2-1 Whether a lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike is automatically illegal?

The Supreme Court in Indian Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. & Another v. Their Workmen (1958 AIR 130, 1958 SCR 667), noted that a lock-out was declared in consequence of repeated illegal strikes by the workmen. The Supreme Court held that the lockout was lawful and that the lockout notice, stating that employees' services "shall be deemed to be discharged," meant a temporary refusal to employ, not a permanent dismissal.

The intention was not termination, but rather the suspension of services due to work disruption. Workers who reported within an extended period retained the right to resume work unconditionally. Further, the Court emphasised that Industrial Tribunals have limited scope to interfere in disciplinary actions and may intervene only where the action is malafide, constitutes unfair labour practice, violates principles of natural justice or is based on findings not supported by material.

Therefore, the prosecution as against A1 company cannot be continued. A further stand has been taken to the effect that the criminal prosecution cannot be proceeded against the new management which has taken over A1 company. It is clear from the above that the criminal liability of a company cannot be transferred to another company or the new management ipso facto. Therefore, the new management, apart from not taking over the criminal liability of the A1 company, cannot also be made to undergo criminal prosecution for the offence committed by the persons in charge of the company during the relevant time.[Emphasis Supplied]

The Honourable high Court stated that the Hon'ble Supreme Court while issuing directions in Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India reported in AIR 2013 SC 93, stated that the report of the ICC shall be deemed to be an enquiry report as the ICC would be deemed to be the inquiring authority for the purpose of disciplinary action. Necessary amendments have been made in the Tamil Nadu State Service Conduct and Disciplinary Rules, Industrial Employment Standing Order Rules, consequent to the direction given by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the order dated 26th April 2004 in Medha Kotwal Lele's v. Union of India and others in Writ Petition (CRIMINAL) NOS. 173-177 OF 1999. Hence the inquiry made by the ICC in the instant case should be deemed to be an inquiry made for the purpose of disciplinary action as done by the Enquiring authority.

(viii)

The Honourable high Court further stated that while considering the ICC as an inquiry authority it was needless to state that a reasonable opportunity should be given to both the parties. But the complication came when the standards of the reasonableness and fairness was set by the ICC. As far as the second respondent is concerned, the respondent, claimed that non- furnishing of CCTV footage had deprived him to get a fair opportunity and the Labour Court had also endorsed his views. In any enquiry made against the delinquent by the inquiry authority, a fair amount of reasonableness should be there in the interest of justice. But the object of reasonableness was to ensure that the respondent should not become a scape goat at the hands of someone due to some malice. However, there cannot be any straight-jacket or a rigid formula to suggest the standards of reasonableness to be adopted during the departmental inquiry. So far as the charges of sexual harassment was concerned, the privacy, secrecy and safety of the victims also need to be given priority and hence the fairness formula to be adopted during such inquiry could be flexible and suiting to the nature of the complaint, type of the institution and even the conduct of the parties also.

(ix)

The Honourable High Court further recorded that in this regard it was appropriate to refer the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court held in Union of India v. P.K Roy reported in (ILLJ 633 SC) wherein it is stated that the doctrine of natural justice cannot be imprisoned with the straight-jacket or a rigid formula and its application depends upon several factors.

(x)

The Hon'ble Supreme Court had taken cue from the earlier judgment rendered in Hira Nath Mishra v. Principal, Rajendra Medical College, Ranchi, AIR 1973 SC 1260 to endorse the above view. In Hiranath's case the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held in paragraph No.11 that the rules of natural justice cannot remain the same applying to all conditions and for a better clarity, it is extracted hereunder: "

Paragraph 11. Rules of natural justice cannot remain the same applying to all conditions.

(xi)

The Honourable High Court further stated that the Honourable Court know of statutes in India like the Goonda Acts which permit evidence being collected behind the back of the goonda and the goonda being merely asked to represent against the main charges arising out of the evidence collected. Care was taken to see that the witnesses who gave statements would not be identified. In such cases there was no question of the witnesses being called and the goonda being given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses. The reason was obvious. No witness would come forward to give evidence in the presence of the goonda. However unsavoury the procedure may appear to a. judicial mind, these were facts of life which were to be faced. The girls who were molested that night would not have come forward to give evidence in any regular enquiry and if a strict enquiry like the one conducted in a court of law were to be imposed in such matters, the girls would have had to go under the constant fear of molestation by the male students who were capable of such indecencies. Under the circumstances the course followed by the principal was a wise one. The Committee whose integrity could not be impeached, collected and sifted the evidence given by the girls. Thereafter the students definitely named by the girls were informed about the complaint against them and the charge. They were given an opportunity to state their case. The Honourable High Court did not think that the facts and circumstances of this case require anything more to be done.

The review procedure and the settlement plan both cover the interests of all lenders, as, according to Sec. 31 of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, if a conflict-solving plan has been accepted; it ties and makes it compulsory to abide by for all creditors. 2.2 Prior Permission for Closure in case of larger undertakings (Section 80) An employer intending to close down an undertaking of an industrial establishment employing 300 or more workers must apply electronically or otherwise in the prescribed manner (As per Draft Rules, 2020, an application for permission must be made in Form X) to the appropriate Government for prior permission at least 90 days before the intended closure.

The application must clearly state the reasons for the intended closure, and a copy of the application must be served simultaneously on representatives of workers in the prescribed manner.

However, this requirement does not apply to undertakings set up for the construction of buildings, bridges, roads, canals, dams or for other construction work.

2.3 Government decision to grant or refuse to grant permission for Closure

The appropriate Government, after making an enquiry as it thinks fit and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the employer, workers, and persons interested in closure, may, by order, grant or refuse to grant permission for closure. A copy of the order must be communicated to the employer and the workers.

If the appropriate Government does not communicate the order granting or refusing permission to the employer within 60 days from the date of application, the permission shall be deemed to have been granted, and the application shall be disposed of accordingly.

Further, the order of the appropriate Government must be final and binding on all the parties and must remain in force for one year from the date of such order.

2.3-1 Whether the power of the Government to deny permission for closure is absolute?

The Supreme Court in Orissa Textile & Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa [2002] 2 SCC 578, held that the Government's power to refuse permission for closure of an undertaking must be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances.

Such refusal is justified only where compelling or overriding reasons exist or where the public interest so demands, for instance, where the establishment is engaged in manufacturing life-saving vaccines or drugs during a prevailing epidemic, or products essential for the defence of India.

2.4 Power of Review or Reference to Tribunal for adjudication

The appropriate Government may, suo motu or on an application by the employer or worker, review its order granting or refusing permission within the prescribed time (As per Draft Rules, 2020, the prescribed time is within 30 days from the date on which the order is made) or refer the matter to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal must pass the award within 30 days from the date of such reference.

2.5 Consequences of Illegal Closure

Where an employer fails to apply for prior permission for closure within the prescribed period or where the permission for closure has been refused, the closure of the undertaking shall be deemed illegal from the date it takes effect. In such circumstances, the workers are entitled to all benefits available under the applicable law as if the undertaking had not been closed down.

2.6 Exemption from Prior Permission Requirement in certain exceptional cases

The appropriate Government may, in certain exceptional cases, such as an accident in the undertaking, the death of the employer, or similar situations, by order direct that no prior permission for the closure of the undertaking is required.

2.7 Compensation payable to workers upon permitted or deemed closure

Where an undertaking is permitted to be closed down or where the permission for closure is deemed to be granted, every worker employed immediately before the date of the application for permission must be entitled to receive compensation.

The compensation payable must be:

(a)

equivalent to 15 days' average pay or

(b)

Average pay of such other number of days as may be notified by the appropriate Government, for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of 6 months.

2.7-1 Whether closure of undertaking amounts to retrenchment of workers?

No, the Supreme Court in S.G. Chemicals & Dyes Trading Employees' Union v. S.G. Chemicals & Dyes Trading Ltd. [1986] 2 SCC 624, clarified that the closure of an undertaking is distinct from retrenchment. Retrenchment means reducing surplus staff in an ongoing business and not ending the entire business.

Further, Insolvency Law Committee ('the Committee') has also discussed treatment of Winding up Proceedings Initiated under 1956 Act/2013 Act vis-a-vis IBC in its report. The Committee underscored the need to avoid multiple and possibly conflicting orders in winding up/liquidation proceedings of the same corporate debtor whether under the 1956 Act or under IBC. The Committee was also mindful of the underlying principle with regards to existence of a moratorium once winding up/CIRP is initiated whether under the 1956 Act (section 446)/2013 Act (section 279) or under the IBC (section 14 during CIRP, section 33 during liquidation). The Committee noted that under the 1956 Act and 2013 Act, during the moratorium, legal proceedings could be initiated or continued with the leave of the Court/NCLT. Accordingly, for cases which were not expressly transferred to the NCLT pursuant to the Transfer Rules, the Committee felt that the assumption was that the case was at an advanced stage and, therefore, the Court hearing the matter was best suited to grant or deny leave to initiate insolvency proceedings under the Code. Finally, based on the available jurisprudence, the Committee felt that the leave of the High Court or NCLT, if applicable, under section 446 of the 1956 Act or section 279 of the 2013 Act, must be obtained, for initiating CIRP under the Code, if any petition for winding up is pending in any High Court or NCLT against the corporate debtor. The Committee agreed that necessary amendments be made to schedule XI of the Code (which will result in amendment to the CA 2013) to ensure that the leave of the High Court or the NCLT, may be obtained, if applicable, where such winding-up petition is pending for initiation of CIRP against such corporate debtor, under the provisions of the Code. Corresponding amendments may also be made to the Transfer Rules.

Conclusion 21. From the above case law, it is abundantly clear that the company has to ensure compliance in all stages i.e. right from the incorporation till the company is finally liquidated through the corporate insolvency resolutions process during which time the powers of the board of directors of the company stands suspended and such power is vested with the resolution professional / liquidator. In the given case, the company had gone to the mode of liquidation through the order of the Honorable National Company Law Tribunal and as per the order, the earlier management i.e. the directors of the company was relieved from all their responsibilities and the same has been taken over by the Liquidator and Insolvency Resolution Professional. By taking over, they became the officer in default and assumed the responsibility of ensuring compliance. Even though the company has gone into liquidation mode, the earlier management had been relieved from their responsibilities, still, for the non-compliance, the Liquidator and the Resolution Professional both were identified as defaulters for the required compliance of filing annual returns and annual financial statements and accordingly the Registrar of Companies penalized them.

In conclusion, we can say that the company is required to ensure all the required compliance at all stages till it is finally closed down and the person whosoever is responsible including Liquidator and Resolution professional have to ensure absolute compliance at all stages and at all time in order to avoid the penal actions from the regulators.

Dilatory part of court procedure is a dampener 1.40-13 In addition to the question on the proper Court of competent jurisdiction discussed above, companies and company affairs that happen to be brought before the courts for adjudication in whatever context are equally subject to the common curse of endemic court delays and related costs largely due to the archaic, outmoded and staid procedural laws made by the imperialist British regime around the 1850’s remaining firm at the core through six decades of India’s Independence to the present electronic era, as a consequence of the law-makers’ choice of creating multiple fast track courts or forums parallelly, to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts which are nearer to people and familiar to them in the view that those courts are super-saturated with other cases and allowing their jurisdiction over company cases to continue would only add to further delays, instead of overhauling the procedural laws to rid them off the dilatory parts for faster disposal of cases by the common law courts and creating more. Unfortunately, seeing the victims sapped by prolonged litigation for years lasting for a generation or over in many cases, there is a misgiving present generally as an aside in the minds of people on ‘who is watching what they do’ about the Judiciary in our system. Overall, so far as companies are concerned, the combined incidence of these factors has gone in favour of the managements to do what they prefer rather than what they should under the laws in matters of the corporate investors or others.

Court in Crompton Greaves Ltd. v. Workmen (AIR 1978 SC 1489) observed that a strike is a legal weapon available to workers. However, its justification depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The Court clarified that even an illegal strike may be justified in rare situations, while a legal strike may still be unjustified if the conduct of workers is unreasonable.

3.1-2. Whether a lockout is the same as the closure of operations? The Supreme Court in Management of Express Newspapers Ltd. v. Workers & Staff Employed Under it (AIR 1963 SC 569) clarified that a lockout is not the same as a closure. A lockout refers to the temporary closing of the place of employment, the suspension of work, or the employer's refusal to employ workers during an industrial dispute. A closure, on the other hand, refers to the permanent shutdown of business operations. Unlike a lockout, a closure signifies the end of business itself, not just the temporary suspension of operations.

Further, in Management of Kairbetta Estate v. Rajamanickam (AIR 1960 SC 893), the Supreme Court elaborated on the distinction between a lock-out and a lay-off. The Court held that a layoff arises when ongoing operations exist but workers cannot be given work due to reasons beyond the employer's control, while a lockout involves a temporary suspension of operations by the employer. In this case, a justified lockout in response to workers' violence cannot be treated as a layoff, and thus, the workers were not entitled to layoff compensation.

3.2 Prohibition on Strikes and Lockouts:

The provisions relating to the prohibition on strikes and lockouts are as follows:

3.2-1 Prohibition on Strikes

No person employed in an industrial establishment must go on strike, in breach of contract, in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving the employer a notice of strike within 60 days before striking or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of strike specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.2-2 Prohibition on Lockouts

No employer of an industrial establishment must lock out any of his workers in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving a notice of lock-out within 60 days before locking out or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of lock-out specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.3 Exemption from notice requirement in case of existing strike or lockout:

The notice of strike or lockout must not be necessary where a strike or lockout is already in existence. However, the employer must send intimation of such lock-out or strike on the day on which it is declared to such authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government, either generally or for a particular area or for a particular class of services.

3.4 Reporting Requirements for Strikes and Lockout Notices:

If on any day, an employer receives from any person employed by him, any notice or gives to any person employed by him, any notice of strike or lock-out, he must report it within 5 days to the appropriate Government or to such authority as the Government may prescribe and to the conciliation officer, specifying the number of notices received or issued on that day.

3.5 Illegality of Strikes and Lockouts:

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 62 or continued in violation of an order made under Section 42(7) of the Code.

3.5-1. When continuation of a strike or lock-out is not deemed illegal

If a strike or lock-out relating to an industrial dispute has already commenced and is in existence at the time an application is filed before the Tribunal or when the dispute is referred to an arbitrator or the National Industrial Tribunal, its continuance shall not be deemed illegal. The only condition is that the strike or lock-out was legal when it began and has not been prohibited.

3.5-2. Legality of strikes or lock-outs declared in consequence of illegality

A lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out must not be considered illegal.

30.15 Powers and Duties of Tribunal on presentation of Petition [Sections 443 and 444]

Stay of suits

30.15-1 Earlier, under section 442 power was vested in the High Court to stay suits and proceedings or restrain further proceedings in the suits or proceedings at the instance of any creditor or contributory at any time after presentation of the petition for winding up and before a winding up order is made, only for that interim period, because once the winding up order is made-section 446 providing for same on its making-will become applicable, but with the omission of the section 442 by the Second Amendment Act, 2002 (not yet notified), this power is no longer available to the Tribunal, which means that the suits and proceedings shall continue until making of the winding up order by the Tribunal.

Relief Undertakings Act and Stay

30.15-2 However, it would appear that the stay of proceedings notified in exercise of statutory power under a State legislation like Relief Undertakings Act having overriding efficacy would be effective and the Tribunal would be bound, having regard to the decision in Jaysinth Dyechem v. Mewar Textile Mills Ltd. AIR 1988 Raj. 16, that such a notification is constitutional and not repugnant.

Tribunal’s powers [Sections 443 & 444]

30.15-3 Further, sections 443 and 444 dealing with the powers of Tribunal on hearing petition and its duty to communicate the order when made to the Official Liquidator, have been substituted in their entirety - only to substitute ‘Tribunal’ for ‘Court’ - by the said Act. Accordingly, on hearing a winding up petition, the Tribunal may, at par with the High Court earlier,

u (a ) dismiss the petition with or without costs,

u (b) adjourn the hearing conditionally or unconditionally, (for example, where family disputes over property ownership exist, Shivraj Gupta v. Hansraj Gupta & Co. (P.) Ltd. [1987] 2 Comp. LJ 74 (Delhi),

u (c) make any interim order that it thinks fit (like the appointment of an interim-Administrator to take charge of the company’s affairs pending a decision), or

u (d) make an order for winding up the company with or without costs, or any other order that it thinks fit, such that the Tribunal shall not refuse to make a winding up order on the ground only that the assets of the company have been mortgaged to an amount equal or in excess, or that the company has no assets.

Petition on ‘just & equitable’ ground

30.15-4 In respect of a petition for winding up on the ‘just and equitable’ ground, the Tribunal may refuse to make an order for winding up, if it is of the opinion that some other remedy is available to the petitioners and that they are acting unreasonably in seeking to have the company wound up instead of pursuing that other remedy.

Default of delivering statutory report as a ground

30.15-5 Further, in the case of a petition for winding up on the ground of default in delivering the statutory report to the Registrar, or in holding the statutory meeting, the Tribunal may-instead of making the winding up order-(a) direct that the statutory report shall be delivered or the statutory meeting held, and (b) order the costs to be paid by any persons who, in the opinion of the Tribunal, are responsible for the default.

Workers’ right to present petition for winding up

30.15-6 In National Textile Workers’ Union v. P.R. Ramakrishnan AIR 1983 SC 75, it was held that though the workers have no statutory right to present a winding up petition, they are entitled to be heard of their interest as interveners but not as parties in a winding up petition, and particularly so because the winding up order after it attains finality the workers have no scope to participate in the further proceedings, except by appealing against the winding up order under section 483.

If an employer intends to close down an industrial establishment, they must give notice in Form XIII to the central government at least 60 days in advance. They must also send a copy to the concerned Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (central) and the authorised representatives of the workers.

7.4 Special Provisions Relating to Lay-offs, Retrenchment and Closure

Chapter X of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, governs special provisions relating to ‘Lay-offs, Retrenchment and Closure’. The provisions of this Chapter shall apply to an industrial establishment in which 300 or more workers or such higher number of workers as may be notified by the appropriate Government18, were employed on an average per working day in the preceding 12 months.

7.4-1 Application for Permission

As per the rules, the employer must submit applications for permission for Lay-offs, retrenchment, and Closure in Form-XIV.

7.4-2 Service and Display of Application

A copy of the application must be served simultaneously to the workers electronically, in person, or by registered or speed post. The application must also be displayed by the employer on the notice board or on the electronic board at the main entrance of the industrial establishment.

7.4-3 Review of Orders by the Central Government

The Central Government may, either on its own motion or on an application made by the employer or any worker, review its order granting or refusing permission for lay-off, retrenchment, or closure of an industrial establishment.

7.5 Worker Re- Skilling Fund ( Rule 37)

As per the rules, every employer who has retrenched a worker in an industrial establishment is required to transfer, within 10 days from the date of retrenchment, an amount electronically equivalent to 15 days of the last drawn wages of such retrenched worker or workers into the fund.

7.5-1 Maintenance of Fund

The fund must be maintained by the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central)/Office of the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central)/Office of the Regional Labour Commissioner (Central)/Office of the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) as required.

7.5-2 Transfer of Funds to Retrenched Workers within 45 days

Further, the funds so received must be transferred by the office of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) or the office of the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) or the office of the Regional Labour Commissioner (Central) or the office of the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), electronically to each of the retrenched worker account within 45 days of retrenchment to enable them to utilise that amount for his re-skilling.

8 Maintenance of Records, Registers, Forms, Notices, and Display Board ( Rule 47)

Rule 47 sets out provisions for the maintenance of records, registers, forms, notices, and display boards. As per the rules, all records, registers, forms, notices, display boards, and other documents required to be maintained under these rules shall be maintained electronically in the required format or containing the required information.

The records and other documents must be produced or shown as and when required by the concerned authority specified in this behalf under the Code.

9 Compounding of Offences ( Rule 38)

9.1 Application for Compounding

The accused to whom the notice is served may send the duly filled-up application electronically in Part III of Form XV to the compounding officer and deposit the compounding amount electronically within 15 days of the receipt of notice.

9.2 Composition of Offence

Further, where the prosecution has already been instituted against the accused in the court of competent jurisdiction, the accused may apply to such court to allow the composition of the offence against him.

The Court may, after considering the application, allow composition of the offence by the compounding officer in accordance with the provisions of section 89 and the procedure specified in this rule.

5. Comparative Study

A comparative overview is as follows:

| S. No. | Key Changes | Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 | Industrial Relations Code, 2020 | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. | Definitions | Section 2(q) defines the term 'Strike' and Section 2(l) defines the term 'Lockout' | Section 2(zk) defines the term 'Strike' and Section 2(u) defines the term 'Lockout' | The Code broadens the concept of strike to cover mass casual leave movements often used to circumvent legal restrictions on strikes. |
| 2. | Notice Period for Strike/Lockout | Section 22(1) – Six weeks' notice required; strike not to commence within 14 days of giving notice Section 22(2) – Similar provisions for lockouts | Section 62(1) & (2) – Notice period extended to 60 days before strike/lockout; cannot commence within 14 days of notice | The extension from 6 weeks to 60 days provides a longer window for conciliation and negotiation, allowing parties and authorities to intervene before a shutdown occurs. |
| 3. | Restrictions during proceedings | Section 23 – Prohibition during pendency of conciliation, arbitration or tribunal proceedings and for 2 months thereafter. | Section 62(d) –(f) – Prohibition continues during pendency and extends for 60 days after conclusion of proceedings. | The Code maintains the spirit of the Industrial Dispute Act but standardises the post-proceeding restriction to 60 days across forums. |
| 4. | Exemption from notice | Section 22(3) - Notice is not required if a strike/lockout already exists; the employer must intimate the Government Authority. | Section 63(2) – Similar provision retained; intimation on the day of declaration to the prescribed authority. | The code clarifies the timing and responsibility of intimation, making it obligatory for employers to report on the day of declaration. |
| 5. | Reporting obligation to Government | Section 22(6) – Employer must report notice of strike/lockout within 5 days to the appropriate Government. | Section 62(6) – Employer must report notice of strike/lockout within 5 days to the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer. | The change broadens the reporting requirement by mandating employers to submit the notice of strike/lockout not only to the appropriate Government but also to the conciliation officer. This enhances transparency and strengthens early dispute-resolution mechanisms. |
| 6. | Illegality of Strikes/Lockouts | Section 24 – A strike or lockout is illegal if commenced in contravention of Section 22 or 23 of the Act or continued despite prohibition orders. | Section 63 – Similar provision; declares a strike/lockout illegal if commenced in violation of Section 62 or continued in contravention of orders under Section 42(7). | The concept of illegality is retained but references are streamlined to new Code framework. The clear cross-linking with Section 42(7) strengthens enforceability by aligning illegality with formal adjudication prohibitions, thereby ensuring that industrial actions cannot continue once legally restrained. |
| 7. | When continuation of strike/lockout is not deemed illegal | Section 24(2) – Continuation of strike/lockout is not deemed illegal if strike/lockout was legal at the time of commencement and dispute can later be referred for adjudication. | Section 63(2) – Similar safeguard retained. | The preservation of this clause upholds the balance between statutory regulation and legitimate right to collective bargaining. It ensures that workers and employers are not penalized for lawful actions that precede a reference to adjudication, thereby maintaining fairness in procedural application. |
| 8. | Legality of consequent strikes/lockouts | Section 24(3) – A strike/lockout declared in consequence of an illegal strike or lockout is not considered illegal. | Section 63(3) – Mirrors this position in the Code. | The continuation of this principle maintains parity in employer-employee rights. It prevents one party from gaining an undue advantage through an initial illegal action and ensures equitable treatment under industrial jurisprudence. |
| 9. | Financial support to illegal strikes/lockouts | Section 25 - No person must knowingly spend or apply any money in direct furtherance or support of any illegal strike or lock-out. | Section 64 – No person must knowingly spend or apply any money in direct furtherance or support of any illegal strike or lock-out. | The provision under the Code retains the same prohibition as the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, reflecting continuity in the law. This indicates that legislative intent remains unchanged, ensuring that no financial support is extended to illegal strikes or lockouts. |
| 10. | Penalties | Sections 26-28 – Provided monetary fines and imprisonment for illegal strikes, lockouts and instigation. | Sections 86-89 – Updated penalty structure with higher fines and graded severity. | The updated penalty structure aligns with current economic realities and acts as a stronger deterrent. It also introduces proportionality – higher penalties for employers or unions depending on the gravity and repetition of offences, ensuring better compliance and enforcement efficiency. |

6. Conclusion

The legal framework governing strikes and lockouts in India aims to balance industrial peace with the genuine rights of workers and employers. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020, is expected to modernize and streamline the law by broadening key definitions, standardizing timelines, strengthening reporting requirements and updating penalties to discourage abrupt shutdowns and encourage negotiations. At the same time, it preserves protections for lawful ongoing strikes and lockouts, ensuring fairness to both parties. Overall, the Code seeks to promote

In conclusion, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, provides a clear and workable framework for employers and workers to deal with situations of lay-off, retrenchment, and closure. The Code requires employers to carefully assess applicability thresholds, follow prescribed procedures, obtain prior approvals where mandated, and ensure timely payment of statutory compensation. Any deviation from these requirements can result in the action being treated as illegal, exposing employers to penal consequences.

At the same time, the Code protects workers by ensuring continuity of service during lay-off, fair compensation, advance notice, and safeguards against arbitrary termination or closure. Overall, the Code encourages lawful, disciplined, and balanced handling of workforce adjustments in line with business needs and worker welfare.
